While The Callisto Protocol may be a bit derivative (I'm not gonna say of which game, you know which one), it's stellar presentation and solid, albeit basic, mechanics, provided an enjoyable 7 hour singleplayer experience. While some mechanics, like quick time button mashing and very predictable jump scares, are quite antiquated, bashing my way through Black Iron Prison was a good time. The enemy and weapon variety is unfortunately rather limited and although the narrative wasn't exactly the most original or surprising, the cast carries it very well and the reveal of the [spoiler]giant alien corpse[/spoiler] was neat. Callisto leans very heavily on it's superb visuals and audio but so much of the story and gameplay feel like iterations we've seen before or ideas that are great on the surface but were never expanded upon enough to become something special. Completed the game on normal difficulty, bought it on sale for about $10. None of the DLC appears to be worthwhile so I've stuck with only the purchase of the main game.

I was honestly waiting for The Calisto Protocol, because I love the Dead Space series. Moreover, there are almost no Sci-Fi horrors. And he's kind of a spiritual heir, also from the author of the Glen Schofield franchise. Then, after the release, I saw ratings and reviews, got upset and forgot about The Calisto Protocol. And in 2024 I tried the game. And I liked it in general. It's not Dead Space, it's a mixture of Dead Space 3 and Resident Evil. And The Calisto Protocol doesn't take the best from these franchises. First of all, the game does not scare at all, it disappoints from the first minutes. Secondly, most of the gameplay is sharpened for close combat, and it is very secondary here. Thirdly, if you consider the plot, this is the weakest part of the game, and the finale and the main twist causes laughter and disappointment. I was still hoping for something more serious. But The Calisto Protocol also has its advantages. Of course, this is graphics and visuals - even after 2 years in 4K the game looks amazing. Technically, the game was able to be brought to a normal playable state. RTX is not badly implemented. But unfortunately, The Calisto Protocol is a creative failure. There was a real chance to create a new franchise. There was both budget and time. But it turned out to be just a passable game, which was remembered only because it was first added to PS Plus and then distributed in the Epic Store.

Reviewing this game is difficult.
The game is trying really hard to mimic the iconic game mechanics of its superior counter part (Dead Space) while also trying to introduce new elements that I believe slow and sour the experience.

[b] Things I loved about the game [/b]

- Graphics are quite insane in this title
- Ambiance and atmosphere are definitely on par with the OG Deadspace
- Using a prison and abandoned mine colony as the setting is brilliant, and the contrast between each place does make it feel very unique. 
- Sound design did a meticulous job and its ear candy.
- While the story is predictable and very similar to other Sci-Fi stories, it servers it purpose.
- Monster design is cool as well, while not a 1 to 1 copy of this brother, it definitely keeps those body horror elements.
- Tension is good for the most part.
- There are so many great death animation for our main character and the game embraces the gory elements in them.
- The game is fairly polished as of the date of this review, I did not encounter any bugs or crashed. An unexpected surprise
- I felt immersed in the universe for the most part, partially due to the lack of HUD and details.

[b] Things that I disliked: [/b]

- Having to crawl through small or cramped spaces in video games usually server the purpose to move to the next section in order to not have a loading screen. However, in this game it slows down the pace significantly for no reason and there is A LOT of that in the game. You will be crawling or squishing your way through so many corridors, tunnels and air ducts and it creates FAKE tension, you can do anything besides crawl, therefore you know you can not get attacked in the air-vents. There was only 1 instance where it was successful at creating tension and a scare for me.
- The combat / melee system is not as bad as people make it out to be but is not good either. Instead of using strategy you just have to use rhythm, which immediately kills off almost all the tension from encounters. 
- Switching off weapons is odd, they tried to reinvent the wheel here but instead made it unnecessarily complicated to do.
- Healing is VERY slow as well, which is a single shot, it should not be. Its a way they decided to artificially increase difficulty.
- Reusing bosses several times is always been frown upon, unless they become a re-acuring enemy later down the line, this is not the case. They re use the same boss 3 times and honestly it makes the game less exciting.

[b] Things that I HATE: [/b]
- Performance is not good and honestly unless you have a beefy card I would say stay away from the game, even with a 4080 I had top use Lossless scaling since the game does not have any frame generation and the upscaling method does not have DLSS.
- Manual / Auto saving is so bad in this game, even if you save before a specific part, the game will respawn you all the way back to a different checkpoint forcing you to sell your items and perform the upgrades again.
- Changing game graphical settings is a pain, you can not do it in game and you have to back out to the menu to test the settings and change them.

Overall, I do recommend the game for enthusiast of horror and ambiance. However, for the amount of content I Highly suggest to GRAB IT ON SALE. the story is about 8 hours long which is on the short side and some replayabilty features are locked behind a paywall which is an L in my book.

The Callisto Protocol — это настоящее удовольствие для любителей хоррор-экшена. Игра моментально погружает в атмосферу ужаса и безысходности: мрачные коридоры тюрьмы «Чёрное железо», пугающая тишина и жуткие крики в темноте создают невероятное напряжение.

Графика — просто потрясающая. Детализация лиц, освещение и анимации сделаны на высоком уровне. Особенно впечатляют звуковые эффекты — каждый скрежет или шорох заставляет обернуться. Боевая система хоть и ближе к ближнему бою, но ощущается увесистой и жестокой, что добавляет реализма выживанию.

Да, у игры есть свои шероховатости: кому-то может показаться геймплей однообразным, а сюжет — слегка предсказуемым. Но в целом The Callisto Protocol — это качественный и атмосферный ужастик, который держит в напряжении до самого конца. Отличный выбор для тех, кто скучал по играм в духе Dead Space.

So I've done a flip on this. Initially I was frustrated with two major aspects: 

1: Hitting an enemy will not cancel their attack animation. You're forced to play reactively. I hate this. If I have a quicker attack than my enemy, and I land it, it should cancel their attack animation as they got hit. They shouldn't get to 'follow through' with their attack despite receiving a hit.

2: It does not save the game at the moment you manual save it. I've died twice at a section where I've needed to replay the same 10 minutes. I usually die because of issue 1.

But having completed the game it's actually been a pretty good experience. It's a shorter, graphical heavy title that focuses on atmosphere and narrative - which I'm cool with from time to time. It didn't overstay it's welcome, provided enough combat variety for it's short run-time, and captivated me with it's story - which is delivered to us by stellar acting performances. The game leaves us with some questions about the wider situation. Credit to what they've already given us; I'm keen to see where it goes.

I think a large problem with these types of games is that they're clearly big budget, but offer a short run time with little incentive to re-play. This causes a big price tag and creates a poor time-to-money ratio which I can't fault people for avoiding. On a steep discount this is worth it though.

If you came here looking for something to scratch the Dead Space itch (like I did), you'll be sorely disappointed. It's an entirely different game with an entirely different vibe. 

It feels like they stripped away all of the survival horror elements in exchange for a highly predictable action story, and swapped out the on-your-toes, calculating combat system of Dead Space for an all too easy, mindless combat system. Right from the start of the game unless you're being swarmed by multiple enemies at once, you rarely feel like you're in any real danger, which certainly takes away from the "survival horror" tag this game has. That being said, if you're a sci-fi or walking sim fan and just want to jump into a cool sci-fi environment and experience the story, I'd recommend it on a deep sale. Some games definitely are worth every penny at this price tag, but The Callisto Protocol is not one of them. I spent $16 CAD and I kind of feel like that might have even been a little steep.

The Callisto Protocol is a game that I think, deserves a sequel. This game really has good bones for something great, I just think they made some strange decisions to differentiate it from its obvious influence, Dead Space. 

The games graphics are quite impressive, and feature what I feel are some of the best facial animations in the business. It at times looks highly photo-realistic, which really elevates the horror theme. 

Unfortunately, where the game shows its issues is the combat. I personally love how the guns feel. They have great sound design and feel punchy. Melee combat at first is kind of interesting, but quickly falls apart once multiple enemies are on screen while you are trying to fight one. It just seems to fundamentally break the game. Oh, and don't try to melee any enemy on an incline/stairs. I think if they just take some of it back to the drawing board it could be so much more. 

Story is somewhat predictable, but decent. Should be really familiar to most fans of sci-fi survival horror. I did quite enjoy the vocal performances from the main cast, solid work. 

Sound design is VERY good. Play with a good headset to experience some great ambient noises that add to the atmosphere.

The game did feel quite easy at times on normal difficulty. I think it would probably be better starting the game on a higher difficulty. At first it felt pretty balanced, but after just a few weapon upgrades I felt as if I was just rolling through most enemies. Also, the GRP (pick up enemies from afar and throw them) is pretty OP even at base level. There are literal hundreds of opportunities to throw enemies into spiked walls/fanblades etc... and that definitely took a lot of the fear out of some encounters as it one shots just about any enemy. 

Speaking of enemies, the variety is certainly lacking. I think there are maybe 5 actual variants of enemies to fight and a large portion of the middle of the game focuses on a certain type that are just not really fun to deal with. The game wants you to use stealth, but I often felt the stealth was completely unnecessary and it was more effective/fun to just start blastin'. Boss fights are basically non-existent and they chose for some reason to repeat the same type of boss several times towards the end of the game. The final boss was a little more enjoyable, but the whole melee system just really makes 1-on-1 encounters completely brainless and not at all scary, which really hurt the quality of the final encounter. 

Overall, this game is definitely not a bad game. I would say its a serviceable sci-fi survival horror experience that could have been so much more with a bit of tweaking of these systems. I would hope that we could eventually get a sequel or spin-off in the same universe with some changes as I really believe there is a great game underneath some wonky design choices. 

7/10 definitely get on sale.

The Callisto Protocol – A Visually Stunning Horror Game with Room for Improvement

Developer: Striking Distance Studios
Release Date: December 2, 2022
Platforms: PS5, Xbox Series X/S, PC

Overview

The Callisto Protocol is a third-person survival horror game set in the distant future, where you play as Jacob Lee, a prison guard caught in the middle of a deadly outbreak that transforms prisoners into terrifying monsters. Initially released in late 2022, the game received criticism for its combat mechanics and repetitive gameplay. However, a series of post-launch updates have enhanced the overall experience, improving combat fluidity and enemy variety. While The Callisto Protocol remains visually stunning and atmospheric, it still faces some challenges in terms of gameplay variety and story depth.

What Makes It Great?

✅ Visually Stunning & Atmospheric Design
The Callisto Protocol is still one of the best-looking horror games out there. The updated visuals in 2025 continue to impress, with incredible environmental detail and atmospheric lighting that perfectly sets the mood for its terrifying world. The game does an excellent job of creating a claustrophobic, oppressive environment that feels truly alive, with every hallway and dark corner evoking a sense of dread. Even now, the visuals are a highlight, immersing players in a gripping, unsettling world.

✅ Brutal Combat & Gore (Post-Launch Improvements)
The combat in The Callisto Protocol has seen several improvements since launch. The fighting mechanics now feel smoother and more responsive, with the brutal dismemberment system remaining a key draw. The violence and gore remain impactful, making every enemy encounter feel satisfying. Although still not perfect, the combat is more fluid than it was at launch, with the improvements making the brutal confrontations more engaging and less frustrating.

✅ Intense Horror Atmosphere
The game continues to excel in creating a spine-chilling atmosphere. With the dark, decaying setting of Black Iron Prison, the terror is palpable throughout. The sound design is a key contributor to the experience, keeping players on edge with its eerie audio cues, distant growls, and the unsettling ambiance of the prison. The combination of atmospheric visuals and sound design creates a feeling of constant fear that works well, even years after the game’s original release.

✅ Immersive Sound Design
Sound plays a huge role in the tension of The Callisto Protocol. From the creaking metal of the prison to the bone-chilling growls of monstrous enemies lurking around every corner, the sound design effectively enhances the horror experience. The use of ambient noise, the subtle but unnerving hum of machinery, and the sudden intensity of enemy sounds keep you on constant alert, making every encounter feel more terrifying. Even with the visuals being top-notch, it’s the sound that truly heightens the sense of dread in this world.

✅ Environmental Storytelling
While the main story leaves much to be desired, the environmental storytelling has always been one of the game’s strongest points. In 2025, the game’s world feels even more detailed and filled with lore, with remnants of the past scattered throughout the prison. These small, environmental clues help paint a picture of the chaos that unfolded before you arrived, adding depth and mystery to the experience. The setting remains a crucial element that elevates the atmosphere and offers a richer understanding of the world.

What Could Be Better?

❌ Combat Mechanics Still Feel Stiff
While post-launch updates have made combat more fluid, it’s still not without its issues. The reliance on melee combat can sometimes feel unresponsive, especially in intense situations where precision is key. Dodging feels awkward at times, and facing multiple enemies can still lead to frustrating moments. The combat mechanics have improved, but they still lack the polish that would make encounters feel more dynamic and satisfying.

❌ Weak Story & Characters
Despite the game’s strong atmosphere, the story remains underwhelming. Jacob Lee, the protagonist, and the supporting characters still lack depth, with the narrative falling into familiar tropes. The plot, while serviceable, doesn’t have the emotional weight or complexity that would make it stand out. Even with updates and patches, the story still feels like a missed opportunity, and the characters don’t leave a lasting impact.

❌ Repetitive Gameplay Loop
While some improvements have been made to combat and enemy variety, the core gameplay loop still feels repetitive. Much of the game revolves around navigating linear levels, fighting off waves of enemies, and solving basic puzzles. This repetition can become tiresome, particularly as the game progresses. The updates have helped to make the gameplay slightly more engaging, but it still lacks the variety needed to keep it fresh throughout.

❌ Limited Enemy Variety & AI Issues
Despite some updates to enemy AI and variety, the game still suffers from a lack of diversity in enemy types. Many enemies share similar attack patterns, leading to repetitive encounters. The AI can also be inconsistent, with enemies sometimes behaving predictably. While some improvements have been made in the post-launch period, the enemy encounters still lack the variety needed to keep players on their toes.

Final Verdict
⭐ 7/10 – A Visually Stunning Game with Solid Horror Elements but Room for Improvement

The Callisto Protocol remains a visually stunning and atmospheric horror game, with some notable improvements in combat fluidity and enemy variety since its original release. The game’s brutal combat, terrifying atmosphere, immersive sound design, and environmental storytelling continue to shine, but it still struggles with repetitive gameplay and a weak narrative. While the post-launch updates have made the experience smoother, The Callisto Protocol still doesn’t reach its full potential. For horror fans and those looking for a visually captivating game, it’s worth playing, but it falls short of greatness.

I bought The Callisto Protocol on 85% sale for 8,84€, and here are my "no spoiler" thoughts on it after 3 hours...

Firstly... Callisto Protocol is a game that tries REALLY hard to mimic Dead Space in many ways, to a point where you might actually Google whether or not it is the same developer.

Most bad reviews you read, will call it "B-tier Dead Space", or criticize it because it's "not as good as Dead Space", and see the differences as a negative, rather than trying to rate it for what it actually tries to be. The main two differences between this game and Dead Space, is that combat is entirely different, and this game feels A LOT more linear.

And because of those two differences, people will see them as negatives because the only thing they can think is "is it Dead Space?"... Which is too bad, since Callisto Protocol is a pretty solid game that holds its own.

[b]THE GAME IS LINEAR[/b]

This is a big difference between Callisto Protocol and Dead Space, since Callisto Protocol is VERY linear, and has you basically go from A to B without much deviation. Same goes from exploring, which there is very little off besides a few "secrets", that you can find easily by simply checking out the area.

However... Callisto Protocol being linear isn't a bad thing, since it is obvious that the game tries to come off as a bit more of a "cinematic experience", than Dead Space did. Basically it half'n-half feels like playing a movie.

[b]"COMBAT IS BAD"[/b]

If you are looking for a challenging "survival horror game", then you might need to amp up the difficulty a bit in this game, since enemies basically just attack you one at a time, even when there are multiple around you. And this is obviously done to make the melee combat feel a bit more forgiving and satisfying. And combat DOES feel satisfying, but some might find it too easy.

While you DO have guns in Callisto Protocol, the combat is mainly focused around melee combat, with you dodging or blocking enemy attacks. This is very different from Dead Space, where combat is more centered around shooting.

The melee combat feels VERY satisfying in this game, but some might find it a bit too repetitive, since dodging and blocking is "half-automatic", where basically you just need to hold down a button, and not "tapping it at the right moment". 

So all in all, combat isn't bad. In fact, it's VERY satisfying. If anyone says it is bad, it's because they can't refrain from comparing it to Dead Space combat.

I personally enjoy the combat because I see it for what it is, and not what it's not.

[b]IS IT WORTH BUYING?[/b]

On the 8,84€ sale I got it on, it was an amazing buy. However the 58,99€ price tag it normally has, might be a bit steep.

The game IS good, but apparently people claim it takes 7 hours to beat, and because of how linear it is, it doesn't have much replay value. So I recommend getting it on sale. :) Not necessarily as cheap as me, but at least 25% off is a good price.

So yes, I arrived for the ghost of Dead Space…

Callisto Protocol is, in essence, Dead Space. I know pretty much every other review here says that, and it's true. You show up to a prison where some sort of infection has gone rampant around the facility, and now you must escape while fending off hordes of deadly enemies, forming tedious friendships with acquaintances, and facing down a greater evil. It's the Dead Space formula.

But I'll start with what I like about Callisto Protocol.

The in-game performance, graphics, and art style are really fantastic, which I was surprised by given it's a modern AAA release, especially being made in Unreal. Typically I'd expect to see my high-end computer struggle to even scrape 50 FPS in intensive rendering situations, but the game is really well optimized for what it is.

The combat, looting, and upgrade system is well done, though it certainly has room for improvement. I love the brutally fast paced melee combat paired with the quickdraw firearm combos the game lets you chain, but I feel it's heavily subdued by most enemies being trivialized by your ability to dodge left and right. Once you gain a basic concept of the dodging system, you're good to go. With that being said though, I can understand how some people would find the combat repetitive after a time.

This is a super small thing I liked, but I really liked how the game actually shows where/how you store your weapons. I hate it when games have the player character just sort of stuff their guns up their ass or put them into some pocket dimension when not in use, but I appreciate the attention to detail here.

Some things I really don't care for/could've been improved upon? Firstly the GRP Module (basically a telekinesis module that allows you to pick up and throw things) just feels really weak. It has a battery, okay fine I understand that so players can't abuse it and spam it on environmental hazards for enemies. But using it AT ALL on enemies sucks energy so fast that I found myself ever hardly using it.

Another thing I feel the need to comment on is the separation of side-exploration paths, and what leads to the primary objective. Throughout the game you can find side paths that lead you to extra lore or loot, which is cool, but the game LITERALLY DOES NOT TELL YOU IF WHERE YOU'RE GOING IS PART OF THE STORY OR NOT. I had SO many times where I was worried going down one path or another in a split in the road would lead to a point-of-no-return, or would just be a place for me to check out, and is incredibly frustrating, but not something I'm going to count against it.

This isn't a complaint, moreso being a general critique, but the game also likes to push the idea of the GRP Module being a crowd-control tool, but it has no *real* utility for that. I would have LOVED to have seen a function for it where players could quickly push enemies back with a burst of energy from it, in exchange for high-battery usage. Without any function besides just tossing enemies into spike walls or into machinery though, I just feel it was very half-baked.

Another thing I would have loved to have seen were more suit options/upgrade options. For the first half of the game you're in your prisoner jumpsuit with bare minimum health and storage space. Then later on you get a tactical/environmental suit with upgraded health and access to all your storage slots. I feel a sort of intermediary suit would have been good, like maybe a leftover guard's uniform or something.

Narratively, Callisto Protocol is VERY close to Dead Space, and a lot of ambiguity is left to form for the first half of the game, before it really begins to make sense and explain itself. The latter half of the game gets really good though, and I thoroughly enjoy some of the narrative elements and story points that the writers implemented, especially when it comes to Jacob's involvement in the whole situation.

Now onto what I didn't really like, the big part of this section namely being the enemy variety.

You have your basic slasher-grunt type enemies, with the only variant of them being a fatter one that has more health. You've got other enemies, like ones that sneak around with camo and try to ambush you, ones that explode when they get close, ones that spit at you, etc. All fine. But unfortunately there just isn't a whole ton of variety in threats. 

Almost all enemies just run at you and start swinging, and the ones that DO have ranged attacks can be turned into basic slashers by blowing their heads off, at which they'll engage you in melee combat. There's no enemies that force you to use guns (yes, including the aforementioned exploding enemies. Your GRP Module can deal with them), no enemies that are actually a hazard to engage in melee combat with (assuming you know what you're doing), and no enemies that really made me go "oh fuck", besides MAYBE the Security Bots, of which you only encounter once or twice throughout the entire game. This goes for the bosses too. The final boss is fine in a general sense, and actually got me moving. But unfortunately, like every enemy, his main melee attacks could just be sidestepped.

As for the scare factor of Callisto Protocol, it really just isn't scary, at least in my opinion. I fear the developers leaned on the "loud noise = scary" trope in horror, and while the atmosphere is sort of unnerving, it was let down by the fact I could expect to see a loud noise or something kinda creepy pop up on my screen. I think probably the only time I actually got sort of scared/unnerved was during the final boss ([spoiler] when Ferris is giving you a monologue in the tower and starts to mutate and transform suddenly [/spoiler]).

I also feel Callisto Protocol suffers from another problem Dead Space had; turning the player into an errand boy. You'll ALWAYS have someone giving you a "Go here", "Do this", or "Find this" order, where it feels Jacob is just sort of a drone and can't figure out what to do without instructions. 

Overall? Certainly not GOTY material by any stretch of the imagination, but definitely not as bad as many people say it is. I welcome anyone to give it a try during a sale, or if you're just that certain this is the game for you.

Ok so, I got mixed feelings about this one. 

I heard a lot of bad things about this game, so I didn't want to buy it when it launched, guess I made the right decision. I found it at a pretty CHEAP price, and when I say cheap, I really mean it. So let's start with the good and then go to the bad.

Firstly, the game is stunning, I am guessing Unreal Engine 5 was used to the maximum capabilities, making the characters look like the real deal. I also love the sci-fi theme, when it comes to movies, books, games and all the other media. Lightning and shadows, monster design, weapon design are solid. I also found quite interesting some of the things the team did regarding the weapons system, the printing your own weapons is really interesting as a concept. 

Secondly, the combat system feels "good" let's put it this way, I hate that the melee consists of dodge this and dodge that, and then stack 3 attacks and then dodge again, I really do hate that. But I am giving the game credit, it doesn't feel as bad to hit with the weapons, I also like the shooting mechanic even though is built upon the melee part.

Thirdly, I think the game is optimised. Sure there are some frame drops and lag sometimes, but it's nothing out of the ordinary, after all Unreal is strange and hard to optimise, and this team did a pretty good job about that I would say.

Now, here comes the bad part. Unfortunately, Callisto Protocol is boring... Well... the characters have no back-bone, you get nothing out of them other than the fact they look good, at least at the time I write this review (which is almost 3 hours), I see 2 hours mark as a standard after all, so that people can refund games if they find them boring or problematic when it comes to optimisation.

A lot of talking but nothing interesting regarding story or characters background, which is not cool, especially taking in consideration we are on the MOON (a moon), give me something to chew on, to submerge in the story or something. 

When we talk about sound design it's weird this time around as well. There are a lot of good sounds, like the weapon shots and some monster growls, but many times you expect to hear at least the game music in certain parts, and nothing is there. I can guarantee you the intro scene can be greatly improved with some moody music, full of eerie sounds. But no, you hear only footsteps and that is all.

The navigation is also bugged and strange, I could access some areas after I get through a zone, and then returning after a while to the same zone. Those areas should not be crossed by the player. How do I know that, you might ask? Well, the music and ambient sounds stop in those areas... Getting from one point to another is boring and sluggish, and sometimes you get to a cool looking area, but nothing is in that area, no item, no monster, no weapon, ammo, credits, nothing.

The settings are also weird. Look I like motion blur, I said it, I like it in single player titles, especially when I play with a controller as I don't pan the camera around fast. In this game it sucks, it makes my eyes hurt and the bad part is you need to return to menu to stop this setting. Sorry, you need to return to menu to change almost every setting in the game, I am sure some of these settings could've been "plug and play" let's say, easily accessible through the pause menu in game, but we don't get that.

There are at least a handful of games I could recommend other than Callisto Protocol, play those instead, trust me, you will be more thrilled than playing this boring game. I only gave it a thumbs up because I got it dirt cheap, and because of the other good points. Will I finish it? Well I probably will, because I always finish games even if I don't really like them, but as it stands now, I got bored after 2 and a half hours of just moving from point A to B and so on... It's really a disappointment, I look forward to all sci-fi related games. 2/10

FULL: Callisto Protocol. This is a misunderstood, underrated gem. This is straight like Dead Space with some like it or not innovation. The only real issues I found after completing this game is 1.) the game has stutters occasionally, and 2.) there is no real actual ending of the main story. 

The graphics looks brutal (beware, even if you turn ray tracing off, there will still be a forced ray tracing), considering you turn off all the upscalers and taa aliasing, which by default makes the game extremely blurry. I was able to make it crisp and native by turning these off, and it still looks way better than Dead Space 1 remake. 

The combat loop feels good in general once you get used to it. It is innovative in some degree compared to Dead Space. The uncomfortable thing I found is that the game usually "soft locks" you into a possible dodge animation "readiness state" for 2 seconds when you stand right next to an enemy (you are in their radius), even if you try to run away. This can result in some frustrating deaths. 

I get the idea of the melee system, and it works in general, but the final 2 major bossfights are just pure bullshi-. The only way to do those, is to follow the orchestration of the game, where you have to dodge 5 times, then do 1 or 2 hits then repeat. No real freedom during these 2 bossfights, especially the first one.
Other than that, I asked a few times myself during the gameplay, that is why did they include this melee system? And the closest answer I made was "this is a survival game where you can run out of ammo". Like in RE or DS123 games you don't really have a viable option to survive when you run out of ammo, essentially you are screwed. But here, even if you don't pick up any, and if you place your hits and dodges just fine, you can progress. Or when you run out of ammo and there is no time to reload, as the enemy is almost at your face, then you can start the melee fight to finish them off. I find this innovative and I kind a like the idea.

To compare this to DS123, there you had maximum of 5% non-locked melee and 95% free aim gunfight, but here especially at first playthrou you will have 50% soft-locked melee and 50% free aim gunfight.

The game is visually stunning, it looks like an animation movie. Everything is super detailed, and the levels are extra creepy along with the enemies. The variety of the enemies and the places we visit are like a mix of DS123 and some RE games. The setting is very interesting in my opinion. It gives those Chronicles of Riddick Escape from Butcher Bay vibes. 

And as a closing word, I the worst thing about this game I can state is the optimization. I had everything on high, RT off (forced RT still on as it seemed), 1440p and no upscalers or TAA. Still, my FPS was ranging between 35-45 fps in general, but I had some really wrong stutters. There are no loading screens or anything, so I guess it was due to the game loading some parts of the map dynamically. Still, this caused significant frame drops, and there were some unoptimized parts of the game (the mining town) where I had the worst framerate. 

To summarize, don't buy this, if you have anything less than an RTX 3080 and a beefy CPU and a fast SSD, or the game will run like literal dogshi-, as it struggles to keep up with fps above 40-50 fps on stronger systems. 

Buy this if you are a fan of the RE and DS123 universe. 7.8 game, highly recommended for the fans of the genre.

In a crowded landscape of modern horror games, it can be rare to find a game that delivers both an intense, visceral experience and a deeply cinematic, narrative driven story. This game does just that while featuring powerful performances from both Josh Duhamel and Sam Witwer. I'm baffled by the amount of negative reviews and the mixed ratings, as I feel this game stands as a unique and exceptional entry into the horror market.
I believe a common point of contention comes from the unfair comparison to the Dead Space series, an understandable but misguided point of view. While it's clear where the dev's roots lie, The Callisto Protocol forges its own identity. It feels like a spiritual successor that further evolves on the formula, creating a unique and impactful experience rather than just being a rehash for old fans.
I've also seen criticism for the melee combat. As for myself, I find it brilliant. Don't come into the game expecting fast paced "kung fu". It feels slow, heavy, and satisfying. There's weight behind each strike from your weapon that emphasizes the feeling of survival that the main character is going through. It makes it feel more personal.
Ultimately, I strongly suggest anyone on the fence pick it up. This is a very cinematic and rewarding horror experience that I can't recommend enough. From the compelling story to the satisfying combat, this is one that stands tall in the market. I'm totally invested in its world and characters and can't wait to play more.

Let me tell you about my wild ride with The Callisto Protocol - the game that made me scream, hide under my blanket, and... buy it twice! First on Xbox, then on Steam, because sometimes you just need to relive that terrifying magic. 


🌌 The Setting: Space Prison Gone Very Wrong
Imagine you're Jacob Lee (who's quite handsome even when covered in blood 💕), a space trucker stuck in Black Iron Prison on Jupiter's moon. Sounds fun? Well, not when your cellmates are mutating into horrible monsters!  

- So dark, so scary, so pretty!🔦 The graphics are amazing - every bloody corridor looks so real you'll want to touch it (but don't)  
- The sounds... oh the sounds! 🔊 Footsteps behind you, metal creaking, growls in the dark... My heart was beating so loud!  

---  

⚔️ Combat: Up Close and Personal  
You can't just shoot everything here - you'll need to learn melee combat! And you know what? It feels great once you get it.  

- Dodge, hit, repeat! 🎮 Every swing feels powerful, especially when enemies go splat
- Guns 🔫 are rare but satisfying. That shotgun? Pure monster-blending goodness!  

---  

👻 Horror Moments: Blanket Required 
If you like scary games that make you jump, this one delivers!  

- The monsters 👹 are disgustingly cool. Those Two-Heads? NOPE. Just nope.  
-  1️⃣ The Grunt (Your Basic Nightmare)
- The standard model, but "standard" here means "flesh melting off bones"  
- Comes in fun variants like Exploders (💥 surprise boom!) and Spitters (🤢 acid attack, ew)  
- Pro tip: Always check ceilings - they love to drop on you like terrible meat 

2️⃣ Two-Head (The Stuff of Nightmares)
- My personal sleep paralysis demon 👹  
- Basically two angry dudes fused together (relationship goals?)  
- That *scream* when it charges? I had to mute my TV twice  
- Funny story: First encounter made me throw my controller at my poor cat (she forgave me... eventually)  

3️⃣ The Blind (Sneaky Scary Boi) 
- No eyes, but HEARS EVERYTHING 👂  
- Tip-toe sections had me holding my breath IRL  
- Pro strat: Throw objects to distract them... unless you enjoy being gutted  

4️⃣ The Final Boss 
- Let's just say it involves creative use of human anatomy  

---  

💻 PC Version: Pretty But Demanding
I played first on console but the Steam version works great!  

- Graphics 🖥️ are gorgeous on max settings  
- Controls 🎮 feel better with a gamepad for dodging  

---  

The Not-So-Good Stuff  
- A bit short ⏳ (10-13 hours) but has replay value  
- Story 📖 is good but not amazing  

---  

💖 Final Verdict: Absolutely Play This! 
If you love horror with amazing atmosphere and visuals, this is a must-play. Even if you get scared easily like me!  

Score: 9/10 🌟 (for making me feel ALL the emotions)

I enjoyed this game, I guess the general reaction has been mixed. Maybe that can be blamed on people expecting Dead Space again. I'm not sure. The game isn't perfect. Most of the complaints you've heard are correct. The melee is janky, it's linear, and the story is simple. The positives are also true in that the game is amazing looking. One of the first games for me to really feel next-gen. It looks like those Unreal tech engines come to life.

I guess I simply have low standards as I liked it and didn't find the flaws people have expressed.

The game is linear and it has no map. No puzzles. The structure is straightforward, but I'm an FFXIII fan so I guess that doesn't bother me. I don't mind linearity and I think it mostly works here. If anything because yes there is no map. While it does lead to some annoying instances where you want to know where the store is to offload things, in general, I think this confusion adds some tension. There are enough little pathways off of the main path to constantly make you feel like you are exploring and that the environment is well-realized. In a way it adds to the tension and mystery as you may not be quite sure you are going the correct way. That's kind of a nice horror feeling and since it is linear it doesn't feel making or like backtracking.

The combat is melee focused for most of the game, but honestly, I don't feel like the game is always throwing tons of enemies at you. Most of the first half is one-on-one and in a way, I feel like what they were going for is head-on tension feeling in the combat. You have to face your fear is perhaps the theme of the game and well that translates to the gameplay. When an enemy comes your way you had to meet it head-on. The melee does feel visceral and it does lend itself to the catharsis of finally waking a monster to death.  As the game goes on it does become more shooter focused. It does throw more enemies at you, but in one of those game segments if you are being swamped by enemies it's because you have failed the game's simple stealth.  Even then it's not like the game doesn't give you enough tools. The telekinesis is always viable and the game really does make you use all your tools.

In a way, I feel like this is an over-the-shoulder game that was not trying to be a clone of RE4 and do its own thing. I don't think it all comes together that greatly. I think if they did make another one simply putting more emphasis on shooting combat, and some crowd control, all while maintaining the dodge system would probably make more people happy. But I don't think it was needed for me. I felt like this is a game that really tried to make its progression and survival horror more natural and in a way more "hardcore". What I mean is I often feel like in say RE4 it's kind of a trick the game pulls over me to make me feel like I really do not have enough ammo. In the end, I usually do. Callisto also seems to have randomized drops of stuff, but often I did feel like I was short on ammo and melee is what I had to do. Of course, as it went on I felt more confident and my weapons were more powerful, but even up the end ammo and inventory were a concern. I legit feel like the developers were trying to make a real survival horror game and not simply an action game pretending to be one.

The story though is as typical as survival horror games go. So much so that you could fill in the blanks yourself. Nothing really exciting happens, but it's all presented well even though it is all pretty mundane.

But in the end, I really enjoyed this game and I really hope they get to make more.

-- The Short Review --
This is going to be long-winded, and probably expanded upon much like my MW5:M review as I play more. The TL;DR is that yes, I think this game is a fun time if you like sci-fi horror and melee-focused action games. However, going in to this game expecting a 'true' survival-horror experience will set you up for disappointment. Graphically impressive and with some tense moments, an open-minded person will still have a good time as long as they feel the price for admission was worth it. For ~$20, I'd say go for it.

-- The Long Review --
To get the technical stuff out of the way: the game is visually stunning. The fidelity of the environments, character models, gore, monsters, etc. is truly impressive and maybe it is partially due to not being 'current' on modern blockbuster-esque games but the graphics alone have left much more of an impression on me than I ever thought they would. The animations have lots of nuance and fluidity and look amazing. I love looking at this game and taking in the carnage of the environments as I walk and run and fight around them. The sound is great as well; I've not noticed any bad or out-of-place effects and sounds are appropriately powerful or guttural for the weapons and monsters respectively. The music has been good, not 'put this in my playlist' good but also the game would lack something without its presence. After close to two years since its release, I have not had any performance issues apart from the weirdness that can happen from running a game on native LInux with Proton. Honestly its ran far better for me than RE4R despite possibly being the more demanding game.

Now, we can get into the real issues.

The monster design is cool! They are gross and mean-looking and are definitely not out-of-place in sci-fi horror. But... they're not scary. I know that I'm also not all of the way through this game and probably haven't seen everything, but I had to start this review because it just doesn't scare me. Sure it has tense moments and some environments are genuinely creepy, but the horror element is severely let down by the mechanics of the game. The game sets you (Jacob) up as a surprisingly durable killing machine, that can swiftly dodge and dismantle the creatures that set upon you. Against a player that can handle the combat system, these creatures don't stand a chance. You will beat the ever-living shit out of them until they are convulsing in a pile of broken bones and mangled flesh and then you stomp on them some more to let them know how pathetic they are (and to get your loot drops of course).

In a real survival-horror game, combat is a gamble. Is the cost of resources worth the investment of dealing with this threat? (ex. Zombies in RE2R) Can I even deal with this threat? (ex. Mr. X or the Ubermorph) Or, for the more apt comparison of Dead Space (2008) or Dead Space 2 (2011), will I be able to deal with the enemies before they ever get close to me? In my opinion, survival-horror is at its best when you can technically deal with the threats before you, but at the same time you are sacrificing something to do so, while also not wanting these creatures to ever even think about touching you because the consequences are severe.

Conversely in Callisto, when I see an enemy I buckle up and charge in to start beating the ever-living shit out of them with a big smile on my face. The combat system isn't even that technically deep like a Souls-like game or a fighting game, but I find it to be quite satisfying. This is the complete opposite feeling I should have about combat in a game that wants to be a horror game, where the game clearly wants you to fear the creatures that you are fighting. While I enjoy Dead Space combat, I don't necessarily *want* to be in combat in Dead Space. I do everything I can to deal with the necromorphs as quickly as possible so that I can stop being in danger. Callisto has for better or worse, turned you into the danger. I am actively looking for fights because ironically that is the safest place to be in as well as the point when I'm having the most fun. Dodging is simple and easy enough to pull off, and is almost completely safe when doing so. Ranged enemies still pose a threat as your dodge animation only saves you from the enemy you are currently engaged with, but management of ranged enemies or the environment will reduce that risk. Getting grappled does not instantly deal damage to you with all enemy types as far as I can tell, or does not deal enough damage to be a big factor because of the ease of dodging. There is at least a balance issue if I'd rather be grabbed than block an attack because blocking feels like I take more damage from bleed-through. At risk of repeating myself, we'll leave it at that until my inevitable comment-extensions.

My only other major complaint is that the first three chapters of the game and somewhat into the fourth, I was drowning in items with not enough places to offload them. We don't have storage this time around so you have to sell or use what you don't need, but you can't pick up everything because the game starts you off with a measly SIX INVENTORY SLOTS. With how much stuff there was to pick up, this was incredibly frustrating. Instead of being relieved that I found another health injector or ammo for the pistol, I had to play the "Do I have enough space for this item?" game every couple of minutes. What added insult to injury was instead of being able to back-track reasonable amounts to pick up items I had to leave behind, the game pushes you forward several times with permanently locked doors or sequences that cannot be undone due to the game's linearity. Dead Space managed this finite balance well, and offset some of the pressure by allowing you to store items for later when in an excess, so that if you ever found yourself in a drought you could address it. What I will say is that I have so far found the ammunition for the pistol to be a pretty good balance of 'just enough'. Once I'm further into the game that may change.

What about the story? Oh yeah, it's there. I'm enjoying the characters enough and I'm engaged because it does feel like a horror-movie story but its not the 'best story ever told'. When thinking about Callisto's story I'm reminded of The Belko Experiment, which while I had fun with that movie it wasn't a movie I'd rush home to tell everybody about.

Despite my issues with the game, I am still having a good time and have been trying to fit it into my busy schedule. Will it hold up on repeat playthroughs? Higher difficulties? I'll know soon enough. More thoughts TBA as I get further along. Although...

This game had amazing promise, as it was literally just Dead Space in all but name. Unfortunately, it's just a pale imitation, which is very ironic and also sad considering it's literally from the creator and (as far as I know) team that made the first 3 Dead Space games. 

And While Dead Space (and the DS Remake) are masterful examples of how to do Sci-Fi horror, The Callisto Protocol falls flat on every single front EXCEPT its amazing graphical elements/models/textures/etc. Altogether the game is fine, but that's about it. Its combat is repetitive and boring, its story is worse than Dead Space in every respect, and while they TRY to do a reasonable amount of world building, it's really not remotely as well thought-out as its "spiritual" predecessor.

Also, the "true" ending of the game is locked behind paid DLC, and that's just crappy behavior, so I don't think you should have to bother with that. I'll just tells you what happens. 

SPOILERS FROM HERE ON OUT: At the end of the core game the supporting female protagonist escapes the prison when your character (Jacob) pushes her into the only remaining escape pod. Jacob is then left behind fighting horrible things as everything crumbles and explodes around him. The DLC begins with Jacob waking up from where the core game ended (seemingly after having killing all the things coming to eat him), and he then proceeds to go through a bunch of objectives to find data to ultimately send a transmission to the larger human government/civilization so as to expose what happened at the Callisto prison. In reality, the DLC is all a hallucination/simulation in Jacob's mind, as he was horribly mutilated when another supporting character finds him back in real-life. We discover he's nothing but a limbless torso with half his skin left, and the supporting character is using his neural implant to package up all his memories (and the data from the prison experiments) into a transmission to expose what happened at the prison. Jacob isn't aware of any of that though, as far as he knows he's fine and he saved the day. The supporting character sends the transmission, and then the ceiling collapses and kills them both. The end! 

CONCLUSION: In short, it's a decent attempt at a game, but they failed on too many fronts, which is a massive loss to everyone, as the potential here was incredible. If it's super cheap, like $10 or less, it's worth a buy and a play, but more than that? I'd say don't bother. But, don't fret! EA allowed the amazing Dead Space remake to be produced. If we're lucky, they'll come to their dumb senses and allow Dead Space 2 to be remade with the same love and attention as the first game. Go play that instead.

HOWEVER -
In terms of the game itself, it really isn't up to my own expectations. The suspense is bare minimal; I wouldn't even consider this a survival horror as it being a Dead Space copycat. Atmosphere in comparison to other popular survival horrors really isn't there and this game really only has aesthetics to compromise the fact. Callisto is much more of a cinematic adventure title. Suspense is nil, though combat does present itself as a "git gud" in terms of being patient and dodging and striking at appropriate times. 

My biggest beef with this game however is how empty it feels. In any adventure/exploration game, regardless if it's a horror game or not, you're rewarded for exploration yet in this game.. You're not. You can go off the beaten path with minimal reward that makes you question why even venture off in the first place. No rarities or collectibles. Rooms that you'd think would have something have absolutely nothing; even if they do have something, maybe it's just petty cash. Progression is very straight forward yet I still came across something that dumbfounded me. I plan to do a full playthrough, the story isn't all too engaging but it's entertaining enough to make me continue. I might update this review if things get better (or worse). But for now, I'd say this game is a 6/10 rating. Just stick with the first two Dead Space games instead.

Callisto Protocol didn't deserve the fate it received and is still a phenomenal take on the dark grounded sci-fi horror many of us love. Sadly, due to this hypocrite mob of people, uncapable of just being adults and admitting the game isn't for them, we will not be getting more from this franchise. It's truly a shame given that there are almost zero attempts at this niche by any sort of  AAA-standard, and that is for reasons like this.

Let's start off with the graphics, the fidelity here is incredible in everything from the art and the models to the geometric detail, texturing and level design. It's oozing with atmosphere and is another take on that very industrial chunky type of future that many of us envision or have seen in similar takes with franchises like Alien, Deadspace, Event Horizon and so on.

The pure engineering here makes it stand out from any of your average template Unreal Engine games or blueprint cheap shot asset flips. The objective criticism valid here is the PC launch, it wasn't okay, but it is in a much better state today.

Animation and acting is on top, smooth, realistic, and they all look excellent on screen, nothing is budget or cheap here. The writing could at times have been better and less cheesy, especially from the main antagonist, but overall it's very well executed. They do the world building good, and it's the sort where one would just love to have gotten more from this world.

Regarding gameplay, it is also very chunky in a good way, you're not spinning your character around like it's souls or quake 3, and it all fits the tone and vision very well. People seemed to have a hard time with the melee system, fine you can subjectively not like it, but really it's a meaty and satisfying system that keeps the combat tense.

A lot of things are close to great in this game and I feel like if it had just gotten a few more  months in the grinder the last bugs would've been ironed out, and we'd also get a more complete set of bosses and combat arenas. 

I originally played it on the PS5 and had a great time even from the early day one version/patch platinizing the game, so the game itself is probably more polished than most of your games out there already. With that said, things I've encountered in rarity are save bugs. If you rely on the auto-save and quit, I have found myself being set back several minutes, which may be a lot more if the difficulty is high. It's a small thing, but it's still in the game and can be frustrating, I'm not sure what triggers it.

Another valid point is the reuse of a certain boss. It is quite obvious this wasn't meant to be and the boss itself is really cool and well done, but the repetitive nature of fighting it X amount of times does shine through as well as a quite simplistic dodge mechanic that could've used some spice, at least for boss battles. 

The same goes for certain combat encounters. Now I'll approach this from a less dicky buhu side and say that this game is meant to make you feel underpowered constantly, way more than Dead Space. It's not a power-fantasy, and that seems to really get to people for some reason. Again, just admit it's not for you instead of whining and complaining. With that said, certain combat setups and encounters does seem poorly tested when it bugs out with the dodging of the melee system and quirks like that.  Given another 6 months of balancing and bug testing and flushing out these combat spaces and chess pieces a bit more, and I think it could've been superb. 

One thing is that if you play on Hardcore and use the explosive tubes you barely get anything out of it when the enemies have evolved. Many times it fails to make any damage/impact and just bounces right off the enemies, and in certain situations the enemy intro animation will make them invincible and therefor you might completely  waste an explosive tube too early. This is very apparent and can happen in the chapter LOST. In those kinds of situations the game really does let the player down. I also think they could've rewarded exploration a bit more, resources are extremely rare which is fine but rarely are you rewarded for going into the extra rooms which is a shame.

Sound then..
Sound design is fantastic, everything from the chunky footsteps of Jacob to the ambient noises and environmental metal-stresses makes for a really enjoyable experience at Black Iron. It is to be said that I've had situations where certain sounds cut out or cut off, it's rare, but another thing that could've been polished away given just a little more time.

Another thing that holds the game back is the requirement to ship on last gen. You'll end up shimmying through tight sections a lot which starts to feel very artifical after a while. It's fine to have your average vent crawl and and trick here and there, but here it's so common and obviously used  for the onboarding and offboarding of resources. Not really the devs fault but it's another small thing that adds up.

So is Callisto Protocol perfect ? No it isn't, but I think the fans of these type of games really let this game down. It's a huge and impressive production that fell on the finish-line, but even with those quirks and given the patches for the PC it defiantly didn't deserve the shitstorm it got or the rating it has. This is as deserving of praise as the Dead Space remake, and I'm glad we got one entry and attempt at this rather than nothing. Defiantly the best looking game of 2022 and one of the best looking games of all time.

Set in a dark, alien-infested prison on Jupiter’s moon, the game knows exactly what you’re here for: bone-crushing survival horror, jump scares galore, and monsters with way too many limbs.

You play as Jacob Lee, a cargo pilot who somehow winds up in a prison where they skip the whole “due process” bit. Things go from bad to worse fast when some genius decides to let a biohazard break loose, turning everyone into mutants.

The Callisto Protocol prides itself on “tactical melee combat,” which is fancy talk for “hit it with a pipe until it’s dead.” Enemies have a real "no personal space" policy, constantly in your face, lunging, growling, and generally being nightmare fuel. The scarcity of ammo and the tactical element of melee make every encounter feel high-stakes, adding to the survival horror feel. There’s also a “GRP” (gravity restraint project) device that lets players lift and throw enemies—into environmental hazards like fans, spikes, or off ledges—for some satisfying and creative takedowns.

The setting of Black Iron Prison is dark, industrial, and designed to make players feel trapped and vulnerable. Every inch of the game’s environment is crafted to exude unease: flickering lights and ominous sounds keep tension high. The art direction has a strong sci-fi horror vibe, blending futuristic technology with the grime and brutality of a maximum-security prison. Lighting and sound work together to create moments where every creak and shadow keeps players on edge.

The sound design in The Callisto Protocol deserves an award for “most unsettling ambiance.” From the soft gurgling of enemies sneaking up on you to the constant hum of malfunctioning prison machinery, every noise is engineered to keep your heart rate uncomfortably high.

It’s a worthy addition to the genre that will appeal to anyone looking for a horrifyingly immersive sci-fi adventure.

[h1]Callisto Protocol is a good game, not a great game, but a good game nonetheless.[/h1] 

You play as Jacob Lee, a freighter pilot that finds himself stranded in the moon of Callisto. Having been unlawfully imprisoned in a correctional facility there, our protagonist must flee the titular moon whilst surviving a deadly outbreak that is turning all inmates in deadly, mindless ghouls. As one would expect, this escape is all but a harmless ordeal, and our hero must face many a significant trial and tribulation before reaching his journey's end. 

I dare not say much for fear of spoiling anything about the story, apart from the fact that while it is nowhere groundbreaking, the whole "jailbreak out of an offworld prison infested with zombies" felt as a refreshing take on the horror genre. The story (borrowing from a netizen's comment I saw on Reddit, IIRC), is akin to that of a B-Movie, but that is not something wrong [i]per se[/i] ; the problem, rather, lies with the execution: the game's characters are a somewhat forgettable cast, and their dialogues (and the momentum leading up to many of the game's setpiece monologues) could use some much-needed polishing. Moreover, the game suffers from a ridiculous excess of jump scares, to the point that after 2~3 hours into the game you can predict every single jump scare that is bound to happen in a cutscene.

Needless to say, this detracts significantly from the horror factor, albeit not entirely, for the game (fortunately) does have more tricks up its sleeve: atmosphere is one of them. The sheer sense of unease (and even dread) I experienced when visiting some of the latter portions of the game is right there with some of the most unnerving locations in horror games. The game simply feels disturbingly [i]wrong[/i] in these portions of the game and while nothing truly gaze-averting happens, you do get to experience that feeling of "I shouldn't be here" many horror games try to nail, but ultimately fall short of achieving.

This was a nice departure from The Callisto Protocol's famous, albeit formally unofficial, predecessor: Dead Space. I played the original back in 2008 and was completely unfazed by its predictable nature. This comes from someone who literally suffered playing F.E.A.R. out of the sheer terror that game instilled in me and even later games such as Outlast and Alien: Isolation posed a challenge to my fear-coping mechanics. Not Dead Space; I found it a boring and unenthusiastic tech demo, which often seemed as wanting to showcase what state-of-the-art technology could do, rather than delivering an actual story worth being told. I am currently playing the Dead Space Remake so I can safely comment on the comparison between Callisto and Dead Space and for me Callisto delivers a more ambitious, even if flawed, experience. That is not to say that Dead Space is a bad game, but I find it sorely lacking in inspiration, even if its execution is safer, as you would have it. Callisto seeks to be more and, at least in the horror and fear department, undisputably succeeds.

Not only in these aspects is The Callisto Protocol a solid installment: the game sports some of the most breathtaking visuals ever seen in a game, and while it does experience some FPS dips every now and then, the average FPS count was remarkably stable for such a fine-looking game.

Moreover, the gameplay in this game is, simply put, amazing. It truly makes up for the story's lack of charm. Unlike Dead Space, where you are given a gun and must (boringly) shoot off limbs to render enemies unthreatening before finishing them off with a flurry of stomps, in Callisto it is all about melee combat: you basically have to dodge the enemies' hits left and right, carefully predicting their incoming attack. Should you rather not risk that, you may block them, taking reduced damage. It makes for some fun, but challenging (and surprisingly intuitive!) combos which later on you may compound with firearms and the GRP. The GRP is Callisto's answer to Dead Space's stasis and kinesis. It essentially lets you lift a myriad of things in the air, ranging from enemies to stuff lying about, thereby turning everything in a veritable deadly projectile. Moreover, this opens up a whole avenue of environmental deaths (sorely lacking in Dead Space), such as throwing enemies into grinders, fans and spikes, when not outright flinging them to their deaths at botomless pits. Moreover, this allows you to quickly maneuver enemies out of your reach, so as not to get swarmed by them, for unlike other games, The Callisto Protocol does not have enemies take turns pouncing at you; rather, they attack you all at once if they can. Gameplay, thus, is an exhilarating experience in this game, compensating for some of the weakest bits of the story.

For in the end, The Callisto Protocol achieved to be much more than a horror game: it was a fun experience, as much as it was unsettling, if not outright scary. Ineed, it feels to be the game that Dead Space (or at least their shared creator) wanted to be. It still falls short of its vision and promise, but it has a solid foundation to build upon.

Right, let me tell you about this game The Callisto Protocol. You know what's mental? They spent millions making everything look gorgeous – proper Hollywood stuff, right? The gore, the blood, the guts – it's like they hired the effects team from Saw and said, "Go mental, make it disgusting." And they did!

The death animations? Brilliant. Absolutely brilliant. Every time you die – which for most of you will be about every 30 seconds – you get to watch your character being ripped apart in new and exciting ways. It's like Final Destination in space, innit? Thank God they let you skip them, or we'd all be sitting there like proper muppets watching our character get dismembered for the 50th time.

Now, the combat... Oh dear. Oh dear oh dear. You know when you're at a party, and there's that one bloke who thinks he can dance but just looks like he's having a seizure? That's what the combat feels like. You're there, swinging away like a drunk at closing time, and the enemies just look at you like "Is that all you've got?" No stagger effect! Can you believe it? You hit them with your best shot, and they just laugh it off and slap you silly. It's like trying to fight Katie Price's bodyguards after ten pints.

And don't get me started on switching weapons. It's... so... bloody... slow. By the time you've switched from your gun to your baton, climate change has flooded half the planet.

The difficulty? Had to turn it down, didn't I? Not ashamed to admit it. Life's too short to be frustrated by a video game. It's like when you're watching Love Island – at some point, you've got to ask yourself, "Why am I putting myself through this?"

They promised us proper horror, right? Said it'd be like Dead Space's scarier cousin. More like Dead Space's slightly dim nephew who tries too hard at parties. There's so much ammo lying around, it's like an American gun shop. Where's the tension? Where's the fear?

Look, for seven quid on sale, it's not bad. The graphics are proper good, and sometimes – SOMETIMES – it all comes together like a beautiful accident. The Callisto Protocol Review: A Stunning Horror Experience with Some Rough Edges

First things first, the graphics in The Callisto Protocol are absolutely incredible. Even in performance mode, everything looks fantastic, from the environment to the detailed blood, guts, and gore. The death animations are particularly well-done and stand out as some of the best I've ever seen for each enemy type. While they can get repetitive if you die often, there’s an option to skip them, which is great for someone like me who takes a few more hits than I’d like to admit.

The combat is... okay. While it’s not without its flaws, it can be engaging once you get the hang of it. Dodging enemy attacks becomes routine after some practice since there’s no timing window for the dodge, making it fairly easy to avoid hits. However, the combat's biggest issue comes when you’re up against multiple enemies. The lack of a stagger feature, even after landing a power hit, can be frustrating. It’s annoying to get the first swing in only to be immediately slapped down by the enemy. And the weapon-switching animations? They're painfully slow and clunky, which can really interrupt the flow of combat.

After a while, I found the difficulty spikes to be too much. I decided to lower the difficulty to "combat" mode, which made things more manageable without completely taking away the challenge. That said, even on this setting, it’s still easy to get overrun in certain sections. I imagine New Game+ would be where the real fun lies, with a more forgiving pace and power-ups making the combat feel smoother—but I’m not sure if I want to replay the entire game to get there.

I love fighting back, tired of puzzle infested horror games with limited combat..  offering an atmosphere filled with tension and fear. Unfortunately, it didn’t quite live up to that hype. While the monsters are terrifying to look at and the gore is top-notch, it didn’t give me the intense, pulse-pounding experience I was expecting. It didn’t have the creeping dread of something like Dead Space, where every corner feels like it could be your last. There’s a lot of ammo lying around, and with waves of enemies constantly coming at you, the game doesn’t build that slow-burning fear that makes a horror game great.

Another downside is the enemy variety—or lack thereof. You encounter the same types of mutated humans over and over, and even the bosses feel repetitive, with a particular fight being recycled three or four times. It detracts from the sense of escalation that should come with each new challenge.

That said, The Callisto Protocol has its redeeming qualities. The visuals are amazing, and when the game works, it really works. The story is solid, and there are some genuinely thrilling moments. It’s just unfortunate that the difficulty spikes, repetitive enemies, and combat mechanics drag down what could’ve been a truly memorable experience.

At its current price point (around $7 on CDKeys), I’d still recommend giving it a try, especially if you’re a fan of horror games. For that price, it’s worth experiencing the great visuals and story, even if the combat and pacing leave something to be desired.

[h2] The Callisto Protocol: A Beautifully Flawed Horror Experience [/h2]

The Callisto Protocol isn't a bad game, but it’s only a good game if you’re willing to overlook several significant shortcomings. It shines in its opening hours, with impressive graphics, lighting, and facial animations. The game’s atmosphere is particularly strong, offering something that Dead Space fans would likely appreciate—if only it maintained this quality throughout. Unfortunately, it falls into repetition soon after, and much of the initial potential feels wasted.

One of the game's biggest weaknesses is its combat design. The shooting mechanics are basic, paling in comparison to a game like Dead Space. However, it’s the melee system that baffled me the most. Every encounter boils down to the same rhythm of "dodge, dodge, shoot." What’s strange is that the dodge system isn’t active like you’d expect in other third-person games. Instead, it’s reactive—hold a directional key (A or D on PC) to auto-dodge incoming attacks, switching directions if a second or third attack comes. This system removes any sense of urgency or danger from combat.

In most survival horror games, keeping enemies at a distance is crucial, and the tension of being grabbed adds to the fear. But in The Callisto Protocol, you want enemies close, because dodging and melee attacks are too easy and repetitive. It saps the game of the dread you’d expect from a true horror title. A stamina-based dodge system might have injected more challenge, though it would have borrowed heavily from other games.

The game’s design also becomes repetitive. You’ll find yourself cutting identical cables, crouching through vents, and squeezing through walls again and again. As strong as the game’s opening is, the repetition that follows drags it down.

That said, I didn’t encounter many of the performance issues that plagued the game at launch. On my mid-range system, it ran smoothly, with DLSS (even modded) helping me maintain 80–100 FPS most of the time. There were rare dips into the 60s, but these were isolated moments. However, ray tracing is still a mess. Not only does it kill performance, but upscaling doesn’t seem to help, and hardware utilization drops drastically when ray tracing is enabled, underscoring poor optimization.

Would I recommend The Callisto Protocol? It depends. If you can get it at a discount—say around €20—it’s worth it. The base game at that price offers decent value, and adding the "Final Transmission" DLC for about €15 adds an extra two hours of content. But at €60 or the €77 deluxe edition price, it’s overpriced for what is ultimately a very atmospheric but mediocre game.

If you’ve never played Dead Space, I’d recommend the Dead Space remake without hesitation. But if you’ve already experienced Dead Space and want something new, The Callisto Protocol does provide a fresh narrative—just don’t expect it to rival Dead Space in terms of gameplay. Ultimately, The Callisto Protocol excels in atmosphere but falls short in gameplay and variety. The game could have benefitted from another year in development to flesh out enemy variety and mechanics.

The story is interesting and keeps you invested, although it's not something you haven't seen before. There are also some twists (in the main story and the DLC), some very predictable, some not.

In terms of graphics, the game looks good. The level design is amazing and there's a sick attention to creepy details and gore. There's also the lights and shadows that add to the atmosphere. There are moments when a slight flicker of light can make you turn around or make you hide. This, combined with the sound effects and soundtrack, makes this a really well-designed horror game.

The game isn't very long. It consists of 8 missions + another one from the DLC. The first mission is the prologue, with more cutscenes than actual gameplay, and the rest, including the DLC, are somewhere between 90 minutes and 2 hours.

Unfortunately, there are bad things as well.

First is the save system. There are checkpoints that work as you'd expect, and then there's the manual save that doesn't work as one would suspect.
While you can manually save the game, sometimes you'd end up restarting from the closest checkpoint, sometimes somewhere between the last checkpoint and the time you saved, and sometimes exactly from where you saved. I finished the game but still haven't figured it out. And something tells me it's by design, not a bug.

Second, there are the bugs. Not as many as 3 years ago, but still quite frustrating. There are moments when you cannot interact with the objective (finding an access card or getting someone else's implant or with a certain console). This forces you to reload and try to see if you can trigger the right event sequence to avoid the bug. And with the save system being what it is, this gets frustrating fast.

There are also moments when the game refuses to load. It just pops a black screen with background music and that's it. Haven't figured this one out either. Some say it's the memory usage, some say it's having a browser or streaming apps in the background, some say it's when you use trainers and cheats.
But unfortunately, I couldn't find a solution. The more you play, the more it happens, up to a point where (in my case) the game became unplayable.
Thankfully, I finished the game but I was unable to finish the DLC since somewhere in the middle, the game stopped loading and, after 2 hours of checking for a solution, I had to give up.

I was really expecting this to be stable after 3 years, but that's not the case. Or it wasn't for me.

But with all the bugs and problems, this is still a great game. Not only does it feel a lot like Dead Space, but it felt like gaming in 2010 all over again. And this was more than enough for me.
