The Callisto Protocol is a lot like Dead Space! Or is it... Follow Jacob Lee, a new inmate locked up in Black Iron Prison, where he bears witness to an outbreak of zombie-like creatures that wreak havoc on the prison. Get up close and personal with some brutal melee action to dismember and destroy the foes in your path as you try to find out just what the hell is going on.

Similar to Dead Space, you play Callisto Protocol in a third-person perspective walking around a dark and creepy environment. Similar to Dead Space, you'll occasionally be assaulted by three to five creatures of nefarious origin and tasked with dismembering them as swiftly as possible. Similar to Dead Space, you can also yeet and pull shit around with a tele-kinetic gravity arm tool thing. Similar to Dead Space, you can keep track of your health via a segmented bar on your back that you can refill with syringe item pickups, and similar to Dead Space you can find said pickups by stomping on an enemy's corpse. Similar to Dead Space, there's also a mysterious cult-like origin to the zombie beings that assail you. And yet with all these similarities to Dead Space, with all these moments where you go "I feel like I've played this game already", Callisto Protocol still manages to separate itself to a decent degree. The primary thing being that Callisto Protocol is incredibly melee-based, with a focus on counter-attacks and dodging and weaving through the swings of the enemy. The big benefit of this is that you really get to fully immerse yourself in the violence, gore, and horror of the action going on around you. And while I love Dead Space, this variation of a classic formula is still really fun to mess around with.

There are some downsides to The Callisto Protocol. For one, the combat can get a little repetitive after a while, as once you figure out the optimal block-dodge-strike sequences the game feels a tad "figured-out". To make up for this the game introduces a lot of new enemies and variants, most of whom feel exciting to encounter (we do not talk about Two-Head holy fuck what a boring enemy). The story definitely leaves a lot to be desired. Ironically, Dead Space actually has a really solid story at least for the first two games, whereas Callisto Protocol is about 9 hours of your protagonist going "what the hell is going on???????" followed by a final chapter of exposition dump and a god-awful ending. One of your primary antagonists has so much beef with you and for frankly no reason considering you've interacted for all of twenty minutes together. The DLC actually wraps up the main game's ending really well for the most part and offers a much better resolution in terms of gameplay and story, but considering this is locked behind a DLC paywall this feels really scummy. The gore is pretty solid, but the blood effects could be better for the type of the game it is and the advertised gazillions of ways your character can die don't really feel that amazing. If anything, you might see a grand total of like, 8 different animations in the whole story, as half the time an animation won't even play and your character will just flop over dead. Finally, the environmental layout feels really cheesy and slapped together. While it's graphically well-developed, it's also filled to the brim with cheap jumpscares and shimmy sequences (you will crawl through so many vents). Also what the hell kinda prison is this, why are there just random walls of spikes and sawblade machines of gore and destruction (besides to give the player some environmental tools to kill enemies with). 

And yet, with all that being said, I gotta say:

The Callisto Protocol's kinda fun.

Does it feel at times like a pretty inferior product to the game it so frequently emulates? Does it get redundant? Does it feel less horror-focused and more cheesy gore action movie at times? Yes to all these things. But if you can get it on a steep discount, say $20 or less, I'd say it's pretty worth it. Just set your expectations low, and go in just expecting to wail on some zombies for a few hours and experience some brain candy popcorn fun.

Despite all the problems at launch, having bought the game on sale a few years later, I'm actually really enjoying this game for what it is, would genuinely recommend for someone who enjoys single player horror/thriller games

Do I recommend TCP? Short answer: yes. Long answer: BIG maybe. If you are into horror games and specifically classic survival horror games, overall you will most likely enjoy TCP, though you will have to deal and accept all its many defects. If you are looking for an action/shooting game with a high-pace gameplay this is not for you, even if you like horror games. If you are looking for a fun combat system this is not for you either. Below I summarize my thoughts on what I think are good and bad points about this game. 

GOOD POINTS
- Story-wise, it is a bit predictable, but it is not bad and it keeps you hooked. However, a bit more of details in the story with collectibles apart from the records you find would have been nice documents, flashbacks, etc). 
- The environment and the horror scenarios are supreme, really well done. You get immersed from the very first time and despite the repetitive jump scares (see below) it is a scary game, especially during the first half of the game when you are really struggling with guns, ammo, health and item management and you are facing terrifying enemies in dark corridors full of blood, corpses and destruction. 
- Although they get repetitive pretty soon, the graphics and models are really good.
- The ways you can kill the enemies with the GRP using the environment is a great idea and adds a fresh mechanic. 
- Duration is perfect, not too short, not too long. 12-15 h first playthrough. 

BAD POINTS: Unfortunately there are way too many
- First and foremost, and the main reason some people hate this game to their guts, is the combat system. I get they were trying to be realistic, but they did not think thoroughly about the consequences. The game is mostly based on melee attacks, and that is fine, but the character engages automatically the enemies in a kind of an invisible Z-targeting system. It all boils down to dodging the enemy’s attacks by simply tilting the left stick to the left or right (you can also “block”, but it is mostly useless), and then attacking with R, then repeat until the enemy dies. Many problems arise with this system. 1) the character feels really “heavy”, he moves really slow and sluggishly which makes attacks take some time to execute, so enemies can still hit you in the process. 2) when facing 2 or more enemies the system is simply unfair and broken, as you are engaged with 1 enemy and can have 1 or more behind you or by your sides which can hit you. This makes most multi-enemy encounters really frustrating and infuriating, as you can’t see the ones on your back or side because you cannot turn around, the dodge system goes crazy and fail most of the times, the camera is too close and you cannot engage/select different enemies at will, or simply flee (they outrun you). In these situations, either you use the GRP to create some space throwing enemies temporarily away, or kill them with powerful guns spending tons of ammo while managing to dodge at the same time the closest enemy. 3) Some bosses that may insta-kill you and cannot be GRP’ed have secondary enemies spamming around, which most likely hit you on your back, interrupting your dodge/attack and making you easy meat for the boss. This was the most infuriating part to me. 
- The pace is really slow and, on many occasions, you are prevented from running, not sure why, when you have to walk great distances or cross giant rooms. Considering the sluggish pace of the character, it ruins all the exploration. Not to mention when you want to do some backtracking… Closely related to this, vents and narrow paths where an automated long animation takes place are way too much overused. Really, there are TOO many of these that kills the fun for me. 
- Item management is terrible and unbalanced. In the first part of the game you have to constantly drop items or not pick up new ones, because there are not upgrading/selling stations nearby, in a range of 1 h of game. Then in the last part of the game you basically have empty spaces all the time because your storage capacity has doubled and there are selling machines every 10 minutes.
- Checkpoint system could be better. Considering in this game you die A LOT, and that manual save does not exist (see below), they should have chosen better automatic checkpoints here. Some make you repeat tedious narrow paths or vents, slow walking areas or dialogues before facing the enemy that killed you. On the other hand, sometimes the checkpoint is automatically made in situations where you cannot go back and if it happens that you are low on resources (health, ammo), you are screwed because you will die again and again and again, making you load previous save points in order to move forward with the game. 
- Manual saving is misleading and a bad joke: There is what they call a “manual save” option in the menu, but it is only a way of saving manually the last checkpoint, in case you want to return to a previous one. Nothing you have done or collected up to that point since your last automatic checkpoint will be saved. 
- There are too many cheap jump scares throughout the game. At first they were scary, but after your 100th it was boring, predictable and even annoying, because some of them cause you damage without the chance to defend yourself. For instance, there are some chests that you open and a bug comes out of it, attacks you and you get nothing in return (empty chest). There is no way of knowing whether the chest is infected or not, or of avoiding the attack. Same goes for the “launching heads”, there are many cocoons in the game, a few of them have enemies inside that launch at you from great distances, unnoticed and without time to counterattack or dodge. Finally, many parts have some enemies appearing literally from nowhere (not talking about vents) after turning the corner to jump scare you.

I paid loose attention to this game when it had initially come out, and after the lackluster reviews and performance hits I decided to give it a pass. Once Humble Bundle included it in their April choice and with a sale looming to pick up the DLCs for cheap, figured why not actually give it a shot. I’m glad I did. With the game having more time to cook and get fixed (funny how playing a complete product will do that) I had a  blast with very few issues (though one critical issue where all my autosaves were “wiped” and I had to manually recover them).

The game stuns with how beautiful it is, and as someone that loves that dark, grimey aesthetic this game knocks it out of the park. From the destroyed sections of Black Iron, to the biophage spreading like slime mold along the floors and walls terraforming everything to its whims, I was always happy to take a second to look around. 

The gameplay is… rough… to say the least. It did eventually grow on me but that initial bit of trying to figure out how it works was harsh. It’s this weird, overly clunky movement that’s somehow too easy once you figure out how it works. I did enjoy the weight of melee weapons when I upgraded the stunstick to max and started to lean heavily into the G.R.I.P. to throw my enemies around like ragdolls. The gunplay is there, I didn’t particularly care for it and the game seems to rely on it too much with certain enemy types. The light puzzle mechanics throughout the game were enjoyable and I liked how I had to scavenge (and I mean scavenge, choosing how much ammo/health I actually needed and constantly ratting to the store was more fun than I thought it would be) to have enough credits to afford upgrades. A big problem here, and I’m sure everyone has read this were vents. I have never in my life seen a game that takes more time in a vent than in this game. Every section of this game had vents you’d be going through, and these are some long vents. 

The story was enjoyable, nothing “groundbreaking” but it was engaging and fun to playthrough. Not a whole lot to say beyond that, you’ll likely see where it’s going and if you listen to the audio logs that can be found throughout the game, you’ll definitely put it together before any reveal occurs. Now, for something I’ve been holding onto but honestly the worst thing this game has done. The actual ending is hidden by the Last Transmission DLC. Honestly, this is nearly inexcusable to me that they did it, and the only solace I’ll give them is that there's rumor that they intended for sequels to come out that didn’t pan out after the games reception leading to them tying a bow around the story with the DLC. Still, it left a sour taste in my mouth, even if I enjoyed the rest of it.

Overall, I really enjoyed The Callisto Protocol. I don’t see myself replaying it any time soon, and I’m definitely not going to try and 100% it (Full play through on the hardest difficulty with no deaths? No thank you.) but I enjoyed my time in it greatly. Strongly recommend giving it a fair shot, though wait to get it bundled on sale to have access to the actual ending.

The Callisto Protocol is another one of those games that leaves you wishing Steam had a "meh" option between "recommend" and "not recommend." If you manage to pick it up during a steep sale and keep your expectations in check, there’s a chance you might find some enjoyment here. However, it's hard to ignore its glaring flaws.

Combat and Gameplay

The combat feels repetitive, with very little variety in enemy types or encounters. It quickly devolves into a rinse-and-repeat cycle, stripping away the tension and thrill that good horror games thrive on. Asset placement feels overly "video gamey," with items and obstacles often arranged in ways that break immersion.

The biggest letdowns are the jump scares and bosses. The jump scares, while numerous, are entirely predictable and lack creativity. You’ll know exactly when and how they’re coming, making them feel more like a beginner's attempt at horror rather than the work of a professional studio.

The boss battles are even more egregious. The game recycles the same boss fight multiple times, and when a new boss does appear, it isn't an improvement. Instead of being exciting, these encounters feel tedious, and any sense of accomplishment after defeating them is replaced by relief that it’s finally over, easpecially since they continue to borrow from other games notion of "don't let them actually beat the main boss until the end, but let them fight them multiple times, that'll be fun, right?" Adding to this, the motivations of the "antagonist", Farris, lack depth or logic, leaving a narrative void where intrigue should have been.

Story and Atmosphere

The story is disappointingly cliche and predictable, offering little in the way of surprises or meaningful twists. It borrows heavily from older horror games but fails to replicate their charm or suspense.

Despite these shortcomings, the game does shine in some areas. The environment is beautifully rendered, creating a visually stunning world that’s brimming with potential. The sound design is equally impressive, enhancing the atmosphere and making the game’s world feel alive—even if the gameplay doesn’t quite match up.

Conclusion

The Callisto Protocol is a game that struggles to balance its ambition with execution. While its environments and sound design are commendable, the repetitive combat, uninspired jump scares, and lackluster story weigh it down. If you’re a fan of the genre and can snag it on a heavy discount, it might be worth a look. Just don’t go in expecting the next great horror experience. Dont worry though, at only around 10 hours, this corridor isn't that long.
Its biggest flaw? Giving us such an interesting world and failing to utilize it properly.

Verdict: "Meh" (If only Steam allowed it).

Let’s start with the positives.
The atmosphere in The Callisto Protocol is absolutely fantastic — the first half of the game is just amazing. The opening sequence is what really hooked me in and kept me playing it till the end. The game does a great job at building tension, mystery, and intrigue at the start. And I won't say anything about the graphics, it is just incredible.

But then things begin to fall apart.
The biggest issue I encountered was optimization. I played the game after the major patches had already been released, but I still ran into noticeable stuttering in several scenes during the second half of the game. This seems to be a persistent issue, and even players with high-end PCs may not be able to avoid it. So be ready for that.

Another major flaw is the story.
The first part had a ton of potential: beautiful environments, intriguing characters, and hints of deep lore. It really felt like the developers wanted to build a rich, immersive world. Unfortunately, the second half comes off as rushed. There are still some good moments and characters that expand the world, but they’re far fewer than what we get at the beginning.

A strong indicator that the game wasn’t ready at launch is the post-release DLC "Final Transmission." It is the actual ending of the game, and that says a lot about how incomplete the original release was.

I honestly wish Striking Distance Studios had one or two more years to finish and polish the game.

The game needed a more complete ending, stronger antagonists, and a few more interesting side characters. The villains especially felt underdeveloped. After brief interactions at the beginning, they largely disappear from the story until the very end, leaving a massive gap in the middle with little narrative tension. I don't want to spoiler a lot, but I think that we needed a more interesting secondary antagonist that would be like Hans Tiedemann from the Dead Space 2 who was EarthGov's Director of Operations on Titan Station and was trying to somehow save that place with the personal in it. 

As you can see I am also a Dead Space fan (especially Dead Space 2, which I consider the best in the series), and that is why I also want to clarify something important: don’t expect similar gameplay like in the Dead Space. That game is not a Dead Space, they are really different, stop expecting the same experience like from the Dead Space, you will just ruin your experience due to that.

The combat in The Callisto Protocol is heavily melee-focused, with ranged weapons serving more as backup tools. It’s a completely different experience. I liked the concept of prioritizing close combat, but the execution felt lacking. The melee system needed more variety, like combo mechanics, to keep it engaging over time.

So, will the story pull you in?
Probably yes, thanks to the cinematic presentation and strong opening. But I highly recommend playing it on a really good PC and giving yourself time to get used to the combat system — especially if you are a Dead Space fan.

Overall, The Callisto Protocol is a good game and has some standout moments, but the execution and technical issues hold it back. With better pacing, antagonist development, and polish, this could have been something even more unique.

Final score: 7/10.
A solid experience if you manage your expectations.

Maybe it was the bad performance at launch, or maybe it was the over-expectation of people. But for me, I failed to see the mind boggling criticism this game received because it is a decent game. The Callisto Protocol hailed itself as a spiritual successor to Dead Space, and it did well enough in that regard. Here is a linear, immersive experience with an engaging survivalist story - basically a good old-fashioned game where you enjoyed for around 10 hours, then come back for the experience when nostalgia hit after some time has passed.

The gameplay loop is basically Dead Space but heavily focused on melee. Maybe for some people, shooting a gun with different trajectory is less repetitive, but TCP gameplay is as repetitive as any game can get, as it can't be more repetitive than games where criticism have praised to high heaven but had even more repetitive gameplay loop.

This game biggest fault would be its checkpoint system, it would often put you back to a long cutscene, or where you had to spend a lot of time thinking on what to upgrade. And not long after said checkpoint, you ended up picking loots that could have spawn earlier before the checkpoint so you could manage your inventory better. And level design is nowhere as sophisticated as Dead Space, it is more linear and you would spend most time sticking to a straight corridor. These are the only criticism I have for this game. 

It's sad to see how TCP could have done well as a horror franchise and a sequel with many improvements. But with its troubled development, the crazy budget it needed and the hyperbolic criticism it received, this game will be a one timed experience. And the circle of the gaming industry cater to people who prefer loot box multiplayer and short attention span experience coils again.

A 2025 REVIEW 

I didn't play this on launch but I have heard it was rough - unsurprising knowing the brass at Krafton and the state of the industry as a whole. 

However, I bought this on sale, because I was craving more Dead Space - and that is more or less what I got. Didn't pay much attention to marketing or post-launch press, just bought it because it was cheap. And I had a pretty good time, and would like to share this positive sentiment for others to see. 

It's not a full on clone of Dead Space, but it keeps the most important parts of DS alive - the vibes, and weighty combat. I'm not a massive fan of the melee focus, but its serviceable enough. TCP even seems to forget that it's meant to be a melee game with the way that guns are provided, ammo supplied, and the enemy composition encourages gun use. If you're not hot on the melee, guns are viable permanently after the 5h mark - which is roughly half of the campaign. you can play the way you want for more than half of the game which I appreciated. 

The presentation and worldbuilding are absolutely stellar, it's a crying shame this game flopped and left the public sour, because a sequel could and would correct many of the issues that elevate this from a 6/7 out of 10 to an 8/9. 

I do like the more cinematic approach to survival horror/SH-like games, it feels intimate and appropriate for the story attempting to be told. Unfortunately it does mean QTEs, but they're not as egregious in TCP as they were in other AAA games from 2010-2015. 

Overall, since the Dead Space 1 reboot exists, this is definitely a second rate product in comparison. But I believe it is good, and I couldn't recommend it enough at the price I paid for it - if you see this game at the price of $30 or less it's worth every penny. I hope the more recent critical praise around the internet grants this game "cult classic" status and they get Glen & Co back to make TCP2. I'll probably buy the expansion when it goes on sale, will update this review after I play that. But I expect more good things.

The Callisto Protocol is to Dead Space like Dark Souls is to Sekiro. 
If you've stepped in to The Callisto Protocol expecting a Dead Space successor, you're clearly mistaken. Yes, the game was created by the same head developer, and the game shows clear signs of inspiration from the Dead Space series. Gameplay-wise, it's gone from a dismemberment-focused shooter, to a bash-em-up melee, and this direction has clearly divided many of the Dead Space fans that the game was advertised to, but for those who welcome the new direction, will surely enjoy it.
When the game works, it works, graphics are stunning and sound design is excellent, with the dodge-and-smash gameplay mechanic being fun as hell, when it works...
The development team tried too hard to keep the game far from being a Dead Space 4, and the game was rushed to meet deadlines, and the game shows that, with heavy stuttering despite pre-loading shaders and inconsistent story-pacing, with the ending left as DLC.
At launch, this game was objectively unplayable, but with years of constant fixes, it's much more stable in comparison and is very enjoyable, and can now be recommended for others. 
All that being said, please buy the Deluxe Edition on sale ($17.54 AUD at time of review) should you decide to purchase the game. It's moronic to keep the base game at $87.95 AUD with cosmetics and extra story content locked behind a season pass for $43.95 AUD.

The combat in itself is fine, though so far it doesn't feel as stressful and intense as it does in Dead Space. 

Combat also tend to take place along walls and in corners of rooms because of the dodge moves and how you get locked in front of enemies when you swing the melee weapon.

When you fight more than one enemy only one of the enemies will focus on you, the rest will stand and wait for their turn (which is the reason why the combats feels way less stressful and intense than in Dead Space) though enemies that can spit on you will still do so while you fight another enemy.


The doors that Jakob has to open manually feels really unnecessary. First you have to press "e" to grab the door, then you have to press "e" to start opening the door, lastly you have to mash "e" while he is opening the door... Pressing "e" once before having to mash "e" would have been fine.

This game relies [b]HEAVILY[/b] on jumpscares. Every single attempt at making the player feel fear is through some kind of cheap jumpscare attempt. 
I am not someone that plays horror or survival horror games, I do not enjoy them and I do not enjoy feeling fear or terror. I avoid them like a plague.

Thankfully (and also unfortunately), this game does not do any of that.

There is nothing frightening or "scary" about this game. There is no terror. 
Every jumpscare is extremely predictable, so they rarely work, if ever. 
Later on in the game it becomes "roll your eyes" laughable even.

I think one big reason why this game also struggles to make the player feel any kind of fear, is that the player is WAY too powerful. Yes, you can run out of ammo, and ammo isn't always abundant, but the melee combat system, while innovative, is also so simplistic that it rarely matters. 

The player is also always aware where enemies will come from or when a fight will take place, as there are environmental objects like conveniently placed spike walls, explosives, grates on the floor, or air vents that always signal this. 

Upgrading your weapons is a chore as credits (in game currency) are difficult to come by. You are guaranteed to not upgrade all weapons or items on your first playthrough. 

Visually the game looks great, but suffers from some performance issues at times. 

Audio and sound design are good. 

Voice acting is good.

Combat is okay. I enjoyed it for the most part, despite how divisive of a topic it is, but it can quickly become repetitive. 

Story is nothing to write home about either. There was great potential in terms of the futuristic setting and politics involving bioweapons and the future of humankind in space, but the game never really dives deeper into it beyond a surface level presentation. 

Everything that happens in the story is also very cliche and predictable. 

Character development of our main protagonist, Jacob, is also pretty mediocre. 

That's a lot of negatives, so why would I still recommend this game? 

It's not a [i] bad [/i] game. It's just okay or "meh". That, and Steam does not allow a "maybe" or "indifferent" vote.  Also, i'm quite convinced this game took an even more major hit in reputation and negativity by trying to "piggy back" or build hype off of the Dead Space name (and ultimately failing to meet those expectations). 

I however, have not played dead space, so I am able to remain completely neutral in that regard.

Dead Space for modern audiences.
It's alright, just manage your expectations: this isn't a game for players, it's a product for investors. It ticks the boxes but it doesn't innovate or respect you.

[hr][/hr]
Good bits:

- Lots of accessibility options: dyslexic font, color-coding for game items (enemies, hazards, etc.), subtitles font settings (size, color, background). Although, font settings apply only to subtitles, and not to other text such as item descriptions in the store which are barely readable.

- Interesting combat system: evading and chaining different melee and ranged attacks. But it gets really boring really fast, I started the game at medium difficulty and quickly dropped to low because having to hit each and every enemy a dozen or two times for them to go down is not that fun.

- Skippable cutscenes.

[hr][/hr]
Bad bits, in no particular order:

- Unskippable intro logos. Fortunately the movie files can be deleted or renamed.

- Stupid save system: there are auto-saves at plot checkpoints, and there are manual saves anywhere, except they also save only the checkpoints. And as far as I can tell, any checkpoint is saved only once, so if you stumble into an auto-save but then backtrack to pickup any leftover items - the only way to save that backtracking is to progress further to next checkpoint.

- Can't use GRP (kinesis) to pick up items like ammo and health.

- Enemies don't drop loot if killed with with certain types of environmental hazards like huge fans or other chopping/grinding things.

- Gamepad controls are not editable, and the default scheme is... suboptimal. Some buttons (d-pad) bind to several actions, while others (L3/R3) are completely unused.

- Ranged weapons are boring. There are 5 types, and they basically differ only in clip size and fire rate. Maybe in damage too but that's not noticeable. In general, they all shoot bullets in one way or another and they all have different ammo types so you have to carry every type separately, but they take extra time and attention to swap between them and keep them all reloaded.

- The "alt-fire" mode is pointless because it spends N times more ammo for N times more damage so it's not in fact an upgrade.

- Selling or otherwise handling items in the store requires long-press (which is good) but buying weapon upgrades is instant so if you accidentally click on wrong thing, you will spend a potentially sizable chunk of your cash on an upgrade that you might not have wanted.

- "Blind" enemies are a joke. You can cram a dozen of them into a room, and stealth-kill ALL of them. None of them will aggro as long as you do not exit crouching state and do not move closer to any of them than certain threshold, even though "stealth kill" itself is accompanied by a hefty amount of screaming and panting. However once they do get aggroed, they will chase you to the end of the [strike]Earth[/strike] Callisto even if you run away and try to hide.

- Closer to the end of the game they trick player by putting a puny enemy (a parasite larvae, found throughout the game) into a box that typically contains valuable loot. I guess the intent was to increase the suspense by breaking player's trust in loot containers, except they did it to three containers in a row, which completely defeats the purpose. Already after the 2nd container I couldn't care less if another slimy thing will jump on me or not, and the 3rd one drove the final nail in the coffin of horror and atmosphere.

- Final boss is impressive visually but poorly executed mechanically. He's invulnerable to bullets when he's in his first, weaker, human form. I unloaded all ammo from half the weapons in his face and the scene didn't change. The way to progress is to smack him a couple times with melee weapon. The logic left the room...

- Characters are pathetic. Kudos to the actors, they did their part well, but the writing is utterly flat. Saying farewell to Lucatiel of Mirrah was moving, watching Elias die was not. And they have roughly the same amount of interaction with their respective protagonists!

- For half of its duration, the game takes away your ability to run. Sometimes the plot "requires" that you walk and talk alongside another character, even though there's loot to gather on the other side of the (sometimes pretty big) room. Other times the main character just randomly slows to a walk. I guess it might have something to do with the terrain but if so then it's extremely unintuitive and inconsistent. Dead Space had a distinct sound and walking animation for "sticky" floor, this game does not. A game is supposed to be an interactive media; I, the player, am supposed to be in control of my actions; limiting that at random for no reason is [b]INFURIATING[/b].

This review WILL contain some Spoilers to story and gameplay!
I don't write a review often, but for this it doesn't deserve the hate it gets.
For my part i sadly (Or probably luckily) got finally around to play it over 1 1/2 years after release so most on launch bugs and crashes most likely have been fixed (I didn't have a single crash in my 13,2 hours of game time.)

Let's start with the negatives.
Combat: Combat is.. very simple and I found a cheese very early on in the game if you continuously press A and D while meeleing you dodge pretty much every attack. I very often looked at my second monitor and reading or watching videos on the side while I just kept fighting against multiple enemies.
Enemies: There isn't a big variety of enemies. Overall there are like 5 different types of enemies (I count the "fat" and blind ones to the nomral ones). Which is fine but I believe the game would have benefitted from some more one off big monsters that you might not be able to really fight, the 2 Heads are put as a miniboss in too many stages of the game imo and after the first 2 times they were more annoying then adding to the game.

Now to the positives.
Story: It is a great story. All the elements for a "Stranded survival" experience are there. Isolated on a dying station. No way to get help other then helping yourself. A very interesting plot with backstories to how the place came to be and an ending that leaves many questions behind that need an explanation in the future projects!
Graphics and Perfomance: Game is running very stable on my PC (I5 Processor, 16Gbyte RAM and a 3060TI), graphics are very beautiful. A lot of gore and scenes that straight up reminded me of Dead Space (Which is a huge compliment imo). 
Weapons and Creativitiy: I really like the weapons, there aren't a lot but they show some creativity in design (Still simple tho) and I thought the "frame" for every weapon to then switch out the top part was fun. I sadly couldn't figure out the point of the tactical pistol until the end haha. The Alt fire modes are pretty fun.
Overal atmosphere: Game captured the atmosphere of what it wants to be very well. A stranded experienced no help from authorities, isolated with some very strong minded NPCs in the game.


Overall opinion:
Is it a masterpiece? Far from it. Is it a bad game? Not at all. 
It is a very solid start from what could turn into a really cool universe with a cult that controls government bodies that want's to bring Humanity to the next stage of evolution by any means necessary. A resistance group that wants to stop them. It is a great concept with A LOT of potential and I hope we can see more in this universe to build on top of this!

The Callisto Protocol sets its sights high, aiming to resurrect the spirit of classic survival horror with a modern cinematic polish. Developed by Striking Distance Studios and helmed by Glen Schofield (Dead Space co-creator), the game promises a spiritual successor to that franchise’s blend of body horror and claustrophobic terror. And while it delivers in atmosphere and presentation, it stumbles in some critical areas of gameplay and pacing.

Visually, The Callisto Protocol is a stunner. The game’s depiction of Black Iron Prison—a facility on Jupiter’s moon Callisto—is oppressive, grimy, and absolutely dripping with dread. Dynamic lighting and environmental detail are meticulously crafted. Flickering lights, claustrophobic hallways, and grotesque mutations lurking in the dark give the game a chilling cinematic quality. It’s one of the most visually polished horror titles in recent memory.


Gameplay and Combat is where things get more divisive. The Callisto Protocol leans heavily into melee combat, with a dodge-based system that’s both innovative and, at times, frustrating. The close-quarters brawling can feel satisfying when it works, but often becomes repetitive and punishing, especially as enemy encounters escalate without enough evolution in tactics or tools. The camera can be an issue in tight spaces, making some fights feel more clunky than terrifying.

Gunplay, while serviceable, takes a backseat to melee—sometimes to the detriment of pacing and strategy. The GRP (gravity weapon) is a standout, allowing players to hurl enemies into environmental hazards, and it provides some needed variety.

You play as Jacob Lee, a cargo pilot unwittingly caught in the middle of a horrifying outbreak. The story leans into mystery and slow reveals, though the narrative beats are often familiar for fans of the genre. Josh Duhamel and Karen Fukuhara provide solid performances, lending some emotional weight to what is otherwise a fairly straightforward sci-fi horror tale.

Unfortunately, character development feels shallow. The game introduces big ideas—corporate exploitation, bioengineering, and prison ethics—but doesn’t explore them deeply. What’s here is more about mood and survival than moral complexity.

What The Callisto Protocol does incredibly well is terror. Its sound design is masterful: distant groans, sudden shrieks, and the ever-present hum of machinery build a soundscape that constantly keeps you on edge. Jump scares are frequent, but they’re earned thanks to the oppressive tension and superb audio cues.

At launch, the game suffered from performance issues, especially on PC. Patches have since addressed many of these, but some technical hiccups may remain depending on your platform. On current-gen consoles, the game runs smoothly and looks phenomenal.

The Callisto Protocol is a gorgeous, gruesome, and atmospheric ride that succeeds in evoking dread and awe. Its visuals and sound design are among the best in the genre, but repetitive combat and underwhelming story elements prevent it from reaching the heights of its spiritual predecessor. It’s a solid entry for horror fans craving a dark, immersive experience—just be prepared for some rough edges.

For a $50 game including the Final Transmission dlc which is basically mandatory to complete the story, I have mixed feelings about it. It does some things quite well, but fails miserably in others. Let me break it down, in no particular order.

Story: It's okay - not too bad, but not very good either, especially with the way it ended; (spoiler alert) [spoiler] it effectively killed any chances of a sequel by killing off the main character [/spoiler]. There were a few moments that felt odd, but for the most part it at least felt cohesive and conclusive, and there were a few surprises. It is quite short though, and my biggest grievance is that you need the dlc to finish the main story. There's a lot of wasted potential for a rich world building.

Music/Sound: Actually pretty good, one of the strengths of the game. Though once again, the short length of the game means that there just isn't a lot of it. 

Voice acting and cinematics: Amazing. Easily the strongest part of the game. Character models are extremely high quality, with great voice acting and mo-cap likeness by actual actors, especially Karl Urban. I feel like he carried the game really hard.

Horror: It's okay; there are a couple of really good moments, but for the most part you're just bulldozing your way through hordes of enemies. Player character movement is sluggish on purpose, which is acceptable in these type of games, but I don't think they managed to take full advantage of it. There is some predictability with the horror, mostly because the game tends to shift from gameplay to cutscene so you know something's about to happen. Not a big deal, but I do think if the horror scenes were more dynamic (mid-gameplay) it would've elevated the scare factor of the game. 

Gameplay: The weakest part of the game. I could see where they were going with the heavy focus on the melee combat, but it felt very undercooked. In fact, undercooked is a very accurate term to describe the entire gameplay experience; you're mostly just walking and collecting stuff, with the occasional shooting/hacking at zombies and even rarely so, stealth. Enemy variety is quite low and there aren't a lot of bosses. There's little to no puzzles, and player actions are heavily scripted so you often feel like you're not really doing much. Weapon variety is okay, but upgrades don't feel as substantial as they should because of how shallow the combat mechanics are.

Graphics: Very, very good. The environments are highly detailed and enemies are well designed. There is something left to be desired with the UI and especially tutorials, but I'd be nitpicking at that point.  

Performance: Excellent. Not that the game would run on a potato, but it does run quite well (1080p Medium 50-60 fps) even on 8 year old mid-range hardware like the RX 580 8GB. I mostly played on my RX 6800 machine, and with everything set to the max (RT off) at 1440p I got a very smooth 90-100 fps experience. Beware about enabling RT, it causes a lot of stutters and isn't really that transformative in terms of visuals, so the massive performance drop isn't really justified whether you use Nvidia or AMD.

Finally, there is a severe issue with the game crashing your whole PC. You read that right, the whole PC. I've had it crash on me so many times that I've lost count, and there doesn't seem to be any trigger for it - it just happens whenever, wherever, and quite frequently at that. I thought something was wrong with my machine because I've never encountered a game that crashed my main rig (5800X3D + RX 6800), but after checking on my other two machines (3400G + RX 580 and a 4700U laptop) I got the exact same behavior. Admittedly I only have all-AMD machines at hand, so I cannot verify if this is or isn't an AMD-specific issue, but going through some of the forum posts it does seem the issue exists on Nvidia too. I just don't know, and I gave up trying to troubleshoot. It was a frustrating experience, and I don't think I'll be returning for achievement hunting unless the devs fix it. 

Overall, not really worth the total $50 price tag. I got the Deluxe Edition for just $10 which includes the dlc, so I can somewhat recommend the game on a sale....as long as you can deal with the crashing.

If you are old enough to have played Dead Space 1 when it was released in 2008, you'd distinctly remember how your mind was blown when the atmosphere was sucked out of a room and all sound went with it. Only the muffled vibrations reaching the spacesuit through physical contact were audible. It was eerie and claustrophobic, heightening that sense of being alone in the vacuum of a derelict spaceship. All UI was diegetic - meaning all UI existed in the game world. Planets were mostly fictional and large enough to believably produce a gravity similar to Earth's and so, all locomotion was normal. In other words, what science there was in the science-fiction of Dead Space felt grounded by design. And then there's The Callisto Protocol. 

Callisto, the second largest real moon of Jupiter, only has 12.5% of Earth's gravity. (For context, our Moon has 16.5%). This means that if you walk on Callisto, you would be leaping large distances like the Hulk or John Carter. Callisto has a negligible atmosphere whose pressure is 0.00000075 Pa while Earth's atmosphere exerts 101325 Pa of pressure on the body. One would spontaneously explode without a spacesuit on the surface of Callisto.

Callisto Protocol is a video game in which all this is summarily dismissed. Why Callisto Protocol failed to incorporate at least some science while blatantly attempting a rote copy of Dead Space is puzzling. And this is just one example. Callisto Protocol successfully copies the superficial bits from Dead Space, even adds its own flourishes, but ignores the deep pillars that make Dead Space the masterpiece that it was.

Here's another pillar that was ignored - mystery. In Dead Space, the thing that turns dead bodies into necromorphs is a giant alien monolith called the Marker. Nobody knows who made the Marker, or what the writings on it say, or how it makes people go insane just by being near them. But some people believe it is humanity's destiny to be turned into necromorphs by the Marker, a process they call Unification. They form a religion called Unitology whose goals are to find new Markers to enable this Unification. (Altman be praised!)

Callisto throws out all attempts at mystery and subtext for yet another virus/bacteria, the biophage, that turns humans into zombies. Very boring! [spoiler]That it is an alien virus first found deep under Callisto does not really change anything. In place of a believably wacko religion, there is an Illuminati-like group who release the biophage in the Callisto prison just to see if something useful emerges out of the shit show that can be used to modify humans for deep space travel. That's the protocol in Callisto Protocol. "And what about you, huh? Watching people die for fun? Is that your 'Protocol'?" is a line the player character says to the main baddie.[/spoiler] But, to be fair, there was a strong sense of mystery to the plot until these deflating details were uncovered near the end.

There are some good things about Callisto Protocol too. The melee combat was not half-bad, especially on Hardcore difficulty. Sure, you can dodge easily, and you can keep dodging easily indefinitely but I didn't do that because I wanted to get on with it. 

The stealth sections were lip-biting good. The environments, guns, and enemies were sufficiently varied. Throwing enemies with the GRP (kinesis module) into spikes, grinders, and fans never got old. The surface of Callisto and the subterranean, decrepit colony of the first settlers were spectacularly rendered and memorable. Although severely linear for most of the playtime, there were occasional branching paths that rewarded mild exploration. Overall, just playing the game was not as bad as most reviews made it out to be. However, it only got really interesting to play after exactly halfway through the game when some new environments, weapons, upgrades, and enemies were introduced and some actual plot development showed up. Pacing was not Callisto Protocol's strong suit.

The most terrible thing in Callisto Protocol is the four encounters with the same "two-head" mini-boss in the last three chapters of the game. In some of these fights, if you don't have enough ammo, you must reload an old save and stock up. It is a really bad design and stuck out like a sore thumb even amidst the other flaws in this game.

One very strange thing about the level layouts was that I always felt as though I was travelling down, never up. I couldn't count the number of times the elevators broke down or I fell into a pit and ended up far below the surface. And yet, there was not enough travelling up to compensate. It left me feeling the game world was not correctly architected.

All of this is to say that The Callisto Protocol is a poor man's Dead Space. If you read this review and know what you are getting into, get it on discount, and enjoy a romp on Callisto. Just don't squint at the details and do not play the DLC.

The Callisto Protocol — A Beautiful Horror That Fell Short of Its Promise

Having completed The Callisto Protocol, one can’t help but wonder: why didn’t this game win over the hearts of a wider audience? It certainly boasts stunning visuals and high-quality sound design. As a horror experience, it successfully builds a chilling atmosphere, embracing the essential elements of the genre. And yet, something fundamental seems to be missing.

The root issue appears to be the game’s overall lack of polish and consistency. While certain aspects meet the standards of a AAA title, others feel rushed, generic, or uninspired.

Narrative Shortcomings

The story is one of the weakest links. While serviceable, it feels derivative, especially within the sci-fi horror subgenre. The plot develops in predictable ways that genre veterans will see coming from a distance. The game misses an opportunity to either deliver shocking narrative twists or build emotional depth that would allow players to truly connect with the protagonist. As a result, the storyline feels flat, and the emotional investment simply doesn’t materialize.
Limited Exploration and Interactivity

A hallmark of high-quality games is offering the player multiple paths to enjoy the experience. Whether one prefers fast-paced action or slow-paced exploration, great games reward both. Unfortunately, The Callisto Protocol provides little incentive to deviate from the main path. Exploration feels unrewarding, with very few secrets, surprises, or meaningful world-building elements to discover.

Combat and Gameplay Depth

Combat is initially intense but quickly becomes repetitive. Weapon acquisition is too straightforward — items are simply handed out along the main storyline rather than earned through effort, boss fights, or side quests. The thrill of unlocking powerful gear is absent.

Enemy variety is also lacking. Most encounters boil down to simple shoot-or-bash mechanics, with only one enemy type that invites stealth gameplay. While the game features a telekinesis mechanic, allowing you to throw objects (or enemies) into environmental hazards, it never evolves beyond a gimmick. Additionally, the near-total absence of mini-bosses is a missed opportunity to break up the pacing and introduce tactical variety.

A Rushed Launch and Lost Potential

What’s most frustrating is the sense that The Callisto Protocol could have been so much more — if only it had been given more time in development. There’s a strong impression that the developers envisioned a long-term plan supported by post-launch content and community growth. However, the rocky launch, paired with underwhelming critical reception, likely derailed those ambitions.

Post-launch DLC may have expanded the content, but by then, the damage was done. Players rarely return to games that fail to grip them on the first try.
Technical Problems on PC

The situation was made worse by the troubled PC release, which suffered from serious optimization issues. Clearly developed with modern consoles in mind, the PC port did not receive the technical attention it needed. In today’s gaming environment, a broken PC launch can tank a title’s reputation overnight — and no amount of patching in the days that follow can fully undo the harm.

Conclusion: A Tragic Misfire with Unrealized Ambitions

The Callisto Protocol had the makings of a great game — atmospheric design, strong audio-visual fidelity, and solid horror roots. But its unimaginative storytelling, shallow gameplay, and rushed development cycle prevented it from reaching its full potential. It’s a shame, really. With a bit more time and focus, The Callisto Protocol might have earned itself a much better future.

Initially, at this games announcement I was very excited for the Callisto Protocol. I was a huge fan of the original Dead Space games (even 3) and wanted nothing more than a bunch of the original devs to make an amazing game, beat the Dead Space remake, and stick it to EA for closing down Visceral Games. And then the game launched showing me wave after wave of negative reviews which cited a glitchy and buggy mess. So, I did the only thing I could and that was wait it out. And, after 3 years, I returned to this game and started to see a small buzz of positive reviews. Thus, when I saw it on sale for $11.99, DLC included, I went ahead and got the game. I then spent the next couple of weeks really hammering away at this game and my experience was interesting to say the least. So, after all the patchwork did the game live up to my expectations?

First off this game is exceptionally gorgeous to look at. Every corridor, the surface of Callisto, shading, lighting, and characters designs were top notch. The voice acting in the game was also exceptional and in some ways I almost wished we had gotten a movie instead. Especially after the live action trailer. And, I will say the game is really nice at the start. Movement was fluid and the controls were intuitive. I found myself quickly sucked into the mystery of the prison and the Biophages, even though I was pretty confident where it was going of which I was right.

However, as the game continued I found my enjoyment kind of waning and then for a good stretch I was playing it just to play it. The middle of the game in particular could have used some more story beats to keep my interest piqued but instead I went into auto pilot mode. In a way it felt like the game was padding itself out otherwise it could have been over in about 6-7 hours. It wasn't until the near end of the game where the story really kicked back in and my interest once again in full force. So, I was satisfied at the start and the end with the middle going up and down but being mostly forgettable.

The game play itself left a lot to be desired as I was expecting a bit more variety. With a good chunk of original Dead Space team I was hoping this game, as a spiritual successor, was going to innovate on the concepts of those three games but instead just recycles them but in a slightly worse way. One thing I loved about Dead Space were the variety of ways to dispatch Necromorphs by cycling through weapons that were sometimes better suited for certain enemies.  In this game the melee mechanic is supposed to be the main mode of battle and, outside of some boss battles, you can dispatch most enemies in the exact same way. The death animations were cool though, almost like Mortal Kombat fatalities. However, I always found I had lots of ammo because I almost never utilized my guns because I never needed to. Dodging is so easy you're going to be successful 90% of the time. I also rarely used the glove because again I was able to just whack most everything with my baton even though the game was begging me to throw enemies at spikes on the walls or other hazards.

The DLC for this game was a little up and down. You get some skins, new games modes, and of course the Final Transmission which is the true final chapter. In regard to that I had to marinate on it because the ending I did not see coming. Which I honestly enjoyed that aspect because in terms of writing it's probably the strongest piece overall. I've seen the conclusion being divisive but honestly I give props to the developers for such a ballsy ending. Not every game needs a happy ending and in that regard I will always remember it. The game also offers a New Game+ mode and I'm always down for keeping upgrades thus I would definitely give it another playthrough to finish upgrading my weapons.

At the end though do I recommend this game? Yes. The major bugs have been fixed and I had a smooth game experience on the Steam Deck. It's also wildly gorgeous to look at along with great voice acting and excellent motion capture. I'm also a sucker for sci-fi horror and I'd be lying if I didn't say I found a level of satisfaction in the game in the same way a low budget B-movie does. Ultimately I wouldn't call this a bad game but I do think it's going to be a matter of personal taste. For those that absolutely love Dead Space there is some enjoyment here with a 2nd act that drags but finishes pretty strong I thought. I will say that I don't think it's worth it at full price but for a good sale I'd say it's decent.

The Callisto Protocol is a game about a man who befriends cute Japanese waifu and they embark together on a journey of self-discovery. At least that's what I gathered from it. The plot really isn't that important anyway, to be honest. The game's a mood piece where the plot is wallpaper and you're supposed to immerse yourself in the horror atmosphere and the environmental storytelling, more so than experiencing a compelling story. What helps to sell it though, is almost Naughty Dog level of cinematic direction, the performance capture, and the inclusion of kino actors. What disappoints is a very limited amount of backstory for this setting and lack of sufficient explanation behind some of the key plot twists.

The game didn't blow my balls off but it was pretty solid. I find that most people simply do not understand what the word "janky" means when describing the combat. A more fitting word here would be "shallow" because by itself, the melee combat requires practically zero skill. The enemies telegraph their attacks from orbit, the timing window for dodging is wider than an interstate, and it's far too easy to dispatch even the toughest enemies, provided that you don't mess it up due to panic or just general lack of elite gamer dexterity (like mine). The real challenge of this game lies in crowd control. It's not impossible to fight more than one enemy, using medkits isn't broken, and you get no invincibility frames for a reason. You just need to understand that this isn't Dead Space, and the method to handling the combat is very different. 

And sure, all of these design choices may send you on a fast lane towards rage town but none of them are janky. Just deliberate. Which seems to be the entire ethos this game's built upon. Right down to your character movements requiring realistic momentum to wind up and wind down, or feeling the pull of inertia with every turn. Every movement in this game has weight. None of it is "janky" either, at least not in my experience. The animations were smooth, the weapons made contact where they should, and none of the physics or camera work ever spazzed out on me. In fact, from a purely technical standpoint - the visuals, the quality of animations, the sound - it is spectacular, and unlike anything I've seen before or since. Every game you've ever played inevitably ends up looking like a video game once you start pushing buttons, but The Callisto Protocol might be the closest we've ever gotten to a video game that not only looks like a bleeding edge CGI movie in cutscenes, but also animates like one in gameplay... mostly. So it's no wonder that the combat would follow that philosophy, and feel a bit sluggish and messy, but weighty and deliberate. That sense of physicality defines the whole game, like it was built around the idea of controlling a real, fragile person in a tactile environment, rather than serving you another power fantasy.

Going into this expecting Dead Space is just setting yourself up for disappointment, because while the game does share a lot of Dead Space's DNA in its presentation and storytelling, gameplay wise it's a completely different beast. It's not by any means bad, but you can easily see how, ironically, the strict adherence to photo-realism holds the game back from being more immersive for the player. The game is a fantastic audio and visual spectacle and when I was focused on exploration and atmosphere, it was amazing. But every time I got into combat or wandered off into an obvious side corridor with some extra loot, I never stopped thinking how great it would be if there was more depth to all of it. That the exploration would work so much better with just a few extra corridors to sidestep into, or how combat would be so much better if the dodge timing windows were tightened and melee expanded with more combos or special moves. It doesn't make the current experience terrible, and I'm sure there are many people who will have a blast with this game. But to me, a horror game where combat is almost trivial and feels very repetitive, kinda deflates the tension that the atmosphere and presentation are setting you up for.

But maybe I'm just being too harsh because, at the end of the day, I had a great time playing this one. It was actually a very welcome throwback to the PS3/X360 era of gaming, where the story mode was straightforward, didn't drag on longer than necessary, and provided an experience with some risky but unique gameplay gimmicks that helped it stand out from the competition. And in today's gaming market, which is overcrowded with homogeneous open world games plagued by never-ending content bloat, something like The Callisto Protocol sticks out even more and is a welcome change of pace. It's not really a horror masterpiece, but it's one of the very few games in the triple-A space today that were bold enough to try some new ideas, even if they landed a bit awkwardly.

Overall, a highly underrated title that truly deserves a second look – especially for fans of sci-fi horror games in general.

🔰SHREDVIEW🔰 - From someone who actually plays and finishes the games before reviewing.

NOTE: If you like my work, please check out the rest of my reviews, I put a lot of work in these to offer the best overall description of what you’re up against. Thank you in advance!

🔷 ABOUT THE GAME & LORE 🔷

Let’s start up with some facts: You cannot spell Callisto Protocol without Dead Space. The game director is the same Glen A. Schofield which brought some former team members to help turn this game into what it is. As history tells, the idea of Dead Space 4 was pitched and refused by EA. After Visceral's studio closing in 2017, these guys were free to use their creative abilities somewhere else and this is it. Simple as that. 

Now Callisto Protocol is a... you guessed it, third person sci-fi and horror action game set in the future of mankind, year 2320. Our protagonist, Jacob Lee, crash lands on Callisto, the moon of Jupiter which holds a prison for very dangerous inmates. Now Jacob, concussed and looking like Mike Tyson’s punchbag, gets immediately thrown into the Black Iron prison, what a day. Predictably, a violent outbreak occurs and turns everyone to downright disgusting and violent f***g mutants. The main d**khead, Warden Duncan has built his prison on top of an ancient site tied to this virus and secretly plans to advance mankind with it. Your mission is to stop him and the virus from spreading further in the solar system. Sounds familiar? 

🔷 THE GAMEPLAY 🔷

👉 GENERAL:
So this game is linear, focused, and claustrophobic to put it short. Exactly what you want from a space horror. Every corridor, vent and flickering light is a setup that can make you soak your chair. It’s polished, cinematic, quite challenging and very f***g disgusting. Here’s the breakdown:  

   •	The game is story-driven. It walks you through chapters and levels with lore encounters happening constantly along the way. The cast is small but very well designed and the characters interact realistically. It does a great job of capturing emotion and racking up the vigilance in the players. The story itself isn’t the greatest. In fact, it’s quite predictable and derivative, it doesn’t relate to “Dead Space” in any meaningful way, however. There’s no connection to that game’s entities, monoliths, or characters, beyond the similarity of a virus creating sickening f****g mutants in space, spreading from a fleet to an extent that isn’t yet clear.

NOTE: The final transmission paid DLC will expand on the story and ending, however, quite disappointing.  

    •	Combat is simple and focused. You can block, dodge, retaliate, shoot, grab, throw with the glove, and use environmental traps to your advantage. Nothing surprising if you played “Dead Space” The key is learning attack patterns and mastering dodges and melee timing. Ammo is precious, and the achievement hunt will push you through multiple playthroughs on higher difficulties.

   •	Limited but very useful arsenal, the right choices for your preference. Two guns at a time, each built to sever limbs, crack mutant skulls and even wipe mechanized units. You unlock weapon schematics as you go, then print them at the 3D printer. Heads up: some schematics are missable if you don’t find them. They can show up again in later chapters, but still in missable spots. Check every corner and make sure you grab these.

   •	Remember the kinesis and stasis from “Dead Space”? You get about half of that here. The GRP (Gravity Restraint Protector) is a kinetic glove that lets you lift, hold, and throw items or enemies, usually into spike walls to thin crowds fast. You can grab one target at a time, but the animation is quick enough to chain multiple throws. Can’t grab heavies!

    •	The Inventory space is fairly small. You start with six slots and reach twelve around the middle of the campaign, so you have to be strategic about what you carry, what you sell, and what you leave behind.

👉 NAVIGATION SYSTEM:
As expected, not open world nor does it had to be. It’s linear corridor-based design with semi-open arensa. You push fight to fight, with short detours for cash, collectibles, and upgrades. Old-school, zero bloat, pure panic and carnage. Watch the environment. No quest tab, no arrow, the dialogue is your guide. Miss it and you will wander.

👉 PHYSICS & MECHANICS:
Weighty combat, sharp physics, clean ragdolls. The GRP gives short bursts of control while environmental kills reward smart play. Enemy animations are deliberate, not spongy and the GRP lets you control the crowds when swarmed. 
The 3D Printer replaces the old bench and kiosk. Print upgrades, print ammo, sell extras for credits. Inventory is tight, six slots early and twelve by mid-game, so manage every pickup. Polished movement, deliberate enemies, and satisfying finishers.

👉  GRAPHICS & OPTIMIZATION:
The atmosphere and eeriness is what compliments the storyline along with the graphic engine and design used. The game is a graphical powerhouse and it may require some resources in order to perform optimally, however, everything is pieced up together to cause panic The overall visual is bloody, gory and somewhat disgusting without a setting to decrease or amortize the creep factor. Basically, if you's a b**ch then go play Yooka Laylee.

👉  ACHIEVEMENTS & COLLECTIBLES:
Achievements swing from constipation to diarrhea. You’re staring down five full runs: Campaign, NG+, Hardcore, Hardcore+, then Riot Mode and Contagion Mode, but guess what?! Both are paid DLC. You cannot 100% without paying up. Riot mode list is doable except surviving 50 waves which may prove the real choke point. Advice: Grind Riot Mode first and then Hardcore/Contagion turn into a walk in the park since you will learn not to depend on ammo as much as well as master dodging and not taking damage. Overall, everything is do-able but this crap will be very time consuming. It's very obnoxious to have to play the game 4 times in a row then pay for the 5th, like, who the fk comes up with this s**t?! 

🔷  CONCLUSION  🔷

An intense corridor fright-train. Predictable in places, derivative on purpose in others but it lands the mood. The gore, and the set-piece have impact on the experience. Linear navigation and a lean arsenal keep the focus on melee/dodge reads and improvisations. This is the best homage paid to Dead Space ever. If you’re chasing 100%, first, do 100 d**k push ups as preparation.

🔷  PROS & CONS 🔷

✔️ PROS:
-	Brutal, weighty combat.
-	Atmosphere is elite. Terrifying at times.
-	Tight, chapter-driven pacing with cinematic set pieces.
-	Small but meaningful arsenal; upgrades actually matter.
-	The best homage to Dead Space.
-       Great performance. 

❌ CONS:
-	Story is predictable/derivative.
-	Small inventory, constant tetris. 
-	100% requires five f****g playthroughs.
-	Achievements tied to paid DLC.
-	No direction indication. Easy to get lost.

I recommend to buy this game only if you know EXACTLY what what to expect from it.
This game, albeit sharing A LOT of themes and story elements with Dead Space, is NOT its spiritual successor.

You take the role of Jacob Lee, as you're approaching Jupyter's moon Callisto to deliver a payload to the Black Iron Maximum Security Prison. However, the ship crashes, and you're picked up by the guards of the prison, which incarcerate you without further explanation. By the time you wake up in your cell, a mysterious disease has turned nearly every living being in the prison into a human-killing monster.
Will you manage to fight your way thtough this hellscape and get out of it alive?

The graphics and sound design of this game are top notch, and they honestly hit a delicate balance between Dead Space nostalgia and new ideas on the Sci-Fi horror setting. There is a lot of gore, both in the environment and enemy design. A part from a few minor hiccups, in-game animations and cinematics' quality are excellent.
The story is original enough, albeit not excessively so, and most of the time it is easy to foresee its developments.

The main drawback of this game is that the combat system is BORING (exception made for the GRP system).
I can not believe that none of the developers came to this same realisation before shipping the game.
Introducing melee combat interleaved with shooting is a smart more, as it gave the developers a chance to highlight the gore and horror themes that this game has to offer.
The problem is that melee combat is basically the repetition of the same "quick time event" for 9+ hours: dodge (move left/right/left in this EXACT order), mash melee attack, shoot, repeat. Shooting most of the time serves the only function of chain-stunning the enemy to restart the same melee combo over and over.
In fights with multiple enemies, each of them waits its own "turn" to engage the player in this "quick time event" of a fight, and this further adds to the boredom, as such fights do not test reflexes or strategic choice, but just patience: it feels like repeating the tutorial level of a rhythm game.
The selection of different enemy types is not that small, but it feels so, as there is no variation in melee combat, which is sadly also true for the bosses.
The only saving grace of the combat system is the reimplementation of the "telekinesis" mechanic from Dead Space in the GRP system, which is the genuinely most fun way of dealing with enemies.

This game's repetitive nature is worsened by the requirement of doing a minimum of 5 runs to get all of the achievements, each taking upwards of 10 hours, with no additional content or variation in the gameplay.
This is a cheap way to foster engagement, and I don't buy it.

As I mentioned before...The Callisto Protocol (TCP) is a survival space horror game, as the genre states for itself...YOU r IN SPACE, fighting for your survival, surrounded by an eerie apocalyptic atmosphere. Year 2320, the story follows Jacob Lee, a starship captain who survives a crash landing on the Jovian moon Callisto, only to be captured and confined against his will in a high-security prison. -BLACK IRON PRISON-...and shortly after that...comes the virus outbreak...and your fight for survival...

In other words...you can easily kill ALMOST all enemies if you time your attacks and blocks right....but if you mess it up you´ll die very quickly...not to mention if you are surrounded by multiple enemies.
 
THE RANGED COMBAT – is in my opinion always superior in this type of games because its always better to maintain distance between your enemies...this is true in TCP too. Again...its just like in Dead Space...you can dismember limbs (hands, arms, legs, heads) thus slowing down and killing your enemies. For that purpose you can choose from many weapon blueprint types...like shotguns, pistols or rifles. To wrap it up...the ranged combat is good...but nothing revolutionary...

GEAR
   
You can also upgrade your gear...wheter its your gun or melee weapon...the upgrades are bought with „Callisto Credits“ which is the in-game curency. Credits can be collected on the way, as you explore your surroundings. In this game...its worth to explore hidden places, instead of pushing forward the main story line. The upgrades are essential...if you want to make your life easier.  I have to mention...that it was a great disadvatage to have a limited inventory space...which forced you to leave essential or valuable items behind...you cannot upgrade your inventory...it upgrades when you are deep in like 70% of the storyline. I think thats a flaw... 
 
THE WORLD in TCP...NOT OPEN WORLD

...strictly only story based areas and hidden rooms. Although the space around you is limited...the quality is on the level...and I mean masterpiece level. It delivers the dark virus outbreak type of feeling. The developers did a really good job there with the prison, the harsh outside frozen world, the underground tunels/colony  or the hyper-modern laboratories where the experimentations took place. All this + with the added jumpscares...random monster noises, the crawlings, crying and suffering inmates and prison guards...makes you feel like you want to get out from that place. You are checking every corner because you never know where you´ll get jumped by the next enemy. The music or soundtracks also adds to TCP feeling. So the music is good and it forms a finished whole. Especially the ending song.  
FOR those who are looking for some interesting features...Dina Nakamura, Jacobs female inmate friend...is played by the actress Karen Fukuhara, she is famous for her role in “THE BOYS“ as Kimiko...(she was one of the reasons I wanted to try out this game)...and daaamn what a performance she delivered with her character in TCP... Also...for the Star Wars fans....the prison guard (he is making your life a living hell) who is played by Sam Witwer...also known as the actor who played Starkiller in “STAR WARS THE FORCE UNLEASHED“ is present in The Callisto Protocol. So if you are deciding whether to play this game...you know, these might motivate you to do so...as it motivated me.

CONCLUSION

So...where lies the problem ? The combat is good, the gameplay is at times great, at times average because of repetetiveness, the world and the atmo. is magnificent, the characters are interesting, the setting is good, the music is unique ...so where is the PROBLEM ? Is it the STORY ? I deliberately left the story for the end…because the story is an absolute…PERFECTION. Yes you heard right, the game has flaws but its not the story…even though you don’t make any own choices the story is so well written…full of ups and downs, moral dilemmas, great protagonist development and interesting characters (Dina, Ferris, Elias)…it keeps you always on the edge, focused on story…”you have to get out of here, you have to survive”, the odds are always against you but you must fight on…

So no my friends…the story is definitely not the problem.

The problem is that the publishers are greedy…you have to pay for the DLC to finish the story…and although you finish the base game…the ending is almost empty…Imagine you are playing for hours, you immerse yourself with the protagonist and the characters and all is for nothing…sure you defeat the boss, some questions are answered but if you want to know the true ending of the story and the fate of Jacob…you have to buy the DLC…I mean… if this is not a dirty cash grab attempt  from the developers…then I don’t know what is… shame on you KRAFTON and STRIKING DISTANCE STRUDIOS... 
...and that’s why I call it a "disappointing" game.  7/10 

Its not a "Dead Space fake" as some people call it because the game is really unique in its own way...but its very similar to it...so you should decide whether its worth it or nah. 

FINAL WORDS
 
Now I know…some of you will say…”Its not a problem for me to buy the DLC”…and you are right…its not a problem for me either…I invested tons of money in games and I don’t regret it. But the game itself was a 7/10  at best, for me…and I don’t feel like buying the DLC because it was not “catchy enough”…even though I finished the game like an hour ago. 

I´m not saying you should not try it…no…I definitely recommend it. Just heed my WARNING…because the cash grab in this case is real…unfortunatelly…and the publishers haven´t delivered the FULL COMPLETE STORY altough you paid them the full price...

I just finished The Callisto Protocol over the course of 4–5 days – and I really enjoyed it.
The graphics, sound design, and atmosphere are fabulous. While the core story isn’t exactly groundbreaking, the details and worldbuilding offer a refreshing, alternative flavor.

The melee system feels a bit unfamiliar at first, but once it clicks, it's really satisfying. What makes it special is that it’s not 100% perfectly “readable” – and that’s a strength. It’s slightly unpredictable, almost raw and tactile in a way that makes every encounter feel intense. It’s this gritty, imperfect combat design that others might dismiss as clunky, but which I found genuinely compelling.

Level design is pleasantly varied throughout. I was surprised by how little the infamous vents and ladders actually bothered me – they’re used reasonably and don't disrupt the flow. Honestly, I don’t understand the heavy criticism on that front.

Small Note: this was the first game to crash my 7-year-old PC. But with some tweaking, I got it running smoothly – and it was absolutely worth the effort.

Neutral:

- Plays a lot like Dead Space, for me personally not an issue since I enjoyed Dead Space quite a lot and a 
  different setting with similar gameplay is always welcome

   regenerates almost completely and that is not quite clear, given the fact that the alive half can be covered 
   in blood and completely destroyed, but still having tons of health.

Negatives:

   need it you dont have any at all (see boss) 
- Theres two boss fights:
   - If you dont know whats coming for you, you are screwed. In my first run I shot all my ammo at the first 
     boss, unaware that this boss doesnt take damage from ranged weapons. 
     This decision basically trashed the rest of the game and I had to fight the final boss with almost no ammo 
     whatsoever.
  - If the first boss didnt makle it clear enough that it cant be hurt by bullets and it still isnt clear while 
     fighting the second boss you will most likely dump all your ammo on the first phase and have none left 
     for the second phase, where you actually need the ammo, and no, you dont get any ammo when entering

     second phase.
