If you're a fan of Dead Space and love the cinematic movement and weight of games like God of War or The Last of Us, then The Callisto Protocol is right up your alley. It blends the relentless tension of survival horror with the immersive, character driven feel of modern action adventure games, creating something that feels both familiar and new.

The combat is heavy and deliberate, forcing you to master timing and positioning rather than rushing in guns blazing. Every encounter feels like a fight for survival, with melee combat that's as brutal as it is satisfying. The movement has a grounded, cinematic weight to it, reminiscent of The Last of Us, making each step through the Black Iron Prison tense and methodical.

Visually, the game is stunning. The atmosphere is oppressive, the lighting is haunting, and the grotesque creature designs make every encounter a nightmare. IT has the industrial sci-fi horror look of Dead Space but with next gen polish that makes it all the more terrifying.

The story takes its time but keeps you hooked, weaving mystery and desperation into a narrative that feels personal and intense. combined with its pacing, it makes you constantly anxious about what's lurking around the next corner.

My personal rating: 8/10. The Callisto Protocol delivers a cinematic and brutal survival horror experience that fans of Dead Space, God of War, or The Last of Us will absolutely enjoy. It's tense, atmospheric, and unrelenting in all the right ways.


FINAL VERDICT: 80/100

Despite living in the shadow of the superior Dead Space, this is still a good game.  A lot of the negative reviews seem to be about issues that have since been patched.  

The main way that this game differs from Dead Space is in the combat, where Callisto Protocol has more of an emphasis on melee combat, using a dodge and counterstrike mechanic.  There's also a few firearms, but they don't really stand out as being unique in the way that Dead Space's repurposed mining equipment does.     It's fun enough though.

The story is fine, but nothing we haven't really seen before.  The voice acting is good, and the character design and facial animations stand out as being really good.  The graphics are really nice overall, with some really cool environments, but some that are rather generic.  The body horror creatures are pretty good, but not nearly as extreme as Dead Space, and the gore and death scenes are pretty good.

Basically this game's biggest flaw is that better games like it exist.  There is one thing that annoyed me though, and that's the fact that the game's actual ending is in the Final Transmission DLC.  The base game basically hits a cliff hanger in the middle of an action scene, with the DLC immediately picking up from that point for a few extra hours of gameplay.  It probably should have just been included in the base game.

Can't say I understand why this game has mixed review score, I assume it had performance problems at the start. Recommended, despite not loving meaty horrors I'd like to play the second game in this series 👏

Pros:
- Great graphics and sound design. This to me does indeed look like a next gen game. I also really like the suit design.
- At times, the game can produce a nice sci-fi atmosphere. Unfortunately, it can also destroy its atmosphere very quickly as well (see below).

Cons:
- Lacklustre combat design. The game's combat is basically an animation based melee system that stops working entirely if more than one enemy is fought. In most scenarios, it makes the game very easy, which renders the gameplay towards the end rather boring. You also fight the same dead easy mini boss four times throughout the game.
There is also a distinct lack of enemy variety that really hurts the game as most of your enemy encounters will be against quasi-zombies (which is just boring)
- Flat story. The game's story is very strongly inspired by the one of Dead Space. However, whilst Dead Space had great lore supporting its story, CP's falls off here. The story is extremely predictable and uninspired. The characters are mostly uninteresting, unlikable and offer no depth such as an intriguing character development.
- Boring gameplay. Gameplay is ofc strongly impacted by the lacklustre combat design, however there is an equally important factor that brings it down: the incredibly high amount of time the player needs to climb ladders, crawl through vents and squeeze through narrow gaps. Certain areas feel like a walking sim because of that. I kid you not when I say that the player spends almost an hour doing these mind numbing bits that offer nothing. Together with long walk and talk sections, this makes the game simply tedious to play.
- Unsuitable environments. Certain areas in the game just do not make any sense from a design perspective. For instance, how likely is it that in 300 years someone builds a mining colony from shipping containers below ground? Another example: the game is set on Jupiter's moon Callisto, whose gravity is about 1.2% of the one of earth. This ofc would have a great impact on how you move on its surface (eg, think how the astronauts walked on the moon). However, in game the player just moves as if they would on earth. A small nitpick maybe but nonetheless an inconsistency in the game's setting.
Questionable environments (and there are a ton in the game) like these really affect the authenticity of the game's setting, which in horror title can immediately destroy the atmosphere.

Conclusion: If I had to describe the game with a single sentence, Id write: "Dead Space like survival horror action game with next gen graphics that is unfortunately brought down by tedious and boring gameplay".
The game is a 6/10 for me, where it makes it hard to choose whether to give a thumbs up or down. If you are into this sort of game or like sci-fi in general, I would recommend that you pick it up in a sale. If you are neither of those things, dont waste your time with it.

[h1]Review[/h1] 
I was waiting for this game. I was hyped up but then sadly saw the reviews. I got the game gifted because I love horror games with combat. I finally decided to play it and decided that I actually enjoyed the game. 

[u]Gameplay[/u]
Forget that the game is a dead space clone. Forget that the games system is in every way inferior. It has everything that dead space has but less. The only feature that is new is a melee combat system. In contrast to other people i deem it at decent and serviceable but not in the context of the games structure.
I played the game on hard difficulty, which makes enemies take 2-3 melee combos or more to die. You dodge automatically by holding the dodge button, there is a block button that makes you get damage thus being absolutely useless aside the fact that it does not make you dodge in a direction. This is useful when trying to melee combat multiple enemies. Upgrading your weapon increases damage and the chance to break enemies’ arms or outright give you a kill animation. Basically, a must. Ranged Weapons can be upgraded too but that’s not as useful to do. You cannot decide what to upgrade first, making you get useless upgrades like less recoil for a revolver first. Also, for some reason you have the need to do an animation when switching weapons. They don’t change themself that much, since you are in melee combat most of the time the weapons just serve to reduce enemy count and later finish mutating enemies.

At 40-50% of the game, the melee combat gets more tedious. If you play on hard, it’s almost impossible to melee kill an enemy without them mutating. This means they change into a harder enemy, regaining health. Therefore, you either use ammo or have to fight an enemy with twice as much health again, repeating the same dodge and attack pattern.

Otherwise, the gameplay loop about the exploring and pressing on is good. There is usually always a change of location, you don’t get bored by same looking rooms. There are no puzzles at all, and the game is very linear. Its hard to figure out which path is the intended one and which gives additional rewards and loops back again.

The melee combat itself gives satisfaction. The animations are punchy, hard and fantastic to look at. Each combat encounter is a decision between being able to maybe stealth it a bit, take out 1-2 enemies in melee or deciding which enemy to kill with scarce ammo. Ammo is scarce making melee the main combat tool.
In general, I never got bored from my playthrough although the “just” serviceable combat system and linear structure of the levels say the opposite. I never got stuck and while you can die easily a checkpoint is rarely far away. Funnily enough there is a horde mode that shows that the combat system, with enough ammo and lower health enemies, can work very well. Enemies are just too few, too long to beat and recourses are too scares to waste.

[u]Story[/u]
You get to a prison colony on a moon for x reason and a biological virus gets out for y reason. Thats it. Goal is to try to escape and explore more of the colony. The latter part is more interesting as it offers various set pieces and memorable levels. This part is the only one that i deem being very, very good in this game.

[u]Sound[/u]
I did not find the OST in any way memorable. Neither the voice acting nor any other things. Weapons are also serviceable, sound effects are decent, aside melee sfx which are absolutely brilliant.

[u]Graphics[/u]
It looks great and from the stutters people complained about: i have had 0 in 2025. Experiences may vary. Game just looks absolutely great. Variety in level design, enemies and animations. While there is that 1-2 kill animation that you see over and over again, there are a few more rare ones that get you by surprise, especially those that cover the main character getting killed.

[u]Conclusion/TL;DR[/u]
It’s an ok game. There are many decisions that are questionable, tying in a melee combat system into a survival horror game plus a ranged combat system with scarce recourses is a unique approach and difficult. They failed. Instead of making the melee combat system rewarding to use, it’s easy to get into but you can never really do much to make it work in a way that it isn’t tedious. It quickly becomes repetitive. It doesn’t help that it has the modern game design philosophy of making all animations long and repetitive, including long vent crawling sequences. Yet the gameplay loop is serviceable, it’s not so bad that its frustrating and the level design is good. Its one of the few games where I wanted to see what the game would throw at me next, while also being able to recall places in the game after finishing it. I would recommend it, but barely. Since there will be never a sequel as it was a massive flop they never have the chance to remake their mistakes.

A fun enough survival horror with strong (if not simplistic) brawler element that works well in a three-dimensional space, The Callisto Protocol is rightfully a divisive game, though one worth buying at a discount. This is a shame since the game play of the melee combat is actually good, or at the very least promising if there is to be a sequel. However, do not go expecting a Dead Space experience in terms of either combat or storytelling or comparable atmosphere.

Pros:
+Genuinely fun melee system incorporating weaves, combos, and firearms in a way that works far better than what was expected.

+Atmospheric setting that comes with being in a prison on an icy and dead moon.

+Environmental kills with the GRP are very satisfying.

+Enemy mutation adds a level of danger and depth to the combat.

Cons:
+Awful boss fights (Two-headed, Ferris) require a very different play style in terms of combat outside of the melee system that defines over 90% of the game, turning the game into a mediocre 3rd person shooter. 

Note to all prospective game developers: If the bosses of your games have a different playstyles than the rest of the enemies, then it is likely a bad boss battle. Don't make most of your bosses be platformers in a turn-based game.

+Nonsensical environmental storytelling that makes for an uninteresting world to explore. Like really, the prison went to shit in like what, a few hours tops? Compare this to Dead Space where it is implied (albeit inconsistently) that it took around a few days for the USG Ishimura to reach a similar level of destruction, or even weeks in the remake. It makes no sense why there are barricades, why there are widespread fires.

Uninteresting world. We learn very little about how the prison operates beyond it is just a front for experimentation, but we hardly hear from the prisoners themselves or even most of the workers about the day to day. By the time the game proper starts, most everyone is dead. For a gameplay mean to evoke the brawling and gritty aspects of prison life, this game merely takes place in a prison setting, but not a prison.

+Story leaves much to be desired in terms of its characters (Jacob's underdeveloped character arc regarding guilt, Dani's entire character, Elias' entire character)

+Making the ending of the game actual DLC.

+Lack of a good range of enemy design and game play that adds to the base gameplay.

5. Brute fights. The game isn't about shooting limbs off. Yes, you can tear limbs, but I played the game on hard difficulty and I can barely cut any limbs. Not until several beating to the enemy. 

Cons:

2. Lacking suspense & intensity. One of my biggest let down and this could be why the game isn't that popular. I think there should be more scene where the MC is being chased in tight and gripping situation. 
3. Not a horror game. No. Callisto Protocol isn't a horror game, duh. It's an action, brute-fight & survival game. But it certainly would be a really nice thing if the game has more horror element in it.
4. A bit too much of moment of silent. Like the game will give you moments to breathe. There are quite plenty areas where there is no enemies. Yes, I agree after a very intense and brutal combat you need some quiet moment to relax & chill. But in that quiet moment should also be given a nice surprise. Something very unexpected. A jump-scare would be nice.

Wish they'll make Callisto Protocol 2.

Pros:
-Weapons are satisfying to use
-Pretty interesting story
-Graphics are fantastic
-The gore/body horror is genuinely horrendous and gross (if you're into that)
-Most of the technical issues with the PC port seem to be a thing of the past
-Determining which path is the main one for progression and which is for secrets isn't usually immediately obvious (good if you're tired of modern games holding your hand like I am)

Cons:
-Melee combat isn't as bad as some people make it out to be, but it is pretty shallow
-Waaaay too much use of "press forward" gameplay to hide loading screens (shimmying through crevices, crawling through vents, etc.)
-Money seems to be doled out pretty thinly. I explored any secret I could find, and I still feel like I don't have much in my new-game+ playthrough
-Without spoiling anything, there's a moment in the game that's filled with a certain enemy type that's not very fun to deal with (not horrible, just tedious)
-Sometimes non-essential items seem to just fall through the floor or disappear
-The checkpoint system can be pretty unreliable. I've quit the game after seeing that the game saved my progress moments ago, only to have to replay those sections again when I boot the game back up. Never anything major like replaying entire chapters, but I had to replay parts of the game a few times
-Related to the last part, I think there's something wrong with the checkpoint/credentials/save-data validation, because there were a few weird things that happened in the main menu (asked to read the EULA again upon booting, telling me I had unlocked New-Game+ after quitting to the main menu DURING my NG+ playthough, etc.). Again, never anything major, as I was able to fix even the "worst" issue just by closing and reopening the game

Overall this game was a lot of fun at its best, but could be pretty annoying/tedious at its worst. Aside from graphics, it lacks the polish and attention to detail that Dead Space has, but I found that I enjoyed this game more the less I compared it to Dead Space, despite the obvious parallels. While the gameplay itself is far from groundbreaking, I enjoyed it way more than I expected, and feel a lot (but not all) of the criticism I've heard online was too harsh. Granted I got this game on a huge sale (85% off), but I'm glad I played it. Maybe I would be much more critical if I bought it at full price

The Callisto Protocol got way more hate than it deserved. Is it a great game? No. Is it an enjoyable game that does a few innovating things and doesn't overstay its welcome? Absolutely.

[h3]What I liked[/h3]
[b]Melee combat[/b] is surprisingly innovative, using movement for dodging and blocking instead of mapping those actions to buttons. Attacks feel solid and brutal. 

[b]Visuals[/b] are great. Environments and facial animations are really solid.

[b]Campaign length[/b] is right in the sweet spot at 12-14 hours.

[h3]What I didn't like[/h3]
[b]Monster design[/b] feels uninspired, and the variety is very limited.

[b]Characters[/b] are kinda bland and one-note - including the main antagonist.

[b]Controls[/b] are sometimes weirdly unresponsive. Grabbing ladders and ledges and opening containers required being in exactly the right position. The ability to run was extremely inconsistent, with the game just disabling it at times for no apparent reason. Aiming also felt pretty bad for some reason.

[h3]tl;dr[/h3]
If you're a fan of survival horror, I'd give it a go. Know that it's not going to knock your socks off, or unseat Dead Space as the benchmark, but it's still a better game that it was given credit for.

Dammit, it was starting so good... I really liked it more than Dead Space (both original and remake). Where Dead Space seemed to build the atmosphere mainly by turning off lights and jump-scaring you with monsters, this one seemed to be doing much more than that.

Firstly, it was using proper cinematics when required to show intense situations, to let you feel "the strain" of it all. The way camera was moving, the way the frame was "dirtied" (this does not necessarily mean actual dirt, it means that a frame is not "perfect" and that can help with immersion). It felt like they are really putting you into the game, at last to an extent.

Secondly, there were just those little things here and there, like little unnecessary movements made by characters, they made it feel just a little bit more "natural". And it was also little details in the environment, too. In Deas Space I always wanted to run, and could not, because I needed flashlight, which works only if you aim. Callisto is much brighter, but I never wanted to run here, because it just felt wrong. Something was telling me, that I need to be cautious, and move slowly, even though logic told me that this is a safe area, and everything is scripted either way.

There was also combat. Yes, it turned out to be somewhat repetitive pretty quickly, but the way you were introduced to it, and the way it felt... Like "heavy", "difficult", "important". You know, like, with fighting scenes in movies: sometimes they have this weight, that you feel even though you are not participating.

My point is, I wanted to play the game further. Yes, the second prisoner (Elias, if I remember correctly) seemed a bit forced as a guide, perhaps, since he is a prisoner, he probably should be that knowledgeable if he is in his cell most of the time. But there is enough doubt regarding him, that maybe there will be an explanation. I really wanted to know what will be next, was really excited...

★☆☆☆☆ – The Callisto Protocol: A $160 Million Tech Demo That Forgot to Be a Game

I usually don’t write negative reviews, but The Callisto Protocol deserves every bit of criticism it gets. This game is a complete mess, a beautiful, shiny, soulless husk of what could have been a great horror experience. I’m glad I paid $6 from a third-party site, because this isn’t even worth $10, let alone the $60–$70 it launched at.

🎨 Graphics: The Only Redeeming Quality
Yes, the game looks absolutely stunning. The lighting, reflections, character models, chef’s kiss. If you're buying this as a graphical benchmark, sure, it’ll impress your eyeballs.

But the moment you pick up a controller, it all goes downhill.

🎮 Combat: Repetitive, Clunky, and Boring
The melee system is laughable. You just dodge left-right-left and mash attack. Every fight feels exactly the same.

Gunplay? Feels like an afterthought. Barely any weapon variety, and aiming is sluggish.

Enemy variety is awful. You'll fight the same handful of enemies over and over with slightly different skins.

At some point I stopped being scared and just got annoyed.

🧠 Story: Generic Sci-Fi Mush
Warden Cole is a one-note villain with some dollar-store "eugenics" ideology.

The plot is a copy-paste of better horror games, but with zero emotional investment.

Jacob Lee, the main character, is boring. I kept waiting for a character arc or twist that never came.

Even the big “twists” are predictable : "evil corporation," "experiment gone wrong," etc. It’s like they wrote the plot in a weekend.

🧬 Enemy Design & Horror: Weak
This is supposed to be a horror game, but there’s no tension.

Jump scares are predictable.

No resource management, no puzzles, no psychological horror. Just linear corridors and recycled enemy ambushes.

The only fear I had was whether I’d have to sit through another mindless combat section.

🧠 Artificial Intelligence? More like Artificial Dumbness
Enemy AI is just “run at player.”

Level design is strictly A to B, no exploration, no branching paths.

It’s not scary. It’s not smart. It’s not fun.

🧠 Final Verdict:
The Callisto Protocol is a $160 million cinematic tech demo disguised as a horror game. It has incredible visuals... and nothing else. No gameplay innovation, no scares, no replayability. Just a shallow, sluggish, and repetitive experience wearing a very expensive coat of paint.

If you find this on sale for $5 and want to see pretty lighting effects while you mash the dodge button for 8 hours, go for it. Otherwise? Skip it. Or better yet, just play Dead Space Remake — everything Callisto tried to be, and more.

What can I say about Carbuncle Protocol?

It’s a game, one they want you to think is of ‘quadruple-A’ quality, so what does that mean, and does it hold up to that claim?

It’s got great sound design, nice graphics, it’ll set your CPU to broil for downloading/installing and shader cache collection on first boot, that guy from every fuckin’ transformers movie except the three most recent ones, and boring gameplay.

There isn’t a real way to summarize that last part effectively. You look at this game, in every review video, and think “wow, it looks so good, no way that is boring to play!”—but it is.
Exploration is composed of walking around and either stabbing in the back, getting jumped by those stupid fucking pod things that can only be avoided if you played the game and remember where they are so you can shoot them ahead of time, cutting the same serial cables on every box, crawling in vents, shimmying through gaps, and occasionally crouching. As a ‘spiritual successor’ to Dead Space, this feels alright, at first, but then you realize there’s no tension.
Despite the sound quality making you think there’s someone around the corner or behind you, 9/10 times you’re alone and don’t need to worry. Enemies are louder than women in spring, so you won’t doubt there’s someone behind you, maybe one will slip past, but you’ll turn the camera and see them just in time. But then there are these screams from the enemy that just grab you, make you turn around—you can ignore those. I’m confident 98/100 are just background sound clips on some kind of shuffle.

The graphics, where do I begin?
They’re ok.
That’s it.
Ol’ Transformer Actor himself is recognizable, but his head activates that part of my brain that makes me remember the uncanny valley. Everyone looks recognizable as humans, but there’s something off. It’s somewhere between Mass Effect Andromeda and Fable. With this absolutely stellar sound design, the visuals are so lackluster in comparison that you are forced to focus on it. You’re not buying this game because it looks good, and if you are, you’re going to be disappointed, especially when you get into—

Combat! Don’t bother shooting. Melee is how you will win, but it’s tedious. Dodge an attack by picking left or right, then tilt your controller in that direction, and start alternating until you’re ready to beat them in the face like they suck.
You will repeat this process from start of game to finish, with the only variety being windows of opportunity, how long you will beat them in the face, or special weaknesses…which are ignorable.
The security bot is the only time you’ll really need a gun. If you need help finding their weak spot schedule a visit with your local lobotomist expert. Enemies fight neatly one at a time which…they’re fucking feral, right? Why are they so Imperialist-era England about it? All they were missing was starting off the battle while standing in a line. You can sever limbs, or shoot them—but this is dead space, so shooting or dismembering the head is worthless, so why have a gun? What about the quick shot system? Honestly, that works well, and all it really does is serve as the gun in Bloodborne; you will use the quick-shot to stagger enemies so you can interrupt their attack and beat them in the face. If you’re not doing this, you’re doing it wrong. So even in combat there’s no tension, no reason for you to feel rushed or intimidated.
What about all those fucking death animations? What ABOUT them?
They shitty, and rarely happen. 90% of the time Transformerdude just falls over dead and I’m wondering when he’ll get up, because he doesn’t look dead when this happens, it looks like a lifealert moment. He’s fallen, and he won’t get up—-oh, wait, he’s dead. That’s awful! I should know when I’m dead immediately, so the moment I actually get a death animation how do you think I react?
I’m disappointed! They’re well made, brutal, but they feel soulless, and without the weight Dead Space 1&2 originally had. You don’t get excited when you see them, you rarely do anyways, so if it’s why you’re buying the game save your money and look up a YouTube video, trust me—please.

And that’s it! Explore through the game, find secret audio logs and shit. It’s not difficult, it’s tedious, and boring. The story never picks up, you’re constantly waiting for things to explode and get real…then it’s over, and they’re asking you to pay for the real ending because it’s hidden behind DLC. With games I’m normally hooked to see how things end, but with this game I’m not. It’s boring and tedious to the point where I don’t even care what the story is, or what will happen.

The Callisto Protocol, much like Mighty No. 9, sold itself as a spiritual successor of an existing IP made by some of the original creators while the IP owners seemingly forgot about it. The appeal of this sort of thing is immediately apparent: as long as your attachment to the franchise isn't relegated to existent characters and story and it's more about gameplay, atmosphere and tone then you'll be happy to move on to a new IP that promises all those things, and the fact that it comes from the original creators means they know what they're doing.

Unfortunately, just like for Mighty No. 9, the creators have oversold their level of participation in the original, and the resulting product, while similar enough to the original (sometimes to a fault), is a major downgrade in every aspect.

Lets get the positive out of the way first: the game's visuals are very good. The likeness to the actors who play the main roles here is astonishing, and unlike in other games, where they look good while static but feel awkarwd in motion, they always look great here, to the point where you'd be excused for thinking some cutscenes are in live action.

Sadly, that's pretty much it for the positives. Everything else ranges from mediocre to terrible.

I resist to call this game a "spiritual successor" to Dead Space because "blatant ripoff" fits it much better. Yes, it comes from some of the original creators, but it feels like it doesn't even try to innovate. The movement feels the same, the in-game UI is similar, the visuals, the pacing and structure are all the same. There's even a dedicated “stomp” button, with the same function. There's not even an attempt to evolve or improve those systems over the onees they're aping. They're either identical or worse.

In the few instances where the game deviates from Dead Space it's always notably for the worse. While in DS you could explore the place mostly at your leisure this one is strictly linear. Exploration is limited to the occasional extra hallway with some loot at the end. And God forbid you pick the path that advances the story first, because then that loot is gone forever, as the game won't let you go back.

The combat is now inexplicably focused on melee, You only have one melee weapon and one strategy to defeat foes, so every fight feels the same. You have a few guns to pick up, but their usage is so situational and their power so low that outside of the very last boss battle you're better off ignoring them altogether. Enemy variety is already ridiculously low, but the fact that you fight them all the same way doesn't help.

The game also puts too much focus into being cinematic and realistic. This means you'll be constantly fighting the camera that insists on putting the attention far from where you need it, and extensive and uninterruptible animations will get you killed more than once. Attempts at drama get so constant and over the top that it borders on parody. If you see your character following another one through a walkway expect it to break down and make you fall through a long tunnel every single time.

Of course, a major issue with the game is that it labels itself as horror but all it ever tries to do is jump scares. And by God, it abuses the hell out of them. There are dozens, maybe even hundreds of them, not one of them is even the slightest bit effective, and It reaches a point where they become so predictable that again it all borders on parody. I feel like I'm a Scary Movie skit where the killer is trying to scare the protagonists and they never react.

Don't expect the story and characters to save this. I can sum up my problem with the Callisto Protocol in one fact.  To dodge enemy attacks you hold left or right on the thumbstick, and then if they try to attack a second time, you hold the opposite direction.  Not hit it in time with the attack but just hold a direction.  If that doesn’t sound challenging, it’s not. 

There was a point also where you changed a club for a stun baton, and the combat didn’t feel like it changed at all.   Callisto Protocol also struggles to be scary, because most of its jump scares are pre-scripted.  But if you ever are afraid something is going to jump out, hold the stick to the Left just in case.   See it’s kind of dumb.

Also just saying I think the third person made it hard to be scared during several of the horror moments because you’re watching actions being done to the player’s avatars, not experiencing those actions.

Pick this up if you were waiting for a heavy discount.  This game got a lot of popularity leading up to release and then kind of disappeared quickly. I’m not the person to ask about a horror game, but I also just found this one to be more lacking than scary.

The Callisto Protocol" is a game that truly shines in its visual presentation. From the moment you step foot on the grim, atmospheric prison of Black Iron, you're treated to some of the most stunning graphics and art direction in recent memory. The character models are incredibly detailed, the environments are beautifully oppressive, and the lighting is a masterclass in building tension. Every blood-splatter and every grotesque creature design feels meticulously crafted, and it's clear that a massive amount of effort went into making this game a feast for the eyes.

However, once you get past the stunning visuals, you're left with a game that feels, for lack of a better term, like "Dead Space at a minimal level." The core gameplay loop, while functional, lacks the polished, visceral satisfaction that made its spiritual predecessor so iconic. Combat feels clunky and repetitive, often devolving into a simplistic dodge-and-hit affair. The much-touted gore system, while visually impressive, doesn't translate into satisfying gameplay mechanics. You're left with a sense of "been there, done that," but without the tight, rewarding gameplay that made the original "Dead Space" so beloved.

Where "Dead Space" offered a perfect blend of beautiful visuals and a genuinely enjoyable, polished gameplay experience, "The Callisto Protocol" prioritizes the former at the expense of the latter. It's a game that promises so much with its stunning presentation but ultimately falls short in delivering a truly compelling and memorable gameplay experience. It's a testament to the fact that great visuals can only carry a game so far.

This is a game that focuses on looking good, which it does sometimes.  It does not, however, capture you in any meaningful way.  Thankfully I bought this on sale, but it would still not be a good buy for me even if it were $5.99. 

Why do I feel this way?  

Simple:  

You don't know who you are, have zero time to figure that out and develop a reason to play, and you have to run around with 1 combat style.  Sure, it is a fight for your life....but even combat doesn't engage you, and it takes way too many hits to drop these enemies.

But of course, the evil Warden has plans for your meaningless life, and whenever someone says your life is meaningless, they have their own plan on how to make it meaningful.  And how that unfolds is like games from the 90's.  It is a poor idea with worse execution.  You listen to random recordings laying around that fill you in on the story, yet the little bits they give you aren't enough to make you want to find another.  

Speaking of holo-cartridges, you can hold as many of those as you want, but you are limited in inventory.  You will find your standard health bits, ammo, and other "loot" you can sell.  It's good to see I can get credits to buy things in a derelict prison...cause inmates need to buy guns at the 3d printing gun stations...and nothing is cooler than the "hand cannon".  Yawn. 

The perspective is really weird for the camera, you can't change it either.  Your character looks awkward most of the time, and sneaking through all the vents in this prison is just to waste my time.  

Your time is wasted, literally.  Slow, tedious, and boring gameplay...like fuse finding and partially working security mechs to sneak around make it feel like the devs had nothing in mind to begin with.  They had to slow you down to make the game last longer.  

Performance on a RTX 4070 is fine, this is not a game that needs more than 60fps either.  It does look really cool sometimes...othertimes the fog effects remind me of 80's horror movies.  It is incredible that they used so much fog.  Someone in a planning meeting mush have had a 10 minute speech on "atmosphere" and the use of fog.  They missed the memo that atmosphere in games means something different than actual atmosphere in real life...but gots to have that scary fog to build intensity...gots to.
  
The jump scares are lame, and almost always the same.  You new friend that helps you navigate the prison has "special" privileges BRUV (but not enough for him to not ask you for help).  After you try to help, he can just go where he wants, but not you.

You have to sloppily tear your way through a crap hole, cutting access shards out of dead employees. 10 hours prior was a functioning facility. Now its a spark shooting hellhole that has some doors locked (privileges), way too many escape vents, and doors that you are somehow strong enough to use your weak, fleshy hands to pull open...but only partway (because it is a prison after all, can't completely open those spring loaded doors).

Truth is that I bought this game because I love ray tracing...I should have listened to the other reviewers who I had a feeling were telling the truth.  This is boring garbage that is getting uninstalled.

I don’t say this often, but The Callisto Protocol is a bad game. It may be priced like a AAA game, but it feels like a janky indie game that spent most of its budget on graphics.

Imagine you finally get to a safe room. You see an upgrade machine and you upgrade your gear, watching the stutter animation. Feeling prepared you decide to continue on. You see a branch in the path and choose to go left. After slowly walking for what feels like multiple minutes until you drop down a hole that you can not climb back up. You are now locked in a room of zombies with seemingly no way back. Carefully, you kill them all, easily dodging all melee attacks in the dodging system that requires no skill or timing while weaving in attacks. Unfortunately, a spitter hits you with its spit during the dodge animation, because that is a thing that can happen in this game. Luckily you don’t die and you manage to kill the spitter as well. You find some loot, including a collectible as well as a vent that you slowly crawl through when the game freezes for half a second and you know there’s going to be a jump scare. BAM! A zombie runs past the outside of the vent, but you’re not scared, you knew it was going to happen. After escaping the vent, you find yourself back near the branch in the path. You take the other route and find another room filled with zombies. After killing a few of them, the game freezes for another half second and you know another jump scare is going to happen. BAM! Something has grabbed your arm and you have to do a quick time event. Luckily you easily defeat the event and continue on. You see a zombie off in the distance. You run to it and smack it once with your baton. It goes to attack and you easily dodge its attacks, but then suddenly the game freezes for half a second. Is this another jump scare mid fight? No. It was just a regular stutter, but this time when the stutter ends you see yourself already dead. That’s fine, you think to yourself. Surely this game had a recent checkpoint. No. It did not. You are back in the safe room. No collectible, no weapon upgrades. You’re a little annoyed, but the game does offer manual saves, so it’s really your fault for relying on auto saves, right? You repeat the sequence. But this time make a manual save after getting the collectible and returning to the main path. You make your way back to your nemesis for revenge. Even though you know you can normally get 3 or more hits in between enemy attacks, you decide to play it safe and only hit twice. You gracefully dodge the first round of attacks. You smack it once. You click to smack again, but then right before contact it rapidly attacks. You shift your fingers to press dodge, but it’s too late. Even though you hit first, the enemy doesn’t flinch. It hits, but because of your attack animation you cannot dodge and your dead. That’s fine, you made a manual save, right? Wrong. Manual saves are meaningless in this game. You’re still back at the safe house, no weapon upgrades, no collectibles.

However, the opponent also enters an "enrage" period at the same time where you must shoot a tentacle on them within 5 seconds to kill them or they enrage. The problem? This can be disabled via the skill tree later in the game, but that is just a joke to have to spec into a fix for the poor gameplay mechanics.

The final boss fight mandates using the assault rifle. I decked out my shotgun and went into the fight and was spawned in with my AR. You cannot readily change weapons on the fly, forcing me to reload a save prior to decking out my shotgun to load up on AR ammo.

The game makes a wonderful first impression as it has wonderful graphics, performance and a top-notch environment. Hello,
This is my first review, so I would like to ask for your indulgence and apologize in advance for any grammatical errors. 
In this article I would like to focus on Callisto Protocol in detail. Obviously, I can't do this without comparing it to the Dead Space series, so I'll spend some time on that part as well. The main reason I'm writing this review is to point out how horribly bad this game is and how much of a disappointment it is. I'd like to point out that while I'll try to be objective at first but I must say I grew up on the Dead Space franchise and have played all games(primarily Dead Space 1 and 3) + the remake several times as well. This review contains light spoilers. Let's get to it...

ACT I. - World without Dead Space:
Let's imagine for now that there is no Dead Space franchise and Striking Distance Studios is releasing a new unseen game in the survival horror genre. I must say that the audiovisual aspect of the game is amazing and immersive and it is clear that the authors know how to walk in this field. Unfortunately, I'm done with praise here.

COMBAT SYSTEM: totally worth a fuck. On paper it looks good that the combination of "melee" and "long range" duels will be fun, but the opposite is true in this case. The controls are incredibly insensitive and stupid since movement is on the same keys as dodging, and if you happen to decide to run away from the fight the next enemy will hit you immediately. There is no "roll" option in the game and the camera itself is pretty stupid when it comes to combat. It is literally a nightmare when you meet more than 2 enemies at the same time. At this point the game really becomes UNplayable. Generally there are few bullets in the game and the game FORCES you to combine "melee" and "longrange" style ergo forget about the choice. The only way to deal with multiple enemies afterwards is to use the "gravity gauntlet" to throw them all into pits or bayonets according to the level-design, which gets really BORING after 2h! It wouldn't even be that bad if you had more weapons to choose from than one electric baton and a couple of pistols. The weapons are boring and the upgrades are overpriced and don't even give you the feeling that you're gaining the upper hand.

STORY AND CHARACTERS: (if we still take into account that there is no Dead Space) is pretty good. The setting is interesting, but the characters are quite shallow and don't develop much.

PLAYABILITY: is terrible. If you are not moving from A to B you will encounter 3 types of challenges:
1) Find the "Fuse" to open the door.
2) Find the dead guy who has the key to open the door.
3) Kill everyone in the room.
And that's the end of it. Every now and then you get a BOSS FIGHT, but if you don't have enough bullets, it makes life pretty uncomfortable and the game just becomes frustrating again. Another drop in the frustration jug is the lack of any orientation. There is no map, no locator, no hint to tell you where to go and what to do. Main Character will only say, "I have to go along the red pipe.", "I have to go along the cables.", etc... it's incredibly easy to get lost in the game. And one more annoying little observation of mine. If you craft at a "station" weapon or ammo, you can only craft "1 pack"/component, and the animations are fucking long for my taste. So if you want, heaven forbid, 3 packs of cartridges and a first aid kit... Spend a good few minutes at the table :)

ENEMIES: they are quite stereotypical. You will encounter these types:
1) The common infected
3) "Babies" from The forest (toddlers)
2) "Clicker" from Last of Us (only hears)
3) "Spitter" from L4D2 (gases acid)
4) "Boss" he's variable

New!!! is a "head" that shoots and knocks you halfway across the room if you don't notice her fast enough.

The game contains quite long passages where there are so many clickers that you simply can't kill them all, but have to sneak past them. Their AI is extremely stupid, so if you want a realistic clicker experience, go play Last of Us.
It's admittedly subjective, but I'll say it anyway. Overall, I found the enemy design lazy and "not enough" scary than other titles such as: Evil Within , or Resident Evil. And there is no "pyramid" to filter the enemies by how dangerous they are. Even the most pathetic zombie has the potential to kill you in two shots.

ACT. II - Dead Space:
It's like chalk and cheese. Dead Space is better than Callisto Protocol in every way imaginable. Gameplay, level-design, audiovisual... No exaggeration, whatever you say, Dead Space is better in that regard (leaving aside the 2008 graphics), but it was great for the time.
In Deadspace you have: a locator that shows you where to go. A range of diversionary weapons. Enemies are intelligent, subversive and scary. The characters have purpose and depth. You have the freedom to deal with enemies and not be crushed by stupid camera and movement. Diverse level design and quests that make sense.

ACT. III - Review:
After reading the following lines, it's definitely obvious that I'm not going to become a Callisto Protocol worshipper. The optimization may be good a year after its release, but that doesn't change the fact that the game is a bad, unreasonably frustrating copy of Dead Space that will only piss off veterans of the series. DEFINITELY NOT WORTH THE 60€ PRICE TAG. I myself bought it for 20€ on sale and I didn't know what to expect. I was in for an incredible disappointment. The Callisto Protocol is definitely NOT THE SPIRITUAL REPLACEMENT to DEAD SPACE and unfortunately I can't recommend it to anyone.

The Callisto Protocol looks incredible — no doubt about it. The visuals are top-notch, from the eerie environments to the detailed character models. It really nails the horror atmosphere. The enemy designs are also varied and creative, which helps early on.

The story is one of the game's strongest points. It's actually pretty interesting and had me invested in figuring out what was going on. There's a solid sci-fi horror vibe that fans of the genre will appreciate.

Combat starts off feeling fresh, especially with the melee system and dodge mechanic. But after a few hours, it gets repetitive. Dodging is super easy to master, and once you do, it’s hard to die in combat. The challenge fades quickly, even for beginners.

One of the biggest frustrations is how the game handles multiple enemies. The camera locks onto the last enemy you hit, and there’s no way to change focus mid-fight. So if another enemy comes at you from off-screen, you’ll probably get hit — not because you messed up, but because the camera just won’t show you what’s happening. It’s clunky and unfair.

On the bright side, the telekinesis power is a lot of fun. It adds a cool dynamic to fights and helps make some tough encounters more manageable. I found myself using it often to control space and deal with enemies more efficiently.

The gunplay is fine, but I barely used it. Melee and telekinesis did most of the work, and I mostly saved bullets for specific moments.

Overall, despite its strong visuals, solid story, and fun powers, I can’t recommend The Callisto Protocol. It has too many frustrating design choices, and once I finished it, I didn’t feel any urge to come back. It’s a one-and-done experience for me.

In just three hours of playtime, I crawled through at least ten vents, climbed and descended the same number of ladders, and squeezed between countless narrow walls. It’s nothing but artificial padding painfully boring. The entire game is just walking down corridors, crawling through vents, climbing ladders, squeezing through gaps, and occasionally fighting monsters. That’s it.

This game had everything it needed. A director of the first Dead Space, impeccable visuals, atmosphere, sound design, superb actors, motion capture and unique setting. Unfortunately all of these make a great movie, not a game.

The Callisto Protocol unfortunately fails at the most important part - the gameplay. It sure does take time to get used to the dodge-attack mechanic, with Callisto focusing primarily on melee combat, which is almost turn-based. However, that is not quite where all the issues lie. A lot of it also comes from the small amount of variety between enemy types, slow pacing, almost situational gunplay and a very lacking usage of the GRP telekinesis. The melee itself, while could be described as satisfying is very limiting your actions in what you can do. 

The story itself is very simple and straightforward, unfortunately a lot is told in logs scattered throughout the game, and the game never makes it clear which path is optional and which one leads to progression of the main story. This means a lot of logs can be easily missed, though there are some important ones on your way through the main story, while the plot itself is slowly getting properly revealed in last few chapters. Up until that point you have almost no idea what exactly is going on and what role do you play in all of this. While the actors' performances were nothing but stellar, their effort was ultimately lost in this messy and rushed scenario.

I would also like to mention the boss fights (especially the last one) are extremely disappointing and anti-climatic, but I won't go into spoiler territory and just want to mention one more thing. The story can be done in 9-10 hours and by design it feels like Resident Evil, where first playthrough takes time but subsequent runs can be done in relatively short time. However the beginnings are slow and the gameplay loop isn't interesting enough to make me do a new playthrough. The "true" ending and various game modes are also locked behind paid DLC, but I honestly do not think that it will make me change my opinion about the game itself.

TL;DR: A lot of potential was wasted and it's primarily fault of the gameplay and lack of fun elements in the game. It's trying to be more story-driven and while it has everything it needs to be (at least) a good movie-game, the story itself is very mediocre. Not great, not terrible.

I don't actually think [i]The Callisto Protocol[/i] is a bad game. My 'thumbs down' here is not saying the game is bad, I just find the game so painfully mediocre and not worth your time when there are so many better games out there. The game visually looks fantastic (though there is still a stutter issue that never got fixed), but the gameplay leaves a lot to be desired.

My main gripe for the game comes from the general level design. The game, features a lot of slow walking, sliding, and crawling sections. A lot of these sections opt to use fairly cheap jumpscares rather than build any horror through tension or atmosphere. Actually, some of those aren't even jumpscares, but whatever you call those sections where there is some monster/shadow/dead body that just moves off screen around a corner - it's not really a jumpscare and isn't particularly good horror. The game in general lacks any interesting exploration and ends up being pretty linear. By linear, I don't mean that I expect the game to be open world or anything, just simply give me the feeling of actually exploring the world and scrounging for resources. That is what I expect from a survival horror - even if the game has linear story progression, I want to feel like I am exploring the location in some way. I think the fact that Callisto Protocol doesn't have any sort of viewable map really shows just how the game is just linear corridors, you will never need to consult a map because you always just go forwards with only an occasional side path.

A very common complaint around this game is the combat, particularly the melee combat that the game focuses on. I actually don't think that making the combat melee focused is an inherently had idea. In a survival horror game where ammo is going to be limited, I think a strong melee focus can make a lot of sense. I first I actually liked the dodge mechanic, but it ends up being pretty damn repetitive the further in you get in the game. As the game tells you in the initial tutorial popup, there is no timing with the dodge so there is no real skill or challenge in the mechanic. The only mechanic that ever expands on the melee combat is once you get a gun and now you can take a shot at the end of a combo. But the gun doesn't really add much to the melee combo and the game doesn't expand beyond that. Guns in general are pretty boring in the game, the game doesn't really have any mechanic like [i]Dead Space[/i] where you are required to shoot off the limbs, so instead it's just shotgun to the face a couple of times to kill. It's not bad, but doesn't have any of the tension that other games like [i]Dead Space[/i] have.

Inventory management is not something I have an issue with in survivor horrors (not that I play too many of them), but I did find it weird that it really feels like getting more guns is actually [i]worse[/i]. Each gun has a different type of ammo and the game only seems to spawn the ammo when you have the gun. This led to my inventory being filled with ammo, but specifically ammo for four different guns which meant I didn't have all that much ammo for a single gun. The additional guns didn't seem that particularly more useful over the pistol and shotgun, so I think I would've been better off not buying new guns. I never bought the assault rifle because of this - maybe it was good, but it's much more expensive and I didn't want to deal with another ammo type clogging up my already limited inventory.

The story is kinda weird. It's fine and I guess it works for a game, but there are a couple of things that keep me from really caring for it. Without going into any spoilers, it's particularly annoying that there is a bit of a reveal that should already seem obvious to the player. If the player doesn't already assume from the beginning, the game pretty much lays it out before the reveal so so the player should already be able to figure it out before the Jacob (the player character).

If you are interested, maybe the game is worth it on a deep sale, but I think there are plenty of other worthwhile games to play. You would be much better of playing any of the [i]Dead Space[/i] games, or even the [i]Resident Evil[/i] games if you are looking for a survival horror game in general. Maybe if you've already played every other survival horror, then you can go for it, I guess.

After playing through this game and really giving it a chance I've come to the conclusion that it fails as a horror/story game but has moderate success in being a action shooter.

The game is beautiful, the visuals are really awesome and is 10/10. Animations are great the atmosphere is stunning.
But it also lacks in being immersive. For example, the game wants you to use the environment to kill your enemies but instead of using immersive objects one would find in a prison it just places random spikes against a wall or blades that spin and is a complete safety hazard to anyone within 40 meters. The amount of yellow spikes screaming "hey throw enemies against me" is absurd. Like come one, why would anyone place deadly spikes in a marketplace bathroom or a bedroom?

The combat also is absurd for being a horror game. Literally all you have to do against enemies is hold A then switch to D, that's it. You dodge every single attack and there is no intense fighting for your life moment. If there are multiple enemies they all wait for their turn, they all don't attack at once. Boss battles are the easiest boss battles i have had in a game, they can't even damage you.

The game fails in being scary. Enemies are as explained earlier not even a challenge, you never feel in danger. The game also never uses tactics that Dead Space used (Same creator that made Dead Space made this game) the tactics I'm referring to being attacked when you don't expect it. Going back to the area you just passed through? Get jumped by a enemy (Sometimes) or even being attacked when standing in the shop. You never feel safe in Dead Space. But this game just goes easy on you, if you back-track you never encounter enemies, NEVER. It's those small things that add up, this game has none of that.

The story feels very weak, generic "unknown virus" that infects a planet. Could've worked but this game just feels to similar to Dead Space for me to not feel like it is.

For being a 60$ game it just absolutely fails. I have no idea how someone who was the creator of Dead Space could make this. I'm sad the studio basically is dead now but i feel like Glen tried and failed and now has to suffer the consequences of his actions.

The only other game I can think of that fails at Dead Space this hard is Dead Space 3. This was clearly put together by a producer that said "I can do it better" that went on to prove that he in fact could not do it better, in the most incompetent way possible. This feels like a vertical slice early development prototype that's been stretched to 10 hours. I suspect that some of the current problems come from attempting to "patch" problems that are fundamentally broken. A certain Yahtzee Crowshaw nails why this is a horrible game in a much more creative way than I ever could but I'll try. 

tl;dr Combat is boring, movement is clunky, difficulty is achieved through by being a cheater, and the story is a poorly done version of Dead Space, and there's little exploration or branching paths

First off, yes this game is Dead Space, no matter what anyone says. Regular Joe doing a regular job? Check. An out of the way facility in a place people aren't going to look? Check. A corporation with a facility out on the edge of space so people can't watch what they're doing? Check. A shadowy religious organization that infiltrates the company and uses it to its own means? Check. That organization releasing a zombie outbreak because it fits in with their beliefs? Check. Holographic HUD on the character? Check. Vaguely Japenese writing all over the place? Check. 

The entire plot is Dead Space with the nuance removed and the obvious being spelled out in minute detail. There's a log in the game that says "I don't know why they want to stop terraforming after spending billions, its like they don't want people here, wink, wink, wink". You don't care about the characters either. One character naturally dies, I didn't care because he wasn't helping.

How is it not like Dead Space? They took all the good things, chucked them in the garbage and replaced them with features a senior game design student would put together over a semester.

Movement is slow and clunky. It takes forever to turn around, even with the mouse settings maxed out. And you randomly run into walls or trip over random objects. Either the hit boxes are off or the Jacob has some undiagnosed illness.

The combat is boring and inconsistent.  Its got 3 main problems, weapon handling, how difficulty is achieved, and the variety of tactics. 

It really shouldn't be "melee focused" it should be "only one weapon at a time focused". I died a couple of times early on and for the life of me couldn't figure out why. It was because the weapon stowing and switching is gawdawully slow and inconsistent. The pistol will come up and you can ADS in a flash. On the other hand you can bake a cake in the time it takes to stow the thing or switch. The baton, you know the thing was built around, is slow at everything. Including getting unstowed. Oh and it'll get [i][b]stowed all the time without you having a choice in the matter[/b][/i]. So you either have to see an enemy coming from far off, or you need to be able to have it ready at all times for it to be useful. The overall effect is that switching from one weapon to the next can take 5 or 6 seconds. Which will get you killed.

And who the f*** thought the [u]quick[/u] weapons switch was quick or a good idea? Over the last 30 years we've converged on few different ways to cleanly select the type of weapon from a pistol to a shotgun. It takes 4 separate button clicks to switch between both of the weapons the game gives you.

Enemy AI is dumb. Enemy's will come straight at you, with the ranged enemies planted in place. Close range you'll do melee. Which is the same sequence of steps for each fight, dodge once or twice, attack 2 or 3 times, repeat until enemy dead. If you're at a distance you can just chuck objects at enemies until they go down, or use the pistol. No thought or effort required. 

To give you any sort of challenge the game has to cheat. It loves forced damage. You'll have enemies that pop out of boxes and piles of goo on the ground. You can't do anything about the ones that pop out of boxes. It got so bad I was just spamming E whenever I opened a box. Some of the piles of goo you can see but they're placed in awkward positions to where you can't it them with rapid flying object or the pistol. And then there's the games favorite trick, dropping an enemy immediately behind you without any sort of clue that it's happening. Of course enemy placement is 100% scripted, so once you die you know when it where, when, and what's going to happen. Die once, kill them second time. At least Dead Space would drop enemies into areas you already cleared. 

There are some other minor issues that could be overlooked if everything else weren't so bad. The facial animations are just this side of the uncanny valley, like early talking stone CGI. The game is very linear. The story feels like its still at the outline stage. And the game is still still buggy, I had to restart a couple of times because a bug stopped me in my tracks.

10 Major Failures of The Callisto Protocol

1. Overly rigid melee combat:
The dodge system tied to directional input feels imprecise and clunky, making encounters more frustrating than genuinely challenging.

2. Poor pacing:
The game relies too heavily on narrow corridors, forced walk segments, and unskippable cinematic transitions that repeatedly break the flow.

3. Lack of enemy variety:
Most enemy types behave similarly, causing combat to feel repetitive halfway through the campaign.

4. Overly linear level design:
Despite its promising setting, the levels rarely offer meaningful exploration or alternative paths.

5. Badly placed checkpoints:
Death often sends players back several minutes, sometimes including repeated cutscenes that can’t be skipped.

6. Technical issues at launch:
Stuttering, frame drops, and visual bugs—especially on PC—seriously harmed immersion (with some issues still lingering).

7. Underdeveloped narrative:
Characters lack depth, motivations feel shallow, and the world-building doesn’t reach the potential the premise suggests. And on top of that, you have to pay for a horribly written ending...

8. Restrictive and awkward inventory system:
The small inventory forces constant item drops, undermining pacing and strategic choice.

9. Limited actual horror mechanics: 
The game leans far more into heavy action than atmospheric horror, failing to deliver what many players expected from a “spiritual successor” to Dead Space.

10. Repetitive execution animations:
While visually impressive at first, the kill animations become repetitive and slow down the gameplay experience.

Reflection

These ten points outline how The Callisto Protocol struggles in execution despite its strong production values. Most of the issues stem from design decisions that prioritize spectacle over fluid, satisfying gameplay. Ultimately, even a visually stunning title can fall short if the player experience suffers. Video games should be an engaging and enjoyable escape—games are meant to be fun, not frustrating.

CP... nah, I'm not using that acronym. I got Callisto in a bundle, went in expecting to gag on a diarrhoea-laced slop... but suddenly liked the taste. I wish I could recommend in good conscience a battered game I so enjoyed, but it still feels a tinge aborted. It came out deformed. Wheezing, gurgling, choking like its very world I waded. And it hasn't bloomed since. I've seen nasty loot bugs, graphical glitches, and unearned framedrops. What's sadder, the game flings a greasy sales pitch in your face even before the main menu pops up. There, Downloadable Content is the top option, which betrays a greedy mindset. The "content": bonus death animations, skins, an ending! This is ASS. To boot, everything transpires in the PUBG universe... eh? Why not FNAF? That's one too many compromises. It could be done more elegantly without inciting a PR disaster, guys. Instead, you played yourselves by alienating the audience. Regardless, bracing for impact, I kept an open mind because the setting is my jam. And I found many things to admire.

After all, this is violent sci-fi featuring an adequate horror score reminiscent of Alien, fleshy visuals, and impactful smackdowns. You play as Jacob, a generic merc man delivering some sort of cargo to a prison planet. You're boarded by terrorists, crash, and get arrested on the spot. Mutants attack, so prison break it is! I love me a saucy prison setting. This one is bulky, gritty, with an almost vulgar amount of gore splattered around. The normally disruptive claustrophobic FOV suits the theme. I'd call Callisto an eraserhead child of The Suffering and the new God of War, bearing a touch of The Evil Within in its monster designs. A high praise coming from me. But everyone expected Dead Space, which it isn't, only having flimsy parallels like your dead co-pilot acting as a guilt-tripping ghost wife for a minute. Jacob soon meets a friendly inmate who guides him, then Kimiko from The Boys. All of them are well-acted yet forgettable, including the main villain, the preachiest one I've ever seen! He operates solely on platitudes in the vein of "humanity must overcome its weakness and embrace evolution". Said evolution is giving everyone cerebral palsy and bloated alcoholic mugs. If you say so, fruitcake.

[h3]Face/Off[/h3]
Welp, the main course is combat. The first fight is done clumsily. I expired twice and had to beat up the 3 tutorial fodder losers again because of the autosave placement. Seldom it forces you to shop for goods again if you die, which can be a hassle. However, it made me learn faster and helped to retain the tension throughout. Besides, I don't remember going for more than 10 minutes without a save. Useful for a crab like me who blocks punches with his face. On the bright side, I got to enjoy the bloodbath of painful fatalities. I wish there were more of th... ah, right, paywalled. Either way, I won't deprive the devs of their grotesque achievement. Callisto celebrates its violence and I'm down with it. Yet, I'm not down with a puny stomp. It doesn't gib right and you can't even mangle EVERY body you come across! The rest fits the bill. It's a forgiving system. As long as you hold the stick down, you block. But why? Hold it left or right and dodge no matter the timing. No need to read the telegraphs, except when an enemy does a combo - swap direction for each consecutive hit. You can perform perfect dodges for a bigger window, but it's optional.

Combat is fun to master thanks to its brutality. It's satisfying to smash someone's skull to pieces in a dilapidated bathroom, covering the walls in teeth and tissues. His face gone, limbs torn off, then you shatter his rib cage. Hell yeah! Enemies do the same to you. There's a learning curve to that simple system and it flows nicely when you get the hang of it. Except most enemies can take way too much beating, turning bigger fights into a slog. During those, you aren't allowed to make more than a few mistakes either. Serves me right for playing on Hardcore. But I'm glad Callisto made me bleed like a virgin for my victories. Oddly, fighting several foes wasn't as bad as I imagined despite the finicky lock-on. The ones you don't fight currently are less aggressive, which is the oldest trick in the book. I've heard this wasn't so from the start. Overall, the game is punchy to the bone and I enjoyed the encounter design, for the most part. Although, there's a power creep problem because enemies get stronger alongside you, partially negating it. If only I could upgrade on curve.

[h3]Survival Hobo[/h3]
There's a progression system in place, which allows you to enhance your baton by turning a block into a riposte or adding a heavy attack. Not to mention the guns. Those look badass and don't interrupt the flow by being weaved into your melee combos, staggering and dismembering opponents. Slick! There isn't enough ammo to go guns only, but you can utilise a telekinetic glove to launch stuff, bring a guy to his knees, or plant him on spikes. Almost free of charge. Great, for Callisto is both bugged and beyond stingy on Hardcore. I welcome the resource scarcity, albeit, here it goes from survival horror to survival hobo. You call 1-7 credits loot? The cheapest stuff costs 200!  Half the time, all the loot in a room DESPAWNED upon loading a save! As a result, I got to tier 2 upgrades just for my baton in the endgame. That evil bug was the offence that turned that thumb upside down. Yet, while having a bug-stifled progression and few weapons to choose from isn't a riot, I liked the combat system. Could it carry the whole game, tho? Not if it was any longer. Because in survival horror exploration is the adhesive holding the loop together.

Here, it's lacking. It's a robust grossout-themed beat 'em up, alas, that's all it is. Callisto was fashioned in broad strokes, short on nuance in anything that isn't innards being ripped apart. Ishimura it ain't. Linear non-interactive environments feature minimal backtracking and many pointless dead ends. Expect unsightly darkness and slow crawls through tight spaces, juggling them fuses, and partaking in inoffensive stealth. I sure welcomed free quick kills. In the meantime, you find valuables, gun schematics, and, again, pitiful crumbs of scrip. If you're lucky. And sometimes you get rewarded for your trouble with chip damage from slugs or heads-in-the-box springing out of nowhere! Lovely. At least every other enemy drops a bit of instant health, for you can't hold too many health items. Or any items. I accept limited inventory space as a staple. I don't accept the game's habit of locking doors behind you, blocking off the loot you left for later. Loaded a previous autosave to sweep up, hotshot? The loot has despawned. A nightmare for us greedy guts.

[h3]Dead End[/h3]
And what are these goofy QTEs? Why does Jacob just stand there while I mash the button? Only then, when I finish mashing, he does something like prying the door open. Doesn't feel tactile, defeating the purpose. I ended up setting those on autocomplete. Probably missed out on a few cool deaths. All that said, I adore Callisto despite being critical of its terrible mercantilism and lousy exploration. It ticked a few boxes. I dig the setting, the brutality, and I enjoyed the difficulty. Hell, the lack of loot sure made for a tense hobo challenge! But I don't expect the same attitude from others. It upsets me, yet how can I ask of you to invest in a game that can do you so dirty? And still it's an endorsement for the brave who crave its things macabre. At its ripped-out heart, it's pure 80s horror pulp. If only they didn't mess up the marketing! No technical or mechanical flaw could cripple Callisto as hard. Better ratings may have paid for repairs. As it is, the game has merits, but it's a forsaken dead end. If you consider a visit, do it at a bargain price.

Callisto Protocol: A Missed Opportunity

So, I just finished Callisto Protocol, and I gotta say, it’s one of the most disappointing games I’ve played in a while. This is supposed to be the spiritual successor to Dead Space? LMAO, no. Let me break this mess down for you.

1. Graphics and Atmosphere
Okay, I’ll give it credit where it’s due—the graphics are insane. The lighting, the textures, and the overall aesthetic are top-tier. The game looks like it was designed to flex next-gen capabilities, and yeah, it nails the creepy space-prison vibe. But atmosphere isn’t enough when everything else feels half-baked. Pretty visuals don’t fix shallow gameplay.

2. Combat System
What the hell is this combat system? It’s clunky, repetitive, and feels more like a bad boxing game than a survival horror title. The dodge mechanic is so poorly explained and implemented that half the time you’re just eating hits because the game doesn’t communicate what you’re supposed to do. And don’t even get me started on the stick-wiggling melee mechanics—it’s like they tried to reinvent the wheel and ended up with a square.

3. Lack of Innovation
This is 2023, and we’re still rehashing Dead Space ideas? The story is generic “corporation bad” sci-fi nonsense we’ve seen a hundred times before. The enemy designs are uninspired, the scares are predictable, and the “survival” elements boil down to resource scarcity instead of meaningful tension. It doesn’t innovate; it imitates, and not even well.

4. Performance Issues
Even on a beast of a PC, this thing chugs harder than a frat bro at a kegger. Stuttering, frame drops, and weird glitches plague the experience. It’s like they decided to skip QA and said, “Eh, we’ll patch it later.” Classic AAA move.

5. Linear AF
The level design is painfully linear. There’s no real exploration or freedom—just a series of corridors with scripted events. It feels like playing a rollercoaster rather than an actual game. Compare this to something like Dead Space, where backtracking and exploration were rewarded. Here, it’s just, “Go down hallway, kill things, repeat.”

6. Lack of Replayability
Once you’ve slogged through the story, there’s zero incentive to come back. No real alternate modes, no meaningful unlocks, no reason to endure that awful combat system again. It’s a one-and-done experience.

Final Thoughts
Callisto Protocol is a classic case of all style, no substance. It’s like they thought the Dead Space name and a pretty coat of paint would carry them through, but the gameplay just doesn’t hold up. If you’re looking for actual survival horror, you’re better off replaying Dead Space or trying something like Resident Evil 2 Remake. Callisto Protocol is the kind of game you buy on sale—or better yet, avoid altogether.

Final Score: 5/10 (and that’s being generous for the visuals alone).
