Every part of the space station looks the same. It might be realistic, but it's not memorable and doesn't create engaging enough visuals. At one point you go into a waste management facility and other than Jacob wading through and getting caked in sh*t there's nothing distinct or interesting about this level. There's not even a great big mutated sh*t monster or something for you to fight. It's just pointless. I'm not even sure if I could explain where in the game I am right now. The chapter is called "Habitat" but it's just a dark metal space station like the rest of the game.

-Most importantly, the core combat sucks. It's all melee focused and it's just hit twice, dodge once or twice, then hit twice again until the creature is dead. Not only that but the fighting feels like a series of QTE animations instead of you feeling in control. There's a gun too but it's clunky, weak, and obviously not what's intended to be used most of the time. Most enemies act the same when meleeing them too which makes it really unfun and tedious. God help you if you have to fight multiple enemies at once. You can block as well as dodge, but the game doesn't explain why you would do one over the other. In fact they don't explain the dodge at all, you will pick up on it eventually (and trivialize every encounter after) but until then it fees like stumbling in the dark, which you already do enough of in this game.

- It's just not scary. Being able to melee enemies means it becomes not a test to conserve ammo, but trying to stay awake during the game's repetitive combat. Melee therefore puts the control back in the player's hands both in terms of not needing to watch your ammo, and also as someone who can easily stand up to the threats, which kind of kills the whole horror aspect. In most horror games if an enemy comes too close to you, you're probably either going to take a huge chunk of damage or just straight up die, but this game insists on you getting up close and personal, which just doesn't work to a horror game's favor. The checkpoint system and linearity help ensure even if you do mess up you can immediately retry anyways. The game tries it best despite this to scare you, often to mixed results at best, but it does so using really overdone horror game tropes and jumpscares. Oh look you just got the power cell you needed to power up the door on the other side of the room, I hope some monsters you've seen a million times don't pop out of vents on your trek back.

- The QTEs are ridiculous. There's way too many monsters that just grab you and force you to mash the button until the enemy is dead or gets off you. You can't even avoid it or get better at them. You just have to watch the animation and mash the button as your health drains, over and over. Every combat encounter in this game feels like a QTE now that I think about it, whether you're doing melee or mashing buttons, it all boils down to the exact same finger dance that you'll tire of in the first hour. Is this 2010 where we need to explain to developers that QTEs aren't fun?

It feels like the creator of The Callisto Protocol took an incredible number of liberties in copying his own work — Dead Space — but not in a good way. It’s as if he cherry-picked the elements he personally thought were the “coolest,” stacked them together, and called it a day. The result feels more like a collage of newspaper clippings than a cohesive vision — glimpses of what could have been a moderately interesting experience, ultimately buried under something half-baked and emotionally disconnected.

There’s little to no connection with the main character; his “guilt” or emotional core never feels strong enough to make you care. Enemies often appear out of nowhere, not in that tense, atmospheric way Dead Space mastered, but in a cheap, frustrating manner that kills pacing and rhythm. Ironically, if it weren’t for those random encounters, the game would probably be much shorter.

But perhaps that’s the real issue here — it’s impossible not to compare it to Dead Space. When a creator imitates his own masterpiece this transparently, the two become inseparable. And that’s the tragedy of The Callisto Protocol: its biggest problem isn’t just what it fails to do — it’s that it was made by the same person who once did it so much better.

In the end, The Callisto Protocol is a decent way to kill a lazy Sunday afternoon — especially if you grab it on sale. It doesn’t bring anything new to the table, and at best, it smudges the legacy of a franchise that didn’t need saving or reviving — just to be left alone, to rest in peace.

Honestly, Callisto Protocol is not a terrible game, it's got some pretty spectacular graphics, nice sequences, and the abandoned locations tickle my urbex fancy. 

However, it's not a good game either: For starters, it's too short. Length is artificially extended by opaque combat and non-interactive transition sequences (if I see another gruff middle-aged everyman squeezing through an opening it'll be too soon), weapon  and enemy variety is limited, and horror aspect relies far, far too much on entirely predictable jumpscares and icky visuals. 

The capital crime for me is the lack of world building. For a game hyped up as the spiritual successor to Dead Space, this is just embarassing. Even if it's just another hellish turbocapitalist dystopia setting, the first five minutes of Dead Space established key motivations, the world, the stakes, the reason why you're out there - and much of it without expository dialogue. In Callisto Protocol nothing of the sort happens: You know for sure that you're a space trucker running some sort of cargo, there's the Outer Way terrorists, who aren't liked by the UJC, the cliche evil megacorporation, and a prison on a frozen moon. I like a fish out of water scenario, but there's a fish out of water scenario, and then there's a fish suddenly landing in magma scenario.

The lack of exposition and world building is just criminal. What's the UJC? What does the acronym actually stand for? Who are the Outer Way and why did they hit your ship? What's their goal and purpose? I gave up on trying to make sense of the world and enjoyed the game, liked the Secret Rooms (oooh, spooky), but the ultimate reveal was just... It fell flat. 

I know we live in a world of Musks, Bezoses and other oligarchs, who are comically evil, but that's no reason to have the big bad of the game be another comically evil rich person, part of an Ancient Cabal(tm). 

Get this from the bargain bin on a sale, if at all. Striking Distance got gutted already, so you won't make a difference if you buy at full price.

EDIT: Quick addendum to the part where I talk about the issues with RTX, you can get past the infinite loading screen by just waiting for an absurdly long time... Another thing I forgot to mention is that RTX also breaks some of the game's scripting, so cutscenes either lose their audio entirely or it's completely disjointed, audio and music cues trigger too late and character dialogue can break as well.

Despite the fact that I kinda like the game from a technical and graphical standpoint, the animations and facial rigging are really good. I cannot recommend this game to anyone because outside of it's technical aspects, it's a very mediocre, poorly designed, badly optimised and barely functional mess.

Let's start with one issue that really grinds my gears: Ray-Tracing:

Simply put, the game completely breaks if you enable it. It may work once or twice, but after that you have to disable it if you want to keep playing otherwise it will just permanently hang on a loading screen and never actually finish loading. What is the point of adding a feature that you don't even optimise the game around? God forbid I want to experience the game with RT on, I want to see how it is utilised and how it affects the atmosphere. It worked for me initially and I got reasonably playable performance, the only downside was the increased loading times however it would actually finish loading, then it just stopped. Krafton is not interested in fixing this problem because they've written this game off as a failure and don't want to dedicate a day or two to troubleshooting the problem... or they can't get ChatGPT to fix it for them.

Gameplay wise, it's extremely repetitive, enemy variety is low and the strategy for every encounter is exactly the same, barring 2 notable examples but those are spoilers. It's a melee focused immersive horror game, the controls are extremely simple and enemy AI has been neutered to the point of being trivially easy and not even remotely threatening, even on the hardest difficulties. Hold left or hold right to dodge and alternate to dodge more than one incoming attack... that's it, there's no timing required, there's no learning patterns, just hold a strafe key, button mash and repeat.

Story is practically non-existent, it's every sci-fi/zombie story rolled into one, characters are one dimensional and have extremely basic one-note motivations. It's as stock as it gets, and the big twist is literally something you saw coming hours before.

Mercifully the game is not very long, so you can get through it in about 6 hours. Why you would subject yourself to a game that is barely functional and a worse version of a better game series that has been left long dormant without a proper ending, is entirely up to you. Me, I like this game as a benchmark for new hardware and to stress test my PC, it's graphically intensive enough to basically be this generation's version of Crysis. But outside of that, there really isn't a reason to play this over games like Dead Space, Alien: Isolation, etc. 

Additionally, Glen Schofield, creative director of the original Dead Space and The Callisto Protocol, left the company in 2023 so fat chance we're gonna see much else coming from this series.

Finished it in 13 hours in normal mode, 2 years after the release. Having very much liked the experience of Dead Sace (16 years ago! Dang time flies). I was looking for this so called "spiritual successor".
I played 2 years after because frankly having heard of save issues and performance issues, I couldn't bring myself to pay full price for it, and I ended up having it for less than 10 EUR/USD.

Be careful, mild spoilers ahead because explaining the mediocrity of the game requires explanations.

Even with that, I find myself not recommending it for the following reasons:
-Inventory management is a catastrophy. 6 Slots (later upgraded to 12 by story) which are never enough and force you to backtrack to sell stuff all the time to get money for upgrade.
A problem which is coumpunded by ..

-..Level design. You spend a LOT OF TIME in vents, then a LOT OF TIME SLIDING BETWEEN METAL/ROCKS. And more often than not, you find pieces of loot which you know will encumber your inventory, 2 ROOMS AFTER THE SELL POINT, so you backtrack and sell because you don't wan to waste ressources down the line. This happens wayyy too often.  In terms of horror atmosphere the game is great, in terms of playing it, it's just not enjoyable except a very very few parts where you have freedom to tackle an encounter how you think is best. Which leads me to..

-Combat design: This is 2022, 14 years after the original dead space. In DS you can choose different weapons for diffrent necromorphs to cut their limbs a certain way. In Callisto Protocol, there is nothing of the sort: ALL weapons do damage, you just care about inflicting maximum damage while minimizing the one you take. And that is done by staggering the enemy with ranged weapons then finishing them in melee while ALWAYS Dodging the same way (Q, then D, or D then Q then rinse and repeat). That is what you will do during the full game, except a few kamikaze. Of course you can use telekinesis to oneshot mobs in environment, which you will do a lot to save ammos. Again,, you end up doing the same, all the time.

A mixed bag of a horror game. 

Created by Glen Schofield, the creator of Dead Space and developed by his new studio, Striking Distance, The Callisto Protocol was meant to be the spiritual successor to Dead Space, ushering in a brand new Triple-A horror IP in a era where survival horror is rarely seen in the Triple-A space. Unfortunately, we got Dead Space at home and after a disastrous PC launch and the fallout of both negative critic and player reviews, we are left with a horror title that could've been so much more but unfortunately ended up as a mediocre dud.

Pros:

Visuals are great across the board, the game runs on Unreal Engine 4 and there's been a incredible amount of care of bringing this world to life as everything from the cold, overwhelming darkness of Black Iron Prison, the game setting to the frozen wasteland of the prison's outside areas help to create a genuinely tense and horrifying atmosphere and with the right settings on PC, the game can look stunning at times. 

The all-star cast on display here is also great like Josh Duhamel who plays the game's main protagonist, Jacob Lee or Sam Witwer who plays one of the main antagonists in the story. Even the smaller roles still shine here, all delivering some good performances with the script that they're given here. 

Unfortunately, this is where the positives end. 

Cons: 

The gameplay of The Callisto Protocol is extremely dull and boring as hell as the game's central focus on melee combat with very little deviation of the formula itself makes every fight feel samey and not scary or tense in the slightest. Here's how most combat encounters go, you walk up to an enemy with your baton out, whack them with it, then they block it or dodge it then you have to evade their attacks using the A or D keys, it does not matter which direction it is, just hold these keys and then return back to whacking them until they fall over dead. Rinse and Repeat for 8 hours straight until the credits roll. Some fights may force you to use a gun every once in a while but the same strategy still remains of dodge attacks and then shoot them some more till they fall over dead. There's one part of the game where they reuse the same mini-boss four times in a single section and it's so BORING. Deadass, who thought that was a good idea? Due to this, combat gets extremely boring as the game rarely tries to spice things up or give you something more interesting to do like puzzles for example. There is a upgrade system but it only helps to make the combat even more dull with the benefit of making combat encounters go by faster. 

The story is everything you expect from a modern horror sc-fi game and with very little punches pulled and every twist you  can see coming from a mile away. While the acting is good, the characters here are bland with very little going on in their respective stories with everyone pretty much spelling out their motivations and with very little nuance or mystery behind their decisions. It's bad when I can relate to Issac Clarke, a silent protagonist from the 1st Dead Space more than a professionally voiced main character throughout the game's 8 hour playtime. It makes for a story that at it's best feels like everything you've seen before in much better games and movies and at it's worst, it's something that leaves you bored and wanting everything to end as fast as possible. 

The horror is extremely lacking here which is damning for any horror title. It's like forgetting your job description while you're still at work. Everything scary here feels like everything you've seen before and done better like the story. For example, Dead Space did space zombies better with the Necromorphs than the Callisto Protocol's Biophages. While the atmosphere here is great, the game's focus on lazy jumpscares, heavy focus on gore, and the extremely boring combat brings that atmosphere crashing down with not much else to replace it with. Nothing here feels distinct and that's my biggest problem with the entire game. It's this heavy feeling of "been there, "done that" that made me feel bored rather than tense and excited to see what the game had in store and that feeling sucks.

Verdict:
The Callisto Protocol was a big disappointment especially coming from someone who was excited for this game and wanted a developer to take up Dead Space's mantle again and give us something new in the sc-fi horror space. Instead we got Dead Space at home with a developer desperately trying to recapture that same spark that Dead Space had but with none of the quality that came with it. I really hope that someone else takes up the dead space mantle and gives something completely unique rather than a big, boring slog of a game to go through while failing to take notes from it's original source. 

5/10. P.S, Wait for a deep sale or buy Dead Space Remake if you're looking for a good sc-fi survival game.

TL;DR: Not a bad game, just mediocre. Would leave a mixed rating if I could. Would not recommend buying without a heavy discount. Even then prepare to waste ~10 hours of your time on a meh game.
This game was supposed to be a spiritual successor to Dead Space, made by some of the same devs. It even had some budget behind it. So it’s fair to says people had fairly high expectations. Well, not me. I like Dead space, but it’s far from my favorite. Also, I read a bunch of reviews beforehand. So I more or less knew what I was getting myself into. Unfortunately, I was still fairly disappointed. Not only this game fails as a Dead Space clone. It’s also a not very good game on it’s own, IMO. 
To me this game feels like a combination of everything I dislike about Dead Space series and modern gaming in general. Prioritizing graphics and story over atmosphere and gameplay, having frequent forced walking or crawling segments, inserting a scripted sequence every 5 minutes, over relying on jump scares, locking an ending behind a paywall. All it’s missing is a crafting system with the ability to pay real money for resources.
This game looks nice, I’ll give it that. When it doesn’t stutter or glitches out. The environments look nice and are highly detailed. Cutscenes are well done, the dialogues are well acted. And the character faces, based on real life actors look great. This game also has some decent gore and dismemberment system if that’s something you like. 
But to me all of this is not enough to consider it a good game. I would rather play a game with PS1 level graphics, but that has great atmosphere (especially important for a horror genre) and gameplay (this is a game after all, not a movie).
Unfortunately this game is not very fun to play, IMO. First and foremost it’s extremely linear with very little room for meaningful exploration. 90% of the time you just go in the only direction you’re able (which is marked with ‘yellow paint’ kind of sign posts for good measure). Sometimes you come across a locked door and have to follow a side path to find a key or a button. There is no map or an objective marker, but most of the time they are not necessary, as it’s almost impossible to get lost. Ironically, the very few times when you do get a fork in a road it’s very hard to tell which path leads to story progression and which contains optional loot. Which normally wouldn’t be a problem, but like I said the game likes scripted sequences very much, and it also likes to lock a path behind you. So if you wanted that optional loot, but accidentally followed the story path, sometimes all you can do is load a prior save. At least saving system is generous as the game keeps track of the last 10 autosaves, as well as allows you to do manual saves at any time.
I also have problem with the game’s combat. Vast majority of the time it’s mandatory. There is a rudimentary stealth system, but most of the time you’re not given enough room to maneuver, so you have to fight enemies head on. I guess, you could try and run pass everything, but that’s inadvisable since defeated enemies drop loot. Early game is very melee focused as you have very little ammo to shoot enemies with. And even if you did find a lot of ammo, the inventory is VERY limited early on, so you wouldn’t be able to carry much. You constantly have to choose between ammo, health packs, and valuable loot. Last, but no least, ammo can be bought and sold at the shopping terminals. And since all weapon and abilities upgrades in the game also require money and not some sort of unique currency, there is not much incentive to waste your ammo on enemies. I personally just sold everything and spend money on upgrades. Not like the combat is challenging anyway. It’s very easy to dodge enemy attacks. And even if you are surrounded, they are very polite and mostly attack one by one. 
And what modern game can do without a semi-obligatory stealth segment involving blind enemies. You’d think these enemies would have improved hearing to compensate. But instead they are laughably easy to avoid. They don’t really react to sound, but to your character running and shooting instead. What’s the difference? Well you could try and distract them by throwing objects near them. And they wouldn’t care at all. They also don’t care when you very loudly “stealth” kill enemies standing right in front of them. If anything, they would rather turn away from the player to make stealth takedowns easier. 
All of this doesn’t do any favors to the horror part of the game. I don’t know about you, but I’m not overly scared by enemies that are easily defeated in a melee fight. The horror atmosphere is further ruined by enemies loudly announcing their entrance, as well as clearly telegraphed combat arenas. At this point it’s no longer a horror game, but more of a cinematic action. Or a horror themed thrill ride. There are only a handful of tense moments when you know enemies are around, but don’t exactly know where. Some of these moments involve heavy fog effects, that limit your vision, some – a bunch of frozen statues that might or might not come to life at any moment. And while there a couple nice moments like these, I don’t find that game all that scary overall. Even despite a somewhat spooky space prison setting and all the grim visuals.
While, as I said, cutscenes and voice acting are well done, the story itself is not that great. It’s all standard stuff about government/corporations researching a virus for their own benefits. All plot turns and twists are fairly predictable. None of the characters are particularly interesting. The dialogues are not that engaging and the villain’s monologues are especially boring.
Honestly, I have no idea for whom this game is made for. It’s not very scary (subjective, I know).It’s not fun to play. It’s not very interesting as a movie either (and could also be watched for free on Youtube). I guess you could buy a horde mode DLC and try and get some enjoyment out of shooting off limbs from infinitely respawning enemies. But personally I would rather replay Dead Space or better yet Resident evil 4.

I want to start by saying The Callisto Protocol is not a bad game. In fact, for the most part, it's a very good one. It’s essentially a B-tec Dead Space, not meant in a derogatory way, just a comparison. It trades the iconic spaceship for a high-security prison on a hostile planet, but the influences are clear: the game design, atmosphere, combat feel, and even the telekinesis ability. It wears its inspiration on its sleeve and, for the most part, pulls it off well.

90% of the story had me hooked. The mystery, the tension, the evolving horrors, all of it had me gripped. I actually cared about Jacob by the end, and that made me want to see his story through. That's why I picked up the DLC for £12 (more than double what I paid for the base game, which already felt ironic).

But here's the problem: the DLC’s "ending" felt like a slap in the face. It's all revealed to be an illusion, none of it really happens. Just as you think Jacob might finally escape, it turns out he’s actually on life support and dies in a miserable state. It left me feeling hollow, like everything I’d invested in just evaporated. It felt cheap, like a story that didn’t know how to end properly and decided to go for shock over satisfaction.

Also worth mentioning: there's a section in the main story after your escape ship gets blown out of the sky, where you fall deep underground and start encountering these mutated, blind versions of the biophages. This part absolutely dragged. It’s a slow, lethargic crawl where you’re silently killing what feels like 50+ identical enemies. The stealth kill animation isn’t even quiet, which defeats the purpose and makes the whole thing feel clunky. It comes off like filler, like the devs were trying to stretch the runtime instead of keeping the pace tight and engaging. The game overall isn’t long, but this section definitely overstays its welcome.

I don’t want to discredit the work that went into the world-building, atmosphere, or gameplay, The Callisto Protocol deserves recognition there. But when a game asks for £50+ for the base experience and then locks the actual ending behind a £12 DLC, only to make that ending essentially meaningless—it’s hard not to feel let down.

In summary, a Solid horror experience, especially if you enjoy Dead Space, Compelling story for most of the journey, One slow, repetitive section that breaks pacing, Poor handling of the ending, especially with paid DLC, Disappointing conclusion that devalues the player’s journey.

I did enjoy the game. But I can't in good conscience recommend a £72 experience that ends with such emotional and narrative emptiness.

[i]The Callisto Protocol is a third person horror brawler, from the creators of Dead Space, which very much wants to be Dead Space while its creators are desperately trying to avoid accusations that they are coping Dead Space, and players going into it are mostly looking for more Dead Space. [/i]

[h1]Flows[/h1][list]
[*]The game looks bloody great. The environmental effects are just eyecandy.
[*]The developers are very clearly building on the foundations of Dead Space, evolving many of its original ideas. Transitional vents now may contain death traps, the protagonist is suffering psychotic episodes which are very trippy, there are attempts at stealth sequences, etc.
[*]The actors just look great. There is absolutely no uncanny valley effect.
[*]The female lead is Japanese while the protagonist is a westerner. More of this kind of diversity please.
[*]Telekenisis is pure sex. It was good in Dead Space as well, but here it's just perfect (WHEN the developers take care to make it an option).
[*]Truly high tension environments in many areas. The game does not hold back on punishing stupid plauer decisions, like being greedy. The prison cells segment in the DLC was just fantastic, as were the stealth segments in the main game, in the old abandoned colony.[/list]

[h1]Flaws[/h1] [list]
[*]The story is paper-thin. Long gone is the lovecraftian touch of Dead Space, the nihilism and the alien aspect of the horror. Here it's just a virus, and your enemies are more or less zombies, which you have seen a million times already.
[*]The player is imprisoned, then immediately the outbreak happens. So the game neither throws us in an already derelict, haunted environment like Dead Space, nor does it allow us to see a "normal" day in the prison so that we can then compare it to the chaos of the outbreak. As a result, you are thrust into action pieces with zero context. The chaos around is as new to the monsters and the people as it is to you, the player.
[*][spoiler]At some point it is (falsely) revealed to the female lead ~who had made our ship crash~ that we were in fact innocent. At that point, from her perspective, she had just f@cked over a completely innocent man in the worst ways possible, getting our partner killed, ruining our business and our ship, and getting us imprisoned. The b!tch just offers us no apology. Instead, she and the protagonist just become friends awkwardly fast from that point on.[/spoiler]
[*]The weak point of your enemies are tentacles sprouting from their chests after they take damage, which you must shoot fast or they transform into much tankier enemies. A good idea to add tension to the fight, except it's much less remarkable than Dead Space strategic dismemberment. 2)It very rarely matters, because the transformed tank enemies can be thrown with telekenisis to multiple instant-kill spikes, fans or death drops.
[*]Survival horror, like Dead Space, needs you to be on close proximity to your enemies, not RIGHT in their face. Enemies are meant to be close enough that you are afraid they will reach you with melee attacks, and you are therefore stressed to deal with them before that happens. Callisto Protocol actually plays as a brawler. You will be fighting enemies one on one with melee, while enemies off-camera basically stand around (even if they are right next to you). Instead of trying to stay away from enemies, you will be intentionally running towards them. The horror aspect is immediately ruined.
[*]Survival horror's dark, claustrophobic environments are a very ill fit for arcade action.
[*]Imagine having to deal with nonsense like invincibility frames or animation mismatches in a survival horror game. Every time I swing or shoot at an enemy climbing up the rails and my attack just passes through them, my excitement vanishes.
[*]The game's difficulty is pretty much determined by how much the environment allows you to abuse telekenisis. Some are filled with spiked walls that give you free insta-kills, others don't have as much as a bucket for you to pick up and throw at your enemies.
[*]Enemy corpses will often be in spots designated as non-interactive. So because the zombie you just killed is hugging the wall, you can no longer loot it, despite it being in front of you.
[*]Severely lacking enemy variety. There's just zombies, the launching head-traps and the spider enemies. Dead Space 1 by comparison, had about 4 times the enemy types.
[*]The game could have used a lot more prison-bot segments. They are a nice change of pace from the regular brawler gameplay.
[*]The DLC's ending is just a middle finger to the players.
[*]The combat basically boils down to blocking till your enemy finishes his combo and then scoring a few hits. It sounds boring, it plays even more boring.
[*]Very limited weapon customization, and no armor customization.
[*]At least in max difficulty (which was my first and only playthrough) there are certain segments, especially in the DLC, which will will drive your patience to its limits. A certain room right before the end, where you are made to fight the new hybrid boss enemies in pairs of two (half-robot, half-zombies that are VERY tanky and are immune to telekenisis) in very close quarters, almost made me uninstall (we are talking 30-40 retries to get through that f@cking thing).[/list]

[b]Thumbs down for a purchase. Callisto Protocol is not Dead Space, despite it trying very hard to be. The environments nail the horror aspect, while the gameplay ruins it with the bizarre brawler approach it has. The difficulty swings from piss-easy to controller-throwing hard, seldom finding the right balance.[b]
